contributions.text_english: Good afternoon, Members. Today, we mark the sixtieth anniversary of the Aberfan disaster, in which 116 children and 28 adults lost their lives on 21 October 1966. Before we begin this afternoon's business, I invite Members to observe a minute's silence in remembrance of Aberfan.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. As you are aware, we are facing a 'not in education, employment or training' crisis in Wales, with everything that that means for young people's life chances, their employment and, of particular concern to me, their mental health and well-being. However, we're not now just facing the prospect of cuts in further education funding, but, as I've highlighted to you in correspondence, providers of services to young people through Jobs Growth Wales+, which is effectively a post-16 provision, are also seeing significant cuts. I'm grateful to you for your correspondence, but I have written back to you explaining that ACT, which has been praised across this Chamber for their transformative work with young people, has currently gone from a confirmed contract value of £18.8 million last year to £13.9 million in 2026-27.

contributions.text_english: Can we have the question, please, Lynne?

contributions.text_english: That is a 26 per cent cut. On the basis of these figures, can we accept that the Plaid Cymru Government is committed to tackling the NEET crisis, and, if that is the case, what are you going to do to reverse these cuts and ensure that all learners have an opportunity to have their education?

contributions.text_english: I am grateful to the Member for her question, and, as I said just now, I have, obviously, had discussions already with Cabinet colleagues to see what more can be done within the resources that we have. I think it is certainly the case that we are seeing not just in Wales, but across the UK, a huge issue in terms of the labour market. It has, obviously, led to the Milburn review, and I agree, actually, with Alan Milburn that working on the supply side, working on employability support programmes, is not going to be enough to deal with the scale of the problem, because the problem is really on the demand side largely. That's where we also need to focus, and I think that, really, the scale of the problem means that we do need a scale of intervention on a similar level to the one that we saw back in 1997—the New Deal for the unemployed. So, we are looking forward to the final report of the Milburn review. We hope that the UK Government will inject the level of investment that is needed not just in Wales, but across the UK, to address the problem that young people and others are facing because of the nature of the labour market need at the moment.

contributions.text_english: Cabinet Minister, I welcome your commitment to extend Jobs Growth Wales+ to consider the incentives for employers, because young people leaving the programme need apprenticeships and jobs to move into. I recently met with Williams Electrical (Cymru) Ltd, a Carmarthenshire firm that wants to take on more apprentices but says it can no longer afford to. Under the reformed qualifications, a first-year electrical apprentice without the relevant foundation qualification must undertake broader construction training and skills. The concern for the firm is that the additional college day in the first year leaves just three weeks on site whilst they're having to pay a full week's wages for that apprentice. Carmarthenshire's over-65 population has grown by almost a fifth, while apprenticeship starts across Wales are at their lowest since records began. Yet electrical contractors are generally excluded from the Construction Industry Training Board apprenticeship grants available to other construction employers. So, will you discuss with the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education how those incentives could include targeted support for smaller electrical firms to cover that additional college day so that businesses like Williams can train the electricians that Wales desperately needs? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Cabinet Minister, I heard your response to Lynne Neagle a moment ago, rightfully outlining the challenge around NEETs, but you need to acknowledge that there's a particular problem here in Wales. In England, the numbers have actually dropped in the last 12 months to 13.3 per cent, whereas, in Wales, numbers have shot up to 17 per cent of 16 to 25-year-olds not in work, training or education. It's vitally important that we get those young people into those positions as quickly as possible. As you know, Jobs Growth Wales+ makes a big difference in that, and you do have already the policy levers to be able to make a difference in this area, and it's about prioritising whether or not you think it's an important matter for you to tackle. I think in particular, in my own constituency of Fflint Wrecsam, that Coleg Cambria run a fantastic summer school with Jobs Growth Wales+, where 100 young people took part in that summer school—a record number so far. So, Cabinet Minister, will you commit today, for the sake of the 16 to 25-year-olds, to ensuring that this is a priority and that you do use the policy levers you already have to ensure that young people have a fighting chance?

contributions.text_english: Where I agree with the Member is that the existing interventions in Wales were not working, and the actual outcomes were worse. As a result of that, we have commissioned, as a Government, work by Professor Melanie Jones, one of the leading figures in labour market economics, to understand, 'Well, let's look across the world at what does work in order to inform our own use of the policy levers that we do have.' But I should say that the consensus view, which is emerging through the work of the Milburn review and economists that are looking at this, is that the supply-side approach, which is basically saying, 'There's an unemployed person here and if we can make them employable, then they can get into the labour market', the increasing consensus view is that that's incorrect, largely. The problem is on the demand side. The jobs are not being generated to a sufficient degree to actually create those job opportunities, and there are particular structural problems in terms of entry-level jobs. That's why I think sector-led approaches, the likes of which we've begun to see, haven't we, in recent weeks and months—the retail sector, the construction sector, coming forward and making commitments to create those entry-level jobs—those kind of approaches are likely to have a better effect. The opportunity for us in Wales is to work with sectors—and we've just heard some specific examples in an earlier question as well—to provide those entry-level jobs, and, yes, make sure that our training skills system is working with employers for real job opportunities that are going to be created.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Cabinet Minister. In Blaenau Gwent, nearly three in 10 residents aged 16 and over have no formal qualifications, which is the highest proportion in the whole of Wales, while neighbouring Caerphilly has the fourth highest. I've seen first-hand the vital role that organisations such as ACT has in Ebbw Vale. They play such an important role in supporting young people facing really complex needs and barriers to education, training and employment. For many of these young people, progress can mean overcoming mental health challenges, gaining qualifications after leaving school without any, finding secure housing or even turning away from crime as well. They need to have a system that can respond to the full range of barriers they face as an individual and gives them the best opportunity as well to fulfil their potential. So, Cabinet Minister, how will the Welsh Government ensure we have a fit-for-purpose system, with the flexibility and stability needed to support young people to fulfil their potential, particularly those facing extreme barriers?

contributions.text_english: I am grateful to the Member for her question. I think that, certainly, we acknowledge the importance of programmes like Jobs Growth Wales. We've committed to continuing that next year, even, as I said, as we begin the work of understanding what more we can do and what we can do differently, because, even though these programmes have made a contribution, they have not solved the problem; the problem has got worse. And so, we need to find out what is missing, what additional can we do. As I was saying, I think the growing view among those who work in and analyse this field is that we need to work more on the demand side to generate the jobs, and also we need to have a place-based approach. So, I think you're absolutely right to focus on the specific needs, which will be different in Blaenau Gwent to other places. The opportunities will be different. The employers that we can work with to create particular sectoral opportunities will be different. So, it's that combination not just of the existing approaches, but blending them with new interventions that are demand led and placed based. That's the way, in a holistic fashion, I think that we can provide a durable and comprehensive solution that will deliver hope to young people and to communities across Wales.

contributions.text_english: Minister, traditionally, entry-level roles have allowed young people to gain the experience needed to progress into more skilled employment. But artificial intelligence now threatens to automate some of those opportunities. What assessment, therefore, has the Welsh Government made of the impact of AI on entry-level employment opportunities for young people in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, and what discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with the Deputy Minister for skills about ensuring that training provision in our constituency prepares young people for the jobs likely to be available in five to 10 years' time?
contributions.text_original: Minister, traditionally, entry-level roles have allowed young people to gain the experience needed to progress into more skilled employment. contributions.text_english: I'm really grateful to the Member for an absolutely vitally important question, which I think is at the forefront of all of our minds at the moment, isn't it? I think it's certainly true that AI is one of the factors that is driving this unique level of disruption that is going on in the labour market. I think that it is a complex picture, and it's fair to say that the evidence is still emerging. We were discussing this at the jobs summit, and we need to have a better understanding and better data. So, there is a live data set that actually looks at what is happening in the American labour market. Month by month, we can see what's happening, and we can see that, particularly, it's young people that are being disrupted most in terms of higher levels of unemployment. We can even be more specific: it's 22 to 25-year-olds who are facing a 20 per cent higher level of unemployment than was previously the case. Now, we need to get that kind of data here and we need to understand how this is playing out across different sectors and across different geographies. That work is ongoing, and I hope to be able to update Senedd Members more in this regard because I think it's one of the central challenges that we're facing at the moment.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Minister, as discussed recently in this Chamber, 500 jobs in Admiral are at risk of redundancy. These are real Welsh people, real Welsh families and actual livelihoods that are now facing uncertainty. Many of those jobs are based across our constituencies in Swansea, Cardiff and Newport. And now we learn that, while Welsh workers face the prospect of losing their jobs, some roles—the majority of those 500 jobs—are going to be outsourced to India. Now, this is a massive slap in the face to all those men and women that have worked hard, paid their taxes, only for their jobs to be sent abroad, and is a firm rebuke to this Government's economic credentials. This should be a massive wake-up call for this Welsh Government. So, Minister, what direct action are you taking to stop skilled Welsh jobs being shipped overseas, to protect workers here in Wales, and to ensure that companies benefiting from operating in this country have a genuine incentive to keep those jobs here? Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Clearly, this was very disappointing news to hear and, obviously, very worrying for the workers and their families involved. I've met with Admiral, and, indeed, with Legal & General as well, to see what we could do—first of all to understand what we could do in the context of those that are at risk of losing their jobs, and we obviously stand ready to do what we can in that regard, but also to understand more about the reasons for these decisions and what we could do, working with these companies and with their sectors, to create additional jobs as well.

Now, Admiral have, in that conversation, confirmed to us that they are going to retain their Cardiff and Swansea offices. In my conversation with Legal & General—and, indeed, with Admiral as well—we did talk about what are the growth opportunities, where we as a Government can work with the companies and with the sectors in order to identify growth possibilities, because we retain important strengths in these sectors, and it's important not to lose sight of that, despite this obviously disappointing news.

Thank you. I thought I was going to get called—excuse me.

Minister, thank you for that, but, as we move on, unlike Plaid's new energy quango, North sea drilling could unlock billions for the UK economy, support thousands of jobs and strengthen our energy security. As Reform UK's Richard Tice has been calling for for years, the Jackdaw project has now been given the green light, and, as we know on this side of the Chamber, that's nowhere near enough. Now, Reform believes the United Kingdom should extract every last drop of oil out of the North sea—and gas—to support our economy, protect jobs and reduce our reliance on imports. Instead, Plaid wants to waste taxpayers' money on another quango and renewable energy schemes that offer absolutely no guarantee of cheaper bills to the men and women of our country. Minister, let's get real for a moment and focus on the action that will actually make a difference to people's pockets here in Wales. What steps are you taking to press Westminster to issue new exploration licences, unlock our North sea resources, boost our economy and bring down household bills for people across Wales?

contributions.text_english: Look, the real opportunity for us—. If you want to talk about energy off our shores, the real opportunity for us in Wales, it's in our floating offshore wind sector, it's in our tidal stream and tidal lagoon industries. That's where the real opportunity, in terms of jobs, is. So, let's focus there, because there are important messages where it would be useful if we could speak with one voice to urge the UK Government, for example, to realise the strategic value of marine energy, of floating offshore wind, of tidal. We have some unique geographic assets. No, they don't involve fossil fuels, but they are definitely sectors of the future that not only will be important in energy terms, but, if we get this right, will create massive supply chain opportunities to build out manufacturing at our ports in Port Talbot and in ports across the whole of Wales. So, let's focus there, where the real opportunity is for Wales, rather than be distracted by issues and questions that are not our responsibility and won't directly benefit us.

Thank you, Minister. The biggest word in that statement I picked up on was 'if' we get this right. That's a very big 'if' indeed.

But, moving on, today, Reform UK will lead a debate calling for a ban on face coverings used to conceal identities and intimidate the public. Wales has become a country where criminals can hide their faces while law-abiding citizens are frightened to walk down their own high streets. Across Wales, hard-working businesses are struggling, shopkeepers face intimidation and theft, customers are being driven away, and once-thriving town centres are suffering, leading to damage to our economic outlook. contributions.text_english: 3. What discussions is the Government having with National Grid regarding the electric arc furnace installation in Port Talbot? OQ64761

contributions.text_english: Welsh Government officials hold regular meetings with National Grid Electricity Transmission. Tata Steel UK’s electric arc furnace installation is a commercial matter. However, we do raise the matter as appropriate.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Weinidog. The decision to close the blast furnaces in Port Talbot was disastrous for my local community. Thousands of jobs were lost and the impact on the wider economy is severe. The National Grid connection offer for the new electric arc furnace was contracted for the end of 2027. However, a range of factors, such as planning and ground conditions, are threatening to delay the project, and some sources are saying that it could be as late as 2029 before the new furnace comes online.

Previously, you've mentioned that the Welsh Government is not a party to the commercial agreement between National Grid and Tata, but I'd like to ask what conversations you've had with National Grid regarding these delays and what further action will you take to prevent any further issues that could harm jobs and the local economy in Port Talbot. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Yes, I'm very grateful to the Member for his supplementary question. I met with Tata Steel UK's chief executive officer, Rajesh Nair, and the steel unions at Tata's Port Talbot site on 24 September to receive a further update on developments. We focused on a whole range of matters, including the issues around connectivity to the grid, which is at the heart of his question, but there were other matters as well around UK Government trade quotas and the effect that that was having on the domestic steel market. Following that meeting, I did meet with the UK Government's Minister for Reindustrialisation, Blair McDougall, together with the Secretary of State for Wales to discuss some of the matters that were raised.

So, we are constantly engaging with the company, with the unions and also with the UK Government to ensure that Wales does—. I absolutely agree with him about the tragedy, really, of the loss of the blast furnaces, but we now need to make sure that we maximise the opportunity represented by the electric arc furnace. It will be the first or second-largest electric arc furnace anywhere in the world. There is the prospect for us to be producing more than 50 per cent of UK domestic steel capacity at a time when the UK Government has said that it wants to increase the level of domestic procurement. So, there is an opportunity there that is massive. We need to stay focused, I absolutely agree, in order to seize that opportunity.

contributions.text_english: Gweinidog Cabinet, I visited National Grid at Margam substation over the summer to discuss the connection to the Port Talbot substation needed for Tata Steel's electric arc furnace. National Grid explained that there were a number of unexpected barriers, as the Member has previously alluded to, for example, poor ground conditions that increase the number of piles required in the ground from the initial 400 to 11,000, adding an estimated 34 weeks to complete construction. They also outlined plans to recover some of that lost time. Given the importance of the project to the future of steel making in Port Talbot, can the Gweinidog confirm whether any progress has been made in reducing that 34-week delay and whether there is scope to shorten the construction programme further?

I think I will have to leave it to the company to share any information it would like to put in the public domain in relation to the current state of play. This is obviously market sensitive information. You can appreciate that it's most appropriate that that comes from the company, and I'm sure that they would want to allow the workforce to hear that information first. 

But I think that one of the positive things that I'm sure that Tata Steel would not in any way have a problem with me sharing was the very positive experience that they had with Neath Port Talbot Council. We often hear, don't we, in the context of economic development, concerns around planning delay. Well, the message that I very clearly heard from the company was that they were incredibly impressed by the way in which the planning officers of Neath Port Talbot Council had really worked at an incredible pace and shown some innovation in how to manage that process. And there may be wider lessons that can be shared with other major projects across Wales. And we talked a little bit about how we could share that best practice.

As a result of this experience as well, we are very conscious of the importance of focusing in a very granular fashion on major developments and what that means for the grid. And we are, as I said, in discussion with National Grid Electricity Transmission and other relevant stakeholders to make sure that we learn from this experience and make sure that we identify areas where we can make progress in terms of the grid connection and its important role in our economy.

contributions.text_english: 4. What measures will the Welsh Government take to support employment opportunities in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64731
contributions.text_original: 4. Pa fesurau y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi cyfleoedd cyflogaeth ym Mlaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64731

contributions.text_english: The programme for government sets out the range of measures that we will take to improve economic opportunities and outcomes for every part of Wales. This includes the national productivity mission, supporting small businesses and high streets to thrive and ensuring Wales has the skills it needs for the future.
contributions.text_original: Mae'r rhaglen lywodraethu yn nodi'r ystod o fesurau y byddwn ni'n eu cymryd i wella cyfleoedd a chanlyniadau economaidd ar gyfer pob rhan o Gymru. Mae hyn yn cynnwys y genhadaeth genedlaethol ar gynhyrchiant, gan gefnogi busnesau bach a'r stryd fawr i ffynnu a sicrhau bod gan Gymru y sgiliau sydd eu hangen arni ar gyfer y dyfodol.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for your response, Minister. My concern is that too many of our talented young people in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni feel that they have to move away to find careers that are sustainable and long term. Beyond the general funding streams, what targeted assurances can the Welsh Government provide to create skilled, futureproofed jobs in their local area so that we can stop exporting our next generation?
contributions.text_original: Diolch am eich ateb, Weinidog. Fy mhryder yw bod gormod o'n pobl ifanc talentog ym Mlaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni yn teimlo bod yn rhaid iddynt symud i ffwrdd i ddod o hyd i yrfaoedd cynaliadwy hirdymor. Tu hwnt i ffrydiau cyllido cyffredinol, pa warantau targedig all Llywodraeth Cymru eu cynnig i greu swyddi medrus sy'n ddiogel ar gyfer y dyfodol yn eu milltir sgwâr fel y gallwn stopio allforio ein cenhedlaeth nesaf?

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for that supplementary question. This question is at the heart of our economic strategy. This morning, I met, for the first time, with the panel assisting us to design the new development agency, and one of the themes that I emphasised was the need to ensure that we do generate good jobs everywhere. We don't want to see a situation where Wales emulates what we've seen in terms of the uneven development across the United Kingdom, where prosperity only accrues in one corner of our nation. We want the south-east of Wales to prosper, we want the north-east of Wales to prosper, and we are very proud of the success that there has been there, but we also want that to permeate through the Valleys, the Heads of the Valleys, into the west, into rural Wales, and into the north-west of Wales. We must raise up the whole of Wales, and that is how we as a Government intend to operate, and that is the aim and the mission that we have already given to the new development agency.

contributions.text_english: Minister, one concern I've got, from speaking to lots of people in the constituency, who feel young people are leaving the area of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni at a large pace now. We can see that the population age is going up in every census, and anyone who's been around the town recently feels that young people are leaving for cities, going over to England or to other parts of the world. What help can you do to incentivise businesses into the constituency, because it's businesses that will create those jobs, but Government have the levers of power to pull? So, I'd be grateful if you could tell us today what levers you're going to pull to bring in those jobs to keep young people here.

contributions.text_english: I think that's a really important question, and Governments, of course, at one level, have to create the broad conditions of economic success, but we also have to work in a very, very focused way, in the near term, which is about job creation in businesses. Ultimately, Governments can help create those conditions, but it's not Governments that regenerate communities; it's communities and businesses within them that regenerate communities and create those jobs. So, certainly, in looking at the role of inward investment, for example, I think it's critical that we think about the way in which we can make sure that there are opportunities for foreign direct investment in every part of Wales. And, interestingly, in a conversation I had with one of the leading firms in the compound semiconductor cluster, they brought many of their suppliers into Wales, they wanted to be close to the cluster, but those companies said, 'We don't want to be in Newport. We don't need to be in Newport. We want to be in the northern Valleys. We think that's a better fit for us. The skills are there. There are advantages for us.' And there are, of course, fantastic transport links. So, there are unique assets, both people based and also physical assets, that can be leveraged in every community. And we need to be thinking in that granular way to identify opportunities that fit, community by community, across Wales.

contributions.text_english: 5. How is the Welsh Government supporting businesses to benefit from public procurement spending? OQ64792
contributions.text_original: 5. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi busnesau i elwa ar wariant caffael cyhoeddus? OQ64792

contributions.text_english: We are determined that more Welsh businesses benefit from public procurement. Business Wales provides tailored advice, while the Procurement Act 2023 requires authorities, in covered procurements, to consider barriers facing businesses and whether contracts can appropriately be divided into lots. We are also developing policy options to strengthen support further.
contributions.text_original: Rydyn ni'n benderfynol bod mwy o fusnesau yng Nghymru yn elwa ar gaffael cyhoeddus. Mae Busnes Cymru yn darparu cyngor wedi'i deilwra, tra bod Deddf Caffael 2023 yn ei gwneud hi'n ofynnol i awdurdodau, mewn caffaeliadau a gwmpesir, ystyried rhwystrau sy'n wynebu busnesau ac a ellir rhannu contractau yn lotiau priodol. Rydyn ni hefyd yn datblygu opsiynau polisi i gryfhau'r cymorth ymhellach.

contributions.text_english: Diolch yn fawr. The Plaid Cymru manifesto sets a target to significantly increase the amount of public procurement spending within Wales to 70 per cent. Given that we spend £11 billion every year on public procurement, there's enormous potential there, isn't there, to better support Welsh businesses, potentially to create tens of thousands of jobs and to boost local supply chains as well. And the best bit, of course, is that this isn't new money; this is money that we're already spending. Yes, absolutely. The formal responsibility is with the finance Minister, but with this, it is very critically, as the Member says, a massive economic driver. It's one of the key tools of industrial policy, actually, public procurement. So, beyond the target, how are we going to achieve it then, getting up to that 70 per cent? We will be setting this out in more detail very shortly. But part of it is working through, as I said, the way in which procurement contracts are structured. So, traditionally, large-scale construction contracts, for example, tend to go to companies the other side of the border because of the scale and the risk involved. Well, just breaking those contracts up into smaller lots, it sounds very simple, but it has a huge impact, and it allows then companies, financially and practically, to get—. The same companies that often end up delivering the project anyway, but now you're taking out a tier and keeping all of that value in Wales.

I think that part of it is also about training companies up, companies that possibly have not been involved in larger scale procurement exercises and might have some fear or inhibition about doing so, so working with them in a different context. I'm going to a procurement exercise in north Wales in relation to the Wylfa project. It's the same kind of approach: how to get Welsh SMEs, many of which have never thought of putting themselves forward, just to understand, 'Look, there's nothing to be worried about; it's a process. You've got the skills, you've got the capacity, you can deliver the product, in many cases at lower cost; you've just got to have the confidence to put your name forward.'

contributions.text_english: Diolch. AI-driven automation is having a growing impact on the labour market and especially on entry-level employment and on workplace learning, and is widening already existing inequalities. Young people at the start of their careers are particularly vulnerable to things like job displacement and a lack of fair access to opportunities and face the collapse of those traditional pathways that let graduates and early-career workers gain that essential experience in learning. contributions.text_english:
The Member raises a really important point. AI must be adopted, in our view, in a way that is fair, transparent and doesn't deepen inequalities. Our approach is rooted in social partnership. Guidance, which has been developed with trade unions and public sector employees, puts worker voice, fair work and human oversight at the heart of workplace AI. We're drawing up a national AI governance framework to provide clear guardrails around accountability, transparency, fairness and risk, and we're still working out, as I said earlier, what the full impacts are on overall employment.

We recognise, though, that AI is changing the skills employers need, and the concerns that I referenced earlier in terms of entry-level roles and traditional routes into work. That's why we're working with employers, with trade unions, with education providers, first of all to understand how AI is changing recruitment, training and workplace learning, while investing, crucially, in digital and AI skills through personal learning accounts and our AI skills pilot.

contributions.text_english: 1. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve educational outcomes for learners? OQ64729
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella deilliannau addysgol dysgwyr? OQ64729

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

contributions.text_english: My priority is high standards and high aspirations for every learner. That is why this Government has worked at pace to develop the 'Foundational literacy and numeracy plan'. contributions.text_english: Thank you for that answer, Cabinet Minister, but there's a clear link also between attendance and educational outcomes, and we know we've got a huge attendance problem in Wales, with over 100,000 pupils every year missing at least 10 per cent of their lessons in the last year for which we have figures. In fact, the attendance records that have been provisionally published for 2025-26 suggest that this attendance problem is actually getting worse, not getting better. There's been a fall in the average attendance to just under 91 per cent in 2025-26. What action is your Welsh Government taking to address these appalling figures—which seem to be on the slide, not getting any better—and why is it that we have such a persistent attendance problem when other parts of the UK seem to be getting their act together and getting kids back into school?

contributions.text_english: It's because they have a Labour Government.

contributions.text_english:
I think that's pushing it rather at this point, but thank you for the contribution.

Of course, this is an important area for us. There has been, you're quite right, a slight reduction on the latest figures, and there are a number of actions we are taking to tackle that. We are aware that school attendance has gone up again incrementally post COVID but is nowhere near the rate pre COVID. We're also aware that the cohort we are now targeting is likely to require a considerable focus and probably considerable support to push that figure higher. 

One of the things we have included in our literacy and numeracy foundational plan is targets on attendance. You will see a 0.5 per cent increase year on year to bring that level up. There's also a focus on persistent absence, which is missing 10 per cent or more of school sessions. A 2 per cent increase year on year is what we expect there.

There are a number of other areas we are focusing on. You will have heard me speak about the national framework on behaviour, attendance and well-being we are now bringing together, in the recognition that no single intervention, albeit we have targets now too, will address those persistent absence problems. They are often complex issues and do require tailored support, which is why we are looking at this framework in the round and making swift progress on introducing that.

Another thing we have done is to look in more detail—. Because often what we find is that reliable, consistent data across Wales is sometimes hard to find, so we've published new school attendance code guidance to give us that greater consistency in recording absence across Wales, to help us to target our work around this area to make a difference and to increase those figures over time. Because I agree with you: you need to be at school to benefit from the education system. It is very much a focus for us. Diolch.

Can I start by declaring an interest? My wife works in an additional learning needs provision within a school in Conwy.

I thank the leader of the Welsh Conservatives for bringing this question forward. Minister, I was speaking to a teacher in Rhyl, and it was explained to me that the school in which that teacher worked can't afford pens or pencils, and staff are currently using their own money to buy learning resources. It's no surprise, then, that the Institute for Fiscal Studies has claimed that students in that local authority area are up to 23 months behind the national average. As we are seeing a shift towards greater school-level flexibility on learning approaches and a more interlinked learning approach, researchers from Cardiff University have warned that schools need significant investment in materials and learning resources to avoid the widening of educational outcome gaps between different parts of Wales. How can we expect teachers in my constituency to achieve the best outcomes for students when their schools can't even afford pens and pencils? Diolch.

Can I thank the Minister for that reply? Perhaps I ought to say that I used to be a governor at Tycoch and my grandchild goes to Bryn Tawe, so I've got an interest, though not necessarily a financial one. I thought I'd bring that up for the record.

One of the issues I think we are all in agreement on is that we do not want young people at 16 to become not in education, employment or training. That means we must have adequate availability of courses in the further education sector. If young people do not continue in education or training at 16, then many will face a life of unemployment. Will the Minister commit to funding further education so that there is a place in college for every young person who wants it in Swansea, so that we don't have people sitting at home who want to be learning?

contributions.text_english:
There are two points there, Mike. The first one is around NEETs. This is an area of great concern for me and the Government. We know the NEET cohort in Wales is increasing. Roughly 17 per cent of the 16 to 24-year-old age group are NEET. That's clearly not where we want to be. We have to put interventions in place to stop them becoming NEET. That takes different approaches. The Alan Milburn report showed that about 70 per cent of those who are NEET are economically inactive—that is, they are not ready for work. That is because they have several barriers in their own personal lives that stop them becoming employable. That could be around mental health issues, it could be additional learning needs, it could be childcare, transport, disabilities, and so on. I am going to lead an inter-ministerial group of people to look at the NEETs agenda and how we can bring different policy areas to play, which would obviously involve health, social services, transport and so on. So, that's the first part.

The second part is ensuring that no young person will be turned away from the course that they want to study. I am committed to reviewing that increased level of participation and the financial pressures over the next month, as we have final figures coming through. We will consider providing additional funding over and above what Medr have already provided, £6.25 million, should that money be available, given the budgetary constraints that we are under.
contributions.text_original:
There are two points there, Mike. The first one is around NEETs. This is an area of great concern for me and the Government. We know the NEET cohort in Wales is increasing. Employers need courses shaped around their businesses, reliable partnerships with colleges and practical help. Announcing an audit does nothing on its own to meet these costs. Since your Government took office, another group of young people have left school hoping to secure an apprenticeship and employment. Your Government is happy to waste our money to fund international projects like tree planting in Uganda, but it seems Welsh employers are being left to shoulder apprenticeship costs. These are our young people, they are our future. What new funding has Plaid made available to help businesses, particularly smaller employers, take on apprentices?

contributions.text_english:
I'll deal with the main and the most important parts of that question, if I may. If I can refer back to a skills summit we organised on 8 October in the Swansea.com Stadium, for the first time ever we brought employers, small and medium-sized and large companies together with education providers. It was a hugely successful event, where employers were telling us that they need to forge a better relationship with apprenticeship providers and vocational skills providers. Employers know what the emerging sectors are. They know what skills they need for the future. So, we need to develop a mechanism where they are telling providers what they need and that we match them both together.

Now, I heard my colleague the Minister for enterprise explain earlier on that we need to create more demand as well. And you heard him explain how we are going to do that through setting up a Welsh development agency and other programmes as well to support industry and SMEs to take on more apprenticeships. I believe that apprenticeships are a great pathway into work and into further and higher education as well. You can earn and learn at the same time. So, we are committed to supporting the apprenticeship scheme, and we will be working with employers to make sure that what they need, in terms of the skills level, matches what education providers can put on in FE colleges, universities and also through apprenticeship schemes.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, additional learning needs funding remains a contentious issue, with a debate scheduled next month in response to a petition. ALN funding by the Welsh Government is up 14 per cent on last year, and has more than doubled in eight years. Inflation over that period has been around 35 per cent. The percentage of the education budget assigned to ALN has risen from just below 15 per cent to nearly 19 per cent over the same period. At local authority level, there have been huge variations, with increases over the last decade ranging from 65 per cent to 297 per cent. One authority now spends more than a quarter of its education budget on ALN. These figures suggest that there has been a rapid change within Welsh education. Whatever is happening looks unsustainable in terms of funding. Minister, what are your thoughts on the reasons for this ALN spending trajectory?

contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr. Thank you for the question. I think we are dealing with two issues simultaneously here. I mentioned earlier on that I was pleased that £60 million had gone into the system this year, as a result of the supplementary budget, to support with immediate pressures. But you are quite right, in the longer term we need to arrive at a system that is more sustainable and is inclusive of the learners in Wales. I think every jurisdiction everywhere over a time, and particularly post COVID, has been dealing with increasingly complex demand from children and families trying to negotiate a range of issues that their learners are facing.

The education system, arguably, experiences changes in society faster than most of us sitting here and probably most of our services as well. So, we have made an effort now to focus on the sustainability of the ALN system over time. You will have seen that a proportion of what was agreed last week has been allocated specifically for that purpose, and we will work now quickly with local authorities and other partners to work our way to a more sustainable system over time. We need this to be a coherent continuum, we need it to be of high quality, we need it to be inclusive, with—and this is the crucial part I think—clearer national expectations of what this system should look like, stronger mainstream capacity, which in turn comes with demand for support, obviously.

One of the first steps is to understand in detail, with all our partners, what an inclusive system looks like and plot our way from here to that system and this commitment—. There is a great willingness amongst all our partners to work on this and we will do so with speed.

contributions.text_english:
Okay, thank you, Minister. I see that later on there's a question regarding teachers leaving the profession. Surveys show that poor pupil behaviour is a factor. However, Plaid's recent programme for government, whilst acknowledging workload concerns, makes no mention of behaviour.

Staff working in schools have a legal right to use reasonable force to control or restrain pupils. Welsh Government guidance explicitly states that no school should have a 'no physical contact' policy. However, there are still occasions when school staff face lengthy investigations and possible suspension for having operated within the law. This can have a devastating impact on both them and pupil behaviour in the school, whenever staff, unsurprisingly, decide that no physical intervention is their best policy.

Minister, will you ask your officials to establish whether schools are advising staff on their legal right to use reasonable force and whether disciplinary processes are being initiated despite staff having operated within the law?

contributions.text_english:
It is obviously important that staff feel safe at school and are able to operate appropriately. It is clear that staff may use reasonable force where necessary to prevent harm, an offence, damage to property or serious disruption, but that intervention must necessarily, and I think we'd all agree on this, be proportionate and use the minimum force required. And it should never be used as a punishment. I think we can all agree on those principles. If there are examples, individual examples, that you have, then I would be glad to look at them.

But we are clear that that is the environment in which our workforce is working. It is also our expectation that restrictive practices are a last resort. And to go back to your first point around behaviour, the behaviour and well-being framework is a priority for this Government, and bringing together a greater national consistency around our expectations and around the support that will help the workforce and the learners in turn is a piece of work that is ongoing.

contributions.text_english:
Okay, thank you, Minister. Finally, the national literacy and numeracy assessments are online and personalised to each pupil. So, they're rather like a flow chart, where the next question depends on the answers to the last one. These tests can be taken whenever the school feels it's appropriate. Pupils can take time out during the assessments, and pupils are permitted to repeat the exercise any time. This is not a standardised test where all pupils in a cohort take the same test at the same time of the year so that judgments can be made about pupil and school standards, including progress.

This is what the tests were originally designed to do when Leighton Andrews introduced them, and that is what happened when the tests were introduced in 2014. This adaptive system, as it's called, has been in place for a decade, but has clearly not led to any improvements in the Programme for International Student Assessment results. Minister, will you reintroduce standardised literacy and numeracy tests to be used by all pupils annually at the end of year 2 to year 9?

We can use the data more broadly that this system gives us, to give us an indicator at year 6, which is what we're doing as part of this plan, and which gives us a place go to, then, as a national trajectory of improvement, and also to make sure that we can align the support available appropriately for those schools and for those learners.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. Last week, as we've heard from Sera Evans, you announced a teacher pay award of 3.5 per cent following the consultation on the independent Welsh pay review body report. That announcement was made during an active industrial dispute, and the National Association of Head Teachers have now withdrawn from talks with the Government and announced that they are moving to a statutory industrial ballot. 

Why did you make that announcement while talks were ongoing, and do you think that is in keeping with the principles of social partnership?
contributions.text_original:
Thank you. Last week, as we've heard from Sera Evans, you announced a teacher pay award of 3.5 per cent following the consultation on the independent Welsh pay review body report. That announcement was made during an active industrial dispute, and the National Association of Head Teachers have now withdrawn from talks with the Government and announced that they are moving to a statutory industrial ballot. 

Why did you make that announcement while talks were ongoing, and do you think that is in keeping with the principles of social partnership?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. I think, as I said in my earlier answer, I remain committed to the social partnership, and I'm always willing to talk to those social partners on issues that we have in common as concerns. 

I announced that fully funded pay award last week, following that consultation, because I wanted to respect the principle of no detriment, so that there'd be no difference between the pay increases here and those over the border in England. I know this has been a continuing debate over many years, to ensure that we remain in that alignment.

I think the previous education Minister will also be aware of the financial environment, and the budgetary environment we are now in, and I judged, at this point, that 4.25 per cent was not affordable when we consider the other priorities of this Government, and Wales more broadly, around, particularly, health service demand—the national health service—and other priorities that this Government is committed to.

The 3.5 per cent was important to me. It was important to most partners. But I remain committed to talking to anybody who wishes to examine areas of mutual interest and concern.

Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Before I ask my questions, I would like to put on record my thanks to Efa Gruffudd Jones for her work as Welsh Language Commissioner. She's been a robust advocate for the Welsh language, and I wish her well for the future.

Minister, the report of the Commission for Welsh-speaking Communities, 'Cymraeg in every community, strengthening the Welsh language', notes that workplaces should be considered as key locations for use of the Welsh language, and the report makes a series of recommendations with the aim of increasing the use of the Welsh language in those settings. What progress has the Welsh Government made in terms of implementing those recommendations, and what evidence do you have that more people are using the Welsh language regularly in their workplaces as a result of that?
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Cyn i mi ofyn fy nghwestiynau, hoffwn gofnodi fy niolch i Efa Gruffudd Jones am ei gwaith fel Comisiynydd y Gymraeg. Mae hi wedi bod yn eiriolwr cadarn dros yr iaith Gymraeg, a dwi'n dymuno'n dda iddi ar gyfer y dyfodol.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much for the question. I would like to add my thanks as well to the Welsh Language Commissioner for her work.

We will, in December, be publishing a consultation on the Welsh language strategy, the Welsh Language and Education (Wales) Act 2025, and the Welsh language proficiency code. I would ask you to look at that point at what we will publish, because we will indicate what the trajectory is to ensure that the use of the Welsh language, access to the Welsh language, the Welsh language in our heartlands, the Welsh language in our schools, all tie together under one co-ordinated strategy that will be based on the concept that the Welsh language belongs to us all. contributions.text_english: 4. How is the Cabinet Minister ensuring community involvement in decisions about the future of Church in Wales maintained schools in Ceredigion Penfro? OQ64786
contributions.text_original: 4. Sut mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn sicrhau bod cymunedau'n cael eu cynnwys mewn penderfyniadau ynghylch dyfodol ysgolion a gynhelir gan yr Eglwys yng Nghymru yng Ngheredigion Penfro? OQ64786

contributions.text_english: Thank you. Local authorities are responsible for decisions on the future of schools, and they must follow statutory procedures when bringing forward proposals. This includes consulting communities, providing sufficient information to enable people to come to informed views, engaging with relevant partners, including religious bodies, and having regard to the wishes of parents.
contributions.text_original: Diolch. Awdurdodau lleol sy'n gyfrifol am benderfyniadau ynghylch dyfodol ysgolion, ac mae'n rhaid iddyn nhw ddilyn gweithdrefnau statudol wrth gyflwyno cynigion. Mae hyn yn cynnwys ymgynghori â chymunedau, darparu digon o wybodaeth i bobl allu dod i farn ddeallus, ymgysylltu â phartneriaid perthnasol, gan gynnwys cyrff crefyddol, a rhoi sylw i ddymuniadau rhieni.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Cabinet Minister. I'm concerned about the low level of confidence that parents, staff and governors in Pembrokeshire have told me that they have in the council involving them meaningfully in big decisions about the future of their schools. Examples include but are not limited to church schools. I wrote to the council back in September around decisions on the future of Cilgerran school, and I'm glad this is now resolved. But, Cabinet Minister, public trust and confidence is easily lost. As Pembrokeshire County Council now consults on proposals to close Tenby Church in Wales VC Primary School and neighbouring Greenhill school, replacing them with a new three-to-19 community school, can the Cabinet Minister assure us that she expects these decisions to be based on the meaningful involvement of parents and the wider community, including open and transparent information on all options available?

contributions.text_english: Diolch. Local authorities are democratically accountable to their communities and are responsible for developing school organisation proposals. In so doing, they must comply with the requirements set out in the School Standards and Organisation (Wales) Act 2013, and the school organisation code, which is quite clear about the processes and involvement that is required in these cases. I do expect all proposers to comply fully with these statutory requirements and to engage openly and meaningfully with all those affected by any proposal. These decisions should be informed by the evidence gathered through consultation and taken in accordance with the legislative framework. You will be aware, because I've said it several times, that the role of Welsh Ministers in the statutory process means that I'm unable to comment on proposals that I may later be required to determine. But, in the context of all decisions, I would expect my first two points to be clear.

contributions.text_english: 5. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the financial pressures facing rural schools in Gwynedd Maldwyn? OQ64722
contributions.text_original: 5. Pa asesiad y mae’r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi’i wneud o’r pwysau ariannol sy’n wynebu ysgolion gwledig yng Ngwynedd Maldwyn? OQ64722

contributions.text_english: Thank you. I seem to have lost you in my book. Wait a second. I'm sorry.
contributions.text_original: Thank you. I seem to have lost you in my book. Wait a second. I'm sorry.

contributions.text_english: We recognise the significant pressures across our schools and local authorities, and acknowledge the commitment of the education workforce in continuing to support learners. Decisions on the level of funding available to schools, including rural schools, are made by each local authority as part of their overall budget setting.
contributions.text_original: Rydyn ni'n cydnabod y pwysau sylweddol ar draws ein hysgolion a'n hawdurdodau lleol ni, yn ogystal ag ymrwymiad y gweithlu addysg i barhau i gefnogi dysgwyr. Mae penderfyniadau ynghylch lefel y cyllid sydd ar gael i ysgolion, gan gynnwys ysgolion gwledig, yn cael eu gwneud gan bob awdurdod lleol wrth bennu eu cyllideb gyffredinol.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. In Gwynedd Maldwyn, we're already seeing the consequences of the financial pressures on these rural schools. Both Gwynedd and Powys have closed rural primary schools and further closures are being considered or progressed. I understand smaller schools can cost more per pupil to run, but these schools are often at the heart of their communities. When one closes, it's not just the school building that is lost; children may have to travel much further, parents have to reorganise their lives, and villages lose something that is very difficult to replace. And, of course, transporting those children elsewhere comes at a cost as well. So, can I ask the Cabinet Secretary whether the Welsh Government is properly accounting for those wider costs and the impact on rural communities when assessing the funding pressures facing our rural schools? Thank you.

Mi fydd yr Aelod hefyd yn gwybod bod fy nghydweithiwr y Gweinidog dros ddygnwch gwledig yn edrych ar fesurau i feithrin a gwarchod dygnwch cymunedau gwledig, a bod ystyriaethau ynglŷn â chynnal gwasanaethau gyda phoblogaeth mwy gwasgaredig, er enghraifft, yn rhan o'r ystyriaethau hynny. contributions.text_english: The challenges facing rural schools like those in my constituency are a symptom of the broader challenges facing our rural areas, with an ageing population, families moving away and local authority services that are more expensive to run and more difficult to administer. For rural schools to flourish, we need high-quality jobs, adequate housing and effective public transport, and I'm very pleased to see the Government taking action on these matters. If rural communities prosper, then rural schools will prosper too. How, then, will the Community Schools Plus plan empower our rural schools, as well as empowering the communities to which they belong?
contributions.text_original: Mae heriau ysgolion gwledig fel y rhai yn fy etholaeth i yn symptom o heriau ehangach ein hardaloedd gwledig, gyda'r boblogaeth yn heneiddio, teuluoedd yn symud i ffwrdd, a gwasanaethau llywodraeth leol yn ddrutach i'w rhedeg ac yn anoddach i'w gweithredu. Er mwyn i ysgolion gwledig ffynnu, mae angen swyddi o ansawdd, cartrefi digonol a thrafnidiaeth gyhoeddus effeithiol, a dwi'n falch o weld y Llywodraeth yn gweithredu ar y materion hyn. Os bydd cymunedau gwledig yn ffynnu, yna bydd ysgolion gwledig yn ffynnu. Sut, felly, bydd y cynllun Ysgolion Cymunedol a Mwy yn grymuso’n hysgolion gwledig, yn ogystal â grymuso'r cymunedau maen nhw’n perthyn iddynt?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much. contributions.text_english: 6. What is the Welsh Government doing to support adult learners who are retraining for new careers? OQ64766
contributions.text_original: 6. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i gefnogi dysgwyr sy'n oedolion sy'n ailhyfforddi ar gyfer gyrfaoedd newydd? OQ64766

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

contributions.text_english: The Welsh Government is committed to lifelong learning and ensuring that adults can access opportunities to develop new skills, retrain and progress throughout their lives. Through personal learning accounts, employability programmes and further education opportunities, we support adults retraining for new careers to realise their potential and progress into sustainable employment.
contributions.text_original: The Welsh Government is committed to lifelong learning and ensuring that adults can access opportunities to develop new skills, retrain and progress throughout their lives. Through personal learning accounts, employability programmes and further education opportunities, we support adults retraining for new careers to realise their potential and progress into sustainable employment.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Weinidog. People retrain for many reasons: after losing a job, returning to work after raising a family, or starting a new chapter following a career break. Others come to Wales with valuable qualifications and skills that go unrecognised, despite the contribution they could make to our Welsh economy. At the Inspire! adult learning awards, I met learners determined to gain new skills and contribute to their communities. For many, adult learning is more than education; it is a vital opportunity to rebuild their careers and their lives here in Wales. One of my constituents, Yassmein Hussein, completed 13 adult learning courses through Cardiff and Vale College and Cardiff Council, leading her to win the shared futures award at the awards. Yassmein's story shows what people can achieve when they have access to the right learning opportunities. But not everyone gets that chance, and many adults still face barriers to retraining. So, I want to know how the Welsh Government is ensuring that adults who want to retrain for a new career can access the learning opportunities and support they need to make that transition.

So, I want to know how the Welsh Government is ensuring that adults who want to retrain for a new career can access the learning opportunities and support they need to make that transition.

contributions.text_english:
Well, like you, I was there in the Inspire! adult learning awards, and what a terrific night it was, to hear the remarkable stories of adult learners across Wales, many who have overcome very personal barriers to achieve in their learning. It really was an inspirational evening and, for me, it's one of the highlights of the year to go to that event. What it shows is that adult learning is about more than just gaining qualifications or skills. It builds confidence, it increases resilience and it improves well-being, and I was delighted to be there to share in Yassmein's success that evening.

In terms of your direct question, the Welsh Government is committed to ensuring that people of all ages have opportunities to learn throughout their lives. We do provide Medr with funding streams, which is allocated to further education colleges and other providers to support learners facing particular barriers. They may relate to disabilities, financial hardship, transport issues, childcare, mental health and well-being. This can include additional learning support, disability-related support, transport assistance, childcare, well-being services and so on, because we want to remove those barriers that stand in their way. Now, in particular, there is a community learning grant worth £6.5 million available to fund adult community learning in general, adult basic education, employability, English for speakers of other languages and well-being courses. These actually help people back into skills and work.

There is also a learning grant for learners over the age of 19, and also a personal learning account programme, which aims to help individuals upskill or reskill, as you mentioned, in priority sectors. So, the Welsh Government is absolutely clear that we do support adults in their retraining and upskilling, and want to be as supportive as we can. Because lifelong learning means exactly that: it never stops. So, we are 100 per cent committed to that programme.

contributions.text_english: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to establish the reasons for teachers leaving the profession? OQ64775
contributions.text_original: 7. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i ganfod y rhesymau pam y mae athrawon yn gadael y proffesiwn? OQ64775

contributions.text_english: Improving recruitment and retention is one of my priorities. We already know that teachers leave the profession for a range of reasons, including workload, well-being and working conditions. We are drawing on national and international evidence and working with our social partners to take practical action to address these issues.
contributions.text_original: Improving recruitment and retention is one of my priorities. We already know that teachers leave the profession for a range of reasons, including workload, well-being and working conditions. We are drawing on national and international evidence and working with our social partners to take practical action to address these issues.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Minister. In March, the Welsh Government workforce plan admitted that they did not have data as to why teachers leave the profession. Estyn noted exactly the same concern 19 years ago. The latest figures from the Education Workforce Council show that more than 3,000 schoolteachers have left the register in the year up to March, the highest number in five years. But we don't know why. There is no national system in place to ask the teachers themselves why they have left. England and Scotland do that. Why doesn't Wales? Will the Minister ask the Education Workforce Council to start asking teachers who are leaving the register why they did so, so that we can understand how we can stop more teachers from leaving in the future?
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Weinidog. Ym mis Mawrth, cyfaddefodd cynllun gweithlu Llywodraeth Cymru nad oedd ganddyn nhw ddata ynghylch pam mae athrawon yn gadael. Nododd Estyn yn union yr un broblem 19 mlynedd yn ôl. Mae ffigurau diweddaraf Cyngor y Gweithlu Addysg yn dangos bod mwy na 3,000 o athrawon ysgol wedi gadael y gofrestr yn y flwyddyn hyd at fis Mawrth, y nifer uchaf mewn pum mlynedd. Ond dydyn ni ddim yn gwybod pam. Does yna ddim system genedlaethol i ofyn i’r athrawon eu hunain pam maen nhw wedi gadael. Mae Lloegr a’r Alban yn gwneud hynny. Pan nad yw Cymru? A wnaiff y Gweinidog ofyn i Gyngor y Gweithlu Addysg ddechrau gofyn i athrawon sy’n gadael y gofrestr pam yr aethant, er mwyn inni ddeall sut fedrwn ni stopio mwy o athrawon rhag gadael yn y dyfodol?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you. I don't think it's correct to say that we don't have any evidence. There are a number of reports that have looked into this specific problem—one quite recently carried out by Cardiff Met, for example, which was published in 2024. The OECD has also looked at these challenges in the context of work that they have done in Wales. One of the Senedd committees has also looked in detail at this issue.

They've all come to the same conclusion, to all intents and purposes, namely that the workload is excessive and is a heavy workload. There's also a feeling that society does not appreciate the efforts of teachers as it did at one stage in the past. I think that we all have a responsibility to examine how we speak about the education profession; we can all be of help in that context, at least. There are also questions about the professional pathway—in terms of promotions and so on, as you move through the system. Then, there are specific subject areas where it is especially difficult to recruit and retain teachers. There is a dependence as well on teachers who are perhaps qualified to teach one subject but are increasingly asked to teach another subject.

These are all issues that influence our ability to recruit and to retain teachers, and this has, clearly, been a priority for me over the recent period. That is why, for example, we provided those additional payments for recruitment to difficult-to-recruit subjects, and also are looking then at the broader requirements with representatives from the workforce itself.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch. Dydw i ddim yn credu ei bod hi'n gywir i ddweud nad oes tystiolaeth gyda ni. Mae nifer o adroddiadau wedi ymchwilio i’r broblem benodol hon—un yn gymharol ddiweddar gan Cardiff Met, er enghraifft, y brifysgol yng Nghaerdydd, a gyhoeddwyd yn 2024. Mae’r OECD hefyd wedi edrych ar yr heriau yma yng nghyd-destun y gwaith y maen nhw wedi’i wneud yng Nghymru. Mae un o bwyllgorau’r Senedd hefyd wedi edrych yn fanwl ar y broblem yma.

Yr un casgliad maen nhw i gyd wedi dod iddo, i bob pwrpas, sef bod y baich gwaith yn ormodol ac yn drwm. Mae teimlad hefyd nad yw cymdeithas yn gwerthfawrogi ymdrechion athrawon fel yr oedd ar un cyfnod. Rwy’n credu bod dyletswydd arnom i gyd i edrych ar siẁd rydyn ni yn siarad am y proffesiwn addysgu; gallwn ni i gyd fod o gymorth yn y cyd-destun hwnnw o leiaf. Mae hefyd cwestiynau ynglŷn â’r llwybr proffesiynol—dyrchafiadau felly, wrth i rywun symud drwy’r system. Wedyn, mae yna feysydd a phynciau penodol lle mae’n arbennig o anodd i recriwtio a chadw athrawon. Mae dibyniaeth hefyd ar athrawon sydd efallai wedi’u cymhwyso i ddysgu un pwnc, ond sydd yn cael eu gofyn yn gynyddol i addysgu un arall.

Mae’r rhain i gyd yn faterion sydd yn dylanwadu ar ein gallu ni i recriwtio a chadw athrawon, ac mae hwn wedi bod, yn amlwg, yn flaenoriaeth i mi dros y cyfnod diwethaf. Dyna pam, er enghraifft, gwnaethom ni roi taliadau ychwanegol yn eu lle i recriwtio i rai pynciau sydd yn arbennig o anodd, ac wedyn yn edrych ar y gofynion ehangach gyda chynrychiolyddion o’r gweithlu eu hunain.

contributions.text_english: And the final question, question 8—Llŷr Powell.

contributions.text_english: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve pupil safety? OQ64768
contributions.text_original: 8. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella diogelwch disgyblion? OQ64768

contributions.text_english: The safety and well-being of learners is an absolute priority for the Welsh Government. We continue to work closely with schools, local authorities, the police and other partners to prevent harm, identify emerging risks and ensure that appropriate arrangements are in place to respond effectively when concerns arise.
contributions.text_original: The safety and well-being of learners is an absolute priority for the Welsh Government. We continue to work closely with schools, local authorities, the police and other partners to prevent harm, identify emerging risks and ensure that appropriate arrangements are in place to respond effectively when concerns arise.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for that answer, Minister. In September, more than 300 pupils in the Caerphilly borough lost their free school transport because, as the council said, they fall within the two-mile measurement of the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008. Now, the problem with that is that the Measure is looking at distance but not incline. I've walked this route with campaigners and parents and children themselves—I went from Aberbargoed to Bargoed—and it's the incline that is the tricky part. During different weathers, whether it's the heat we experienced in the summer, or even cold winter days, when that road can be slippery, it does become a risk. Will the Government now look at reviewing the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008 and look to include the advice on inclines and the difficult weather paths that this could create?

contributions.text_english: 1. How does the Commission's procurement support businesses in Wales? OQ64772
contributions.text_original: 1. Sut mae caffael y Comisiwn yn cefnogi busnesau yng Nghymru? OQ64772

contributions.text_english: The Commission supports Welsh businesses by making procurement opportunities both visible and accessible. All suppliers are treated fairly and consistently under procurement law. Contracts worth more than £30,000 are advertised on Sell2Wales, allowing companies to express an interest and to tender. We also explore the market; we identify potential Welsh suppliers and alert them to suitable opportunities. We monitor spending with Wales-based suppliers through a corporate key performance indicator reported annually. At present, that is being exceeded—it's 55 per cent against our target of 50 per cent. For larger contracts involving subcontractors, we seek opportunities for Welsh businesses to join supply chains. These measures strengthen participation while maintaining an open, transparent and legally compliant procurement process for all involved.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. The Senedd should lead by example in how public money is spent. In 2018-19, the Commission introduced a performance indicator tracking procurement spending with Welsh suppliers. Following scrutiny of its 2020-21 accounts, the Public Accounts and Public Administration Committee recommended splitting the contracts into smaller lots so that the smaller Welsh firms could compete. The Commission accepted that recommendation. The Welsh Government has now pledged to increase public procurement spending with Wales-based suppliers towards 70 per cent. Small and medium-sized businesses account for over 99 per cent of enterprises in Wales. Businesses across Carmarthenshire, from Llanelli to Ammanford and Carmarthen should have a fair opportunity to compete for those contracts funded by Welsh taxpayers, but knowing how much the Commission spends with Welsh suppliers tells us little about whether that money is reaching businesses across the whole of Wales. So, will the Commission publish a regional breakdown of its procurement model spending, including how much goes to small and medium-sized businesses? And what practical steps is it taking to ensure that the smallest firms in areas such as Carmarthenshire can compete for contracts, including splitting larger contracts into smaller lots where appropriate?

contributions.text_english: 2. What safeguards will the Commission put in place regarding the use of smartglasses on the Senedd estate? OQ64771
contributions.text_original: 2. Pa fesurau diogelu y bydd y Comisiwn yn eu rhoi ar waith o ran defnyddio sbectolau clyfar ar ystad y Senedd? OQ64771

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. The Commission already has safeguards in place that restrict filming and recording on the Senedd estate without relevant authorisation. Importantly, those restrictions are technology neutral, and they apply regardless of whether recording is undertaken using conventional equipment, a phone, smartglasses or any other device.

However, we recognise that wearable and AI-enabled technologies are developing rapidly. I've therefore commissioned a review of our policies and guidance to ensure that they remain effective and keep pace with these developments. Our aim is to ensure that Members and their staff, Commission officials and the Senedd estate are properly protected, while allowing the legitimate benefits of new technologies, including, by the way, accessibility benefits, to be realised where their use is appropriate and properly authorised.

contributions.text_english: The Member says his glasses caused a stir. They certainly did. The Commission is undertaking a review, the Cabinet Office has enforced a ban, and it's only a matter of time before other organisations follow suit. The review isn't the problem; the gap before it concludes is. The Cabinet Office has already taken action very swiftly, so I'd be grateful to know the Commission's position while that review is under way. I would also argue that this is a question of equity. Everyone should be on a fair and equal footing. A Member wearing a recording device has an advantage over every other person in the room, and they have no idea that they may be filmed. So, whether the glasses weren't filming isn't the point—nobody else can tell, and a rule that depends on checking after isn't a safeguard.

Thank you very much. First of all, on the Cabinet Office, the Cabinet Office may have made a decision on this, and it's perfectly open to Welsh Government to make a decision on how they pursue this policy as well. Also, courts and tribunals have banned the use of film and recording devices outright. Just to reiterate, there is a clear ruling here already, in a technology-neutral way, on any filming and recording device on the Senedd premises. I shouldn't need to remind Members of that. They're fully aware, they went through induction, everybody's aware. I've written out subsequently as well.

On the issue of equity, that's a valid point. It's been raised by other Members. I've actually had some very good written representations about ideas that could be fed into the review. So, I would strongly suggest that all Members, actually, contribute to this review going forward, but recognising that some of this assistive technology has benefits, not least that it has been identified by many within the disability lobby as well to say, 'We want to see the proper, appropriate, authorised use of this in the right situation.'

So, I can just give a further brief update. The initial review of smartglasses and other advancing technologies is now well advanced. I'll be writing to Members before recess to set out further explanation of the way in which the review will carry out its work, including the ways in which Members will be able to participate so that all views can then be taken into account. Just to say, if we get to this point at the speed that we are going, we will be ahead of other Parliaments in actually putting the right procedures in place for this technology.

contributions.text_english: 3. Has the Commission obtained independent advice on whether its broadcasting policy is fair, proportionate and consistently applied? OQ64743
contributions.text_original: 3. A yw'r Comisiwn wedi cael cyngor annibynnol ynghylch a yw ei bolisi darlledu yn deg, yn gymesur ac yn cael ei gymhwyso'n gyson? OQ64743

contributions.text_english: Thank you. The Commission’s broadcasting policy drew on a report by an independent adviser, which examined the Senedd’s historical position, looked at five other legislatures and considered relevant policy principles. I recently agreed that this policy could be reviewed. In September, Commissioners were asked to consider four options. It was determined that further consultation was required between the Commission and party groups, and this is now under way, with officials already having met or briefed most party groups.

Diolch. GB News is still excluded from the Senedd's internal television screens, and the justification was that comments made were contrary to the Parliament's values. However, the very broadcasting protocol itself was developed by an unnamed independent adviser to the Senedd Commission. So, what are the values of this adviser and on what political spectrum do they lie? The fact is the inclusion of Sky News as a commercial broadcaster undercuts the rule of allowing only public service broadcasters on the internal Senedd television screens. GB News is also a licensed news and current affairs broadcaster like Sky News, and its programmes cover issues affecting people across Wales, including perspectives that challenge the Welsh Government's policies.

So, while I recognise the Commission's responsibility to maintain appropriate standards, these standards must be applied fairly, consistently and proportionately. So, could we have discussions on this sooner rather than later, and can we all have an opinion on this, so that we can get GB News back where it belongs on our internal tv screens?

contributions.text_english: 4. What consideration has the Commission given to introducing mandatory safeguarding training for all Members of the Senedd and their support staff? OQ64741
contributions.text_original: 4. Pa ystyriaeth y mae'r Comisiwn wedi'i roi i gyflwyno hyfforddiant diogelu gorfodol ar gyfer yr holl Aelodau o'r Senedd a'u staff cymorth? OQ64741

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. The Commission cannot formally mandate training for Members, who are of course elected office holders, or their staff, who are employed by those individual Members. However, the Commission treats learning or briefings that inform and protect Members, their staff and the Senedd from legal, regulatory or reputational risk as necessary and recommend them as essential.

We provide training and support to help Members understand their responsibilities and ensure their staff are appropriately trained, and we continue to promote participation through accessible, appropriately sequenced provision. Participation by Members and Member support staff is vital. It has been particularly helpful in the past when party groups have required their Members to attend particular training, while employing Members may require—and, depending on the subject, may be responsible for ensuring—that their staff complete appropriate training.
