contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Nick. I think that's a very fair point. I absolutely recognise the concerns that Members will have about the potential disruption to work. The original intention was to keep Members in Tŷ Hywel while the refurbishment took place, precisely to minimise those disruptions. However, having tested the options carefully, it became clear that the risks from noise, vibration, dust and potential delays were simply too great. We could have ended up with far more disruption and much less certainty for Members and for staff.

We're now working to secure high-quality alternative accommodation very close to the Senedd, which will retain the full range of support services that Members need to do their jobs efficiently. Importantly, moving everyone out temporarily will also allow for refurbishment work to progress much more quickly. The savings from that should at least offset the additional accommodation costs and could potentially deliver an overall saving.

A detailed relocation plan is being developed, and I agree with Nick that Members need to understand exactly what those arrangements will mean for them and their staff. Our priority must be to make the transition as smooth as possible, minimise disruption to the work of the Senedd, and ensure that Members can return to a refurbished Tŷ Hywel under the current programme by April 2030.

contributions.text_english: 7. Will the Commission publish the whole-life costs and options appraisal for the future of Tŷ Hywel before signing any further binding contracts? OQ64760
contributions.text_original: 7. A wnaiff y Comisiwn gyhoeddi'r arfarniad o gostau oes gyfan ac opsiynau ar gyfer dyfodol Tŷ Hywel cyn llofnodi unrhyw gontractau rhwymol pellach? OQ64760

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Steve, for your question. The Commission has undertaken a public, open and competitive procurement process to look at the options available to us when the current lease of Tŷ Hywel comes to an end in 2032. Throughout that process, value for money has been absolutely central to our considerations. We've looked not just at immediate costs, but at the longer term financial implications of each option, including the cost of doing the bare minimum and remaining in Tŷ Hywel under the current arrangements. That work identified the options we're now taking forward as offering the best value for money and at a considerable margin.

The final financial details are still being worked through and will form part of the full business case, which will inform the Commission's decision in December on whether to proceed. I fully appreciate that the Member will want to see those figures, and rightly so. However, we're dealing with commercially sensitive information, and publishing it before contracts are signed could undermine our negotiating position. But I want to reassure Members that we will share that information with them as soon as we're in a position to do so.

contributions.text_english: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister make a statement on the widespread fuel leak in the River Taff? TQ1507
contributions.text_original: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet ddatganiad am y gollyngiad tanwydd eang yn Afon Taf? TQ1507

contributions.text_english: Diolch yn fawr iawn. contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Natural Resources Wales has confirmed that the fuel discharge has now stopped, with mitigation measures preventing residual fuel from reaching the River Taff. Clean-up and assessment of potential environmental impacts on the river habitat and wildlife continue, and NRW will of course continue to monitor developments closely.

contributions.text_english:
Cabinet Minister, last Friday evening, residents of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf in Nantgarw and Taff's Well, as well as communities in Tongwynlais and Gwaelod-y-garth, alerted NRW to a pollution incident in the River Taff, following a toxic leak from GE Aerosapce Wales's engine maintenance plant. We have been told that up to 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled into the river. The impact on people's health and the environmental damage, at least 2 miles downstream, was immediate. Members of the community we have met have spoken of unbearable conditions, which cause headaches, sickness and drowsiness. And then there has been the deadly impact on wildlife and the natural environment all along the river.

We have spoken to South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, who were called by NRW, and were first on the scene. They suggested that an incident occurred on the site sometime before they arrived. Finally, we have met with GE Aerospace, who have confirmed that they were the source of the leak and have assured us that the fuel lines have now been isolated to prevent any further spillage. We welcome the ongoing work being undertaken by Natural Resources Wales, Public Health Wales and the emergency services to assess and respond to this extremely serious incident, but many questions remain to be answered.

What assurance have you received regarding the volume and chemical make-up of the fuel released, and what further risk is there given that this is an area prone to flooding? What discussions have you had with Natural Resources Wales regarding the next steps being taken around the clean-up operation and habitat restoration, and how long this is likely to last? When can we expect a full and transparent review to identify how, why and when exactly this incident occurred, what safeguards are in place, and what is being done to ensure that this won't happen again? Diolch.

I fully recognise the concern that it has caused for local communities and for those with an interest in or an involvement with or living nearby the River Taff. NRW have confirmed to me, as I said in my initial answer, that fuel discharge has now stopped and that current mitigation measures are preventing residual fuel in the tributary from reaching the River Taff, and clean-up and environmental assessments are continuing.

You asked about the volume particularly, but also the source and maybe a little bit about the precise circumstances of the release. Those remain matters for NRW's ongoing investigation, but you're right: early reporting made claims that a considerable amount, estimated at up to 25,000 litres, may have been lost into the site's surface water drainage system. But I wouldn't want to present that estimate as some sort of final confirmed figure, because, as I say, investigations continue. For example, my understanding is that the tank could potentially contain that much; it's not clear yet how much was in it. And, of course, not all of it would have found its way into the river—some of it would have been contained or collected on site before reaching there. So, we need to be mindful of that, but, obviously, this will become clearer over time. The pollutant has, though, been identified as kerosene.

I've discussed the ongoing response with NRW, and I'll continue to keep closely sighted on developments there. The site operator's specialist contractor, who they brought in very early on, continue recovery and clean-up activity, including maintaining and replacing containment booms, whilst NRW continues to assess the environmental impact. NRW officers have observed impacts on aquatic invertebrates, which may be linked to this incident. The information currently available doesn't provide a firm timescale for completion of the clean-up—which is another question you asked—or any subsequent habitat restoration that might follow as a consequence. Again, I wouldn't want to speculate on that today, but that work is ongoing. NRW will continue to work with the site operator to establish the cause, and they will ensure that all possible steps are taken to prevent further spills.

The circumstances of the incident and its environmental impacts remain under investigation, and it would therefore not be appropriate for me to speculate on who is responsible, or anticipate any regulatory or enforcement action that might follow. But, again, I would reiterate—I'm sure, on behalf of everyone here—our thanks to all of those who have been involved in the response effort, which, I have to say, happened promptly and in a very effective manner.

Thank you to the Member for raising this. Cabinet Minister, I spent over 20 years with South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, so I recognise the efforts of crews, Natural Resources Wales officers, and everyone containing pollution. But the facts are deeply concerning: kerosene from GE Aerospace's Nantgarw site has affected around 4 km of the Taff. Dead fish have been recovered, residents have been advised to close windows and doors, and fumes are present. GE Aerospace said it isolated the source on Friday, yet on Monday Natural Resources Wales said it was still investigating the drainage system to stop further pollution. Stopping the original leak is not the same as stopping pollution reaching the river. And this is not the first time; in 2024, pollution from PB Gelatins UK in Treforest killed fish. The outcome announced this June was the enforcement undertaking, including a £50,000 donation and nearly £15,000 in costs.

Cabinet Minister, you chaired the committee that reported Natural Resources Wales's own concerns that its fines and sanctions weren't enough to deter polluters. You now oversee Natural Resources Wales. Our Reform manifesto commits us to dismantling and fundamentally restructuring Natural Resources Wales, bringing strategic policy under ministerial oversight while environmental protections continue without interruptions.

The public deserve to know what went wrong, who is accountable and who will pay to put it right. So, Cabinet Minister, will you commit to a written statement to this Senedd within 14 days, setting out how much fuel was released, the damage identified so far, the timetable for Natural Resources Wales's investigation and any enforcement decision, and how all legal recoverable costs will be pursued from those found responsible and not the Welsh taxpayer? Diolch.

I was appalled at the weekend to learn about the kerosene leak from the GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw in my constituency. I'm really concerned about the environmental impact of this pollution as it seeps into the waterways and into the River Taff that runs right through the heart of our city, right down to this place. I understand Natural Resources Wales were made aware of the incident on Friday and have been taking action with fuel-absorbing barriers at the confluence between the tributary and the Taff, but there are some discrepancies between the two organisations' public statements that we've seen. GE Aerospace claimed that the source of the spill was fully identified and isolated on Friday, but NRW have said that they're still seeking to confirm the source.

Cabinet Minister, I'm glad to hear that you're being briefed by NRW. Could you confirm whether or not GE Aerospace are fully co-operating with the investigation? Will GE Aerospace be held fully accountable for their failures, which allowed this to happen? And what will be done to assess and remediate impacts on the fish and animals that live in and around the River Taff, and how will that be paid for?

Look, until the investigations have been completed, I am loath to point the finger as much as Members would like me to. Clearly, where liability is identified—let's put it that way—then NRW will take appropriate action. That is their role and that is what we all expect of them.

In terms of seeking the source of the incident, my understanding is that whilst maybe it had been identified early on, once it was in the drainage system, which can be very complex, it's very difficult then to know exactly where that goes. So, maybe there's a bit of confusion around the source as opposed to the numbers of ways that that water could actually escape the site. But again, all of this will come out in the wash once the initial response and recovery has taken place. There will be a process then to make sure that we look at the results of all of that.

In terms of the environmental impact, of course—and that is clearly an important factor here—NRW are waiting for results of samples for biological and ecological investigations. Drone surveys have been conducted so that they can visually assess the impact as well. I am told that 10 dead fish have been recovered from the river as a consequence of this. Ten dead fish. But, of course, impacts on invertebrates will mean greater ecological impacts as well, and I'm not downplaying that for a second.

Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I recently had the pleasure of visiting Big Pit National Coal Museum in Blaenavon, where I met with staff and learnt about the excellent work they are doing to preserve and promote Wales's rich industrial heritage. What impressed me most was the museum's commitment not only to protecting our history, but to engaging people of all ages, through education, community outreach and innovative exhibitions. Big Pit continues to play a vital role in ensuring that future generations understand the sacrifices and achievements of those who built our coalfield communities.

During my visit, I also had the opportunity to see the Stories from Aberfan exhibition. And as we mark the sixtieth anniversary of the Aberfan disaster today, this exhibition is a poignant and powerful reminder of the 144 lives lost, the devastating impact on the community and the extraordinary courage and resilience shown in the decades since. The personal stories and artefacts on display help ensure that the memory of Aberfan endures and that the lessons of that tragedy are never forgotten. I would like to thank everyone in Big Pit for their dedication to preserving these important stories and sharing them with future generations, and I encourage all people to visit.

Last week, I was, along with you and other cross-party colleagues, delighted to welcome Danielle Webb to the Senedd women's caucus. Danielle is an inspirational woman and I am fortunate to call her a friend and know her as a former colleague. As vice-chair of Little People UK, she spoke passionately about her experiences as a little person as part of Dwarfism Awareness Month. She highlighted the everyday challenges that many little people face—as students, when entering employment, commuting or simply navigating spaces that too often fail to accommodate them.

There are between 3,000 and 7,000 people with dwarfism in the UK and over 200 different types of dwarfism. Depending on the condition, people may experience significant medical complications, including spinal stenosis, hydrocephalus and arthritis. Diagnosis and treatment can require genetic testing, scans and x-rays, as well as a co-ordinated team of medical specialists. Dwarfism Awareness Month is an opportunity to challenge misconceptions, raise understanding and confront the barriers that people with dwarfism face every day. We must listen to people like Danielle, champion their experiences and ensure our public spaces, workplaces and services are accessible and inclusive. Greater awareness must be matched by practical action so that people with dwarfism can participate fully in every aspect of life in Wales. Diolch.

Dirprwy Lywydd, this month marks Menopause Awareness Month, and on Sunday just gone, we recognised World Menopause Day. Until recently, when I thought about menopause, I naively pictured what I assume many people do: women of a certain age, hot flushes and many a conversation about the temperature of a room. Perhaps that highlights a lack of appropriate education around menopause growing up. I was wrong, and I'm learning that the hard way.

Menopause can cause chronic pain, but also cognitive and mental health challenges that can affect work, relationships and everyday life. And for women who are neurodivergent, in particular those with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, those changes can bring additional challenges that we need to understand and talk about too. We also need to challenge the assumption that menopause only happens to women of a certain age. I want to take this moment to acknowledge premature ovarian insufficiency, or POI—something I had never heard of until I was diagnosed with it at 36. This coming Sunday marks the second-ever World POI Day, which in itself shows how much more awareness and understanding is still needed.

Dirprwy Lywydd, I'll say it again: this Chamber works best when we use our time to shine a light on aspects of people's lives that too often go under the radar. So, to those living with menopause and POI, you deserve to be listened to, understood and supported. And during my time here, I will do what I can to make sure these experiences are seen, heard and taken seriously. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to congratulate Cwm Taf Morgannwg public health team and the Treherbert learning community team, who recently won the inclusion and respect award at this year's Seren awards. Their work forms part of the wider Treherbert initiative, with Grow Rhondda as a key partner. The initiative asked one simple question: what was needed to help people in Treherbert to live healthier lives? This question was taken directly to the people and some clear themes began to emerge: affordable healthy food, mental health support, youth facilities and much more. Importantly, following this, work has started to act on some of these priorities, resulting, for example, in the creation of a low-cost fruit and veg market at Grow Rhondda's cafe, where nothing costs more than £1.50. This shows the importance of working with and listening to a community when looking for concrete actions to improve people's lives. So, congratulations once again to Cwm Taf Morgannwg public health and Treherbert learning community team, and I look forward to seeing what the future holds and what further activities they deliver. Diolch.

Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. This debate, in a nutshell, is, essentially, about putting the NHS first when deciding how to reduce waiting lists, and I'm grateful for the cross-party support on this matter.

I should declare an obvious interest, which you're all expecting me to say anyway, that I'm a consultant eye doctor at Singleton Hospital in Swansea. I've worked in the NHS for 23 years as a doctor and 10 as a consultant. I believe in the NHS, work in the NHS, and I've seen the problems and opportunities first-hand. Our clinicians know their patients, they know the hospitals and, more importantly, they know the systems that they work in. We should give them the opportunity to put forward plans for reducing waiting lists before asking private providers if they can do so. And this is not party political, or at least it shouldn't be.

I believe we all want people across Wales to receive safe, timely care. We want waiting lists to fall and we want public money to deliver the greatest possible benefits for our patients. So, what does this proposal ask for? Three things: to favour NHS-led provision; to give clinical leads the power to reject unsafe private proposals or inadequate follow-up arrangements; and to demand transparent publication of data on private provision from every health board. And why? Because I believe that putting the NHS first can help us deliver safer care, work more efficiently and make better use of NHS money. And I will take each one of these things in turn.

Deliver safer care. One appointment or a surgery is only one part of the process in a patient's diagnosis and treatment journey. It isn't, and, indeed, can't be, a stand-alone thing. Likewise, an operation also. What happens afterwards matters too, and, indeed, before, with listing and pre assessment. It's obviously not hugely safe to send one link of this chain to an unfamiliar provider and then the patient is returned. Clinicians all over Wales can speak about experiences, for example, with patients returning to the NHS with some form of complication following a cataract operation, for example, privately via outsourcing. These complications can and should require urgent treatment, which then takes priority over elective cases, such as macula hole repairs. The proposed legislation would give clinical leads the authority to refuse private arrangements they consider unsafe or which lack appropriate follow-up care. The people responsible for patients' care must have a say in how that care is provided—the people who mop up the mess.

Secondly, to work more efficiently. Local NHS teams know the patients, the department and the systems, yet decisions to outsource or insource work to companies can be taken several levels above them, before they have the opportunity to offer an in-house solution. Oftentimes, if the patients are not known to the company clinicians, who also can't access records and are not responsible for follow-up—we don't have an electronic patient record all around Wales, for example—decisions are deferred, as it is merely an exercise in kicking the can down the road to make the figures look temporarily better. But it always catches up worse than before. I'm a fan of the HBO miniseries Chernobyl, where Professor Valery Legasov says,

'Every lie we tell incurs a debt to the truth. Sooner or later that debt is paid.'

And when is that? When the contract ends in this case.

This proposal would require health boards to seek the development of those solutions first: additional waiting list initiative clinics and operating lists within the NHS, planned by the teams who understand the service. And we also need to consider the effect on our workforce. When clinicians cut their NHS hours to do more private-provider work, which does remunerate better, it has to be said, the private sector grows and the NHS capacity atrophies. We become more dependent on the very provision that is drawing our staff away, and we're, in fact, paying to drain the very service we need to strengthen. If an NHS team cannot undertake all the additional work, private provision would remain an option. This proposed Bill would merely establish a presumption in favour of NHS-led plans.

Thirdly, to make better use of public money, if indeed we do put the NHS first. Private contracts use public money. I think Mabon recently quoted £1.5 million that was spent over the past few years on outsourcing. That money used in an NHS setting would have helped develop services and make a permanent improvement to departments all over Wales. We need to appreciate and understand the full cost of the contracts, including follow-up, complications and any work that then returns to NHS services.

Cataracts, for example—obviously, I'm biased towards cataracts—[Laughter.]—are not undertaken and simply sent back. Complications are needing extra surgery, appointments in eye casualty, as well as administrative problems caused by one eye being operated on privately via outsourcing and the other eye falling through the cracks, which is a terrible image. [Laughter.]

Health boards should publish transparent data on their use of private provision so we can see what has been purchased and assess what it delivers. And why does this matter to constituents across Wales? Because behind every waiting list figure is a person waiting for treatment. They need safe care, timely treatment, and confidence that someone will take responsibility for their follow-up. The decision we make today affects the NHS's ability to treat patients tomorrow. We need to reduce waiting lists while strengthening the service people will continue to depend on.

And why does this matter to me personally? Because this is why I'm here. This is why I came into this job and why I sit in this chair: to give the clinicians delivering care the opportunity to put forward solutions. We have an opportunity to put NHS capacity, clinical judgment and accountability at the centre of decisions about waiting lists—not an expensive, unsafe, can-kicking, sticking-plaster exercise that erodes the health service upon which we depend. Let's stand up for the NHS. Let's put the NHS first. Let's show the people of Wales that we take their safety, their waiting times and their public money seriously, by giving the people who know the patients and deliver their care the opportunity to lead. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Reform UK, we support the NHS. We believe in an NHS that is free at the point of need. And we believe in an NHS that is properly funded and an NHS that puts its patients first. Too many people in Wales are waiting too long for treatment. Roughly a quarter of people are on a waiting list, and two-year waits have not been eradicated as was promised. A&E departments across Wales remain under tremendous pressure, and our planned care capacity is still short of what is required. Everybody who interacts with our NHS can see that the staff are under pressure, the estate needs investment, and the system is not delivering the outcomes that the public deserve.

But we also know that throwing money at a problem doesn't automatically solve it. We cannot fix capacity issues in our NHS if we refuse to look at every practical tool available to us. Therefore, we cannot risk totally excluding independent healthcare providers if they can provide quality care that clears backlogs. I'm not interested in privatisation or charging patients. I'm interested in utilising additional capacity funded by the NHS purse and free to the patient.

Now, I don't believe that the motion before us today seeks to completely exclude the private sector. But I'm concerned that, ultimately, the Bill could result in a set of legal requirements that make it too difficult for us to make use of independent capacity when it is needed. Patients want to be treated in a reasonable time and receive care that is safe and effective. If this Bill leads to a situation in which people are waiting years for NHS care because the system cannot utilise its independent capacity, then it would have failed in achieving the core mission of our NHS: putting patients first.

I'm not opposed to the principle of ensuring that the NHS is properly managed and resourced before seeking alternative solutions. And I'm supportive of the measures that strengthen the NHS, improve the accountability of our health boards and encourage investment into our workforce and estates. But any Bill that effectively rules out practical capacity solutions could, ultimately, end up failing the very people it seeks to protect. Therefore, I will be looking forward to the detail of this Bill, and I will judge it on its ability to get people treated sooner whilst protecting the NHS's founding principle of free care at the point of need. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Can I thank Gwyn for bringing this before us today? I'm a member of the Socialist Health Association, and committed to a publicly funded and publicly provided health service. The NHS, despite the waiting times and financial pressures, is supported by the vast majority of people in Wales. When you consider the cost of health provision in the USA, the NHS is excellent value for money. In the USA, medical costs are the major cause of personal bankruptcy.

I believe in the direct provision of a publicly funded health service by publicly funded and employed health professionals. The private sector see opportunities to profit from the health service, taking the easy-to-provide services, not providing the expensive and difficult-to-provide. I support, wherever possible, delivery of waiting-list initiatives, surgeries and clinics within the NHS rather than through the private sector. The private sector is looking for opportunities to make a profit out of publicly funded health. My aim is a completely directly provided health service with no publicly funded health expenditure leaking out to the private sector.

I support increasing surgical activity through weekend and evening clinics, opening new diagnostic and treatment centres and creating more community-based services to reduce hospital demand. We also have the advances in AI giving us analysis and treatment. All health boards should develop costed plans for additional clinic activity from departments within their organisations before considering entering into contracts with private providers. They must empower and trust clinical staff. I think that's one of the big problems we have: a lack of being prepared to trust the clinical staff.

The BMA has expressed concern about the increasing role of private healthcare provision in the NHS, particularly regarding the privatisation of NHS services. They argue that private healthcare companies should be held to the same standards as NHS providers, including transparent reporting of patient safety incidents and performance. The BMA supports a new NHS provider selection regime to limit procurement arrangements with independent sector providers and ensure the sustainability of the NHS. They also advocate for better oversight of privatisation and recommend that independent sector providers for NHS services should be subject to the same requirements as NHS providers.

I share the concern of many in the health service that increasing the reliance on private providers will erode the NHS's long-term sustainability and will end with us not having a national health service, but a publicly funded health service being used by the public in private hospitals and private areas. And the problem then becomes that the private sector won't want to do accident and emergency. They won't want to do anything that is difficult. They'll want to do the easier-to-deal-with. I think it really is important that we stand up for the NHS, which is what I'm doing now. Can I just, finally, say that the health service is funded to provide services, not as a cash point for the private sector?

contributions.text_english:
My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I absolutely believe that we need to be doing more to increase capacity within the NHS. We need to be doing much more to drive down those shamefully high NHS waiting lists, which are leaving our constituents languishing in pain. We do need to have better data sharing and give consultants and specialists more control as well as authority. But that should not be at the expense of the private sector. The private sector has a place within our healthcare system. It is not the enemy. It can complement and build on the NHS offering. The NHS will always be the crème de la crème, but we should have as many weapons in our arsenal when it comes to providing patients with the best possible care. And that, as far as I'm concerned, includes the private sector. We should be utilising private providers. But, by going after the private sector, you're running the risk of increasing pressures on our already overstretched NHS. Not only can private providers be used to help bring down waiting times, but they can actually alleviate pressure on the health service in other ways too, by providing extra capacity and specialist expertise.

I recently met with the Icon Group, an Australian firm, which is poised to reopen the old Rutherford cancer centre in Newport. Yes, it is a private company, but it stands ready to work with the Welsh Government and the health boards to see NHS patients. That's just one example, but there are many organisations out there in a similar position. Look at Newmedica. They are one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded ophthalmology services, treating nearly 14,500 patients all across Wales. Why would we actively seek to prevent them from carrying out their vital work?

The motion before us would force all health boards to develop costed plans for extra NHS activity before entering into a private sector contract. Some would argue that this sounds reasonable on the face of it, but what happens when the NHS does not have the capacity to deliver quickly enough? Are we going to make patients wait even longer than they have to whilst another plan is drawn up? If an NHS department can deliver treatment promptly and cost-effectively, it should be given every single opportunity to do so. If an independent provider can safely treat a patient sooner, and at an appropriate cost, health boards must retain the flexibility to use that as an option. We do need to see more joined-up working between the NHS and the private sector, not less of it, which I fear is what is going to happen if this motion goes through. We are going to be supporting this motion today, and I will put on record that I do, in fact, fear that this is a case of cutting off your nose to spite your face against the private sector at the same time. Thank you.

I, too, declare an interest as a consultant ophthalmologist working in the NHS in Swansea.

Expensive contracts, fragmented care, lost opportunities to strengthen our NHS: these are the concerns that I recognise not just as a Member of the Senedd, but also a treating clinician. I thank my colleague Gwyn for bringing forth this proposal, which I support. We all want shorter waiting lists. We all want patients to be treated sooner. And we all recognise the extraordinary work that NHS staff are doing to make that happen. But the question is not simply how many patients we can treat today, but whether we can build the capacity to treat patients tomorrow. 

Let me explain what I have witnessed. Patients that have had cataract pre-assessment by an external provider, that arrangement ends, the patient returns to the NHS, sometimes requiring another assessment before surgery proceeds. That's another appointment, another cost, and another delay. And when complications occur, patients rightly return to the NHS teams, adding to the workload of a service already under pressure. Colleagues in other specialties have reported similar frustrations.

Deputy Llywydd, this is not about criticising individual providers. It's about questioning whether our system is making the best use of public money and clinical expertise, because waiting lists can appear shorter without the NHS becoming stronger. So, that's at the heart of this debate.

In Swansea bay, our performance report identifies gaps in cataract pre-assessment capacity and opportunities to improve theatre utilisations. We have the clinicians, we have the expertise, and what we need is the capacity to deliver. And that means investing in assessment clinics, our theatres, our workforce, and the clinical leadership needed to redesign services. That means asking our front-line teams what they can achieve with the right support. And it means ensuring that our clinical leads are involved in decisions about external contracts, patient safety and continuity of care. And we also must be transparent about costs, outcomes and who remains responsible for patients when contracts end.

Deputy Llywydd, I'm not arguing that external provision should never have a role. I'm arguing that temporary solutions must not be a substitute for permanent NHS capacity. Every pound that we spend should do more than reduce today's waiting list. Where possible, it should strengthen tomorrow's service. We're treating patients today, we're training the clinicians for tomorrow, and we're building our NHS for the future. And this principle is why I believe that this proposal should be advanced, and that's why I support it. Diolch.

I believe that the NHS first Bill has worthy ambitions, as long as the NHS is able to deliver the care when required. All my constituents ask for is a local medical centre or a hospital that can treat them quickly, with local expertise.

Gwyn Williams has often talked about how health board boundaries stop the movement of patients, staff and experts. This means that services are fragmented, duplicated and delayed. Patients should not be refused access simply because they live on the wrong side of a health board boundary. There must be no postcode lottery in treatment or outcomes. The ministerial advisory group recognised last year that de facto regional arrangements are already widely established and called for stronger regional working.

To support the Bill, there is clear need for more medical staff. I welcome the Government's announcement of 253 additional graduate nursing jobs recently, but the Royal College of Nursing has said that the uncertainty has caused a huge reduction in people accepting nursing degrees in Wales.

This Bill should also call for greater transparency. Health boards should publish clear information about the use of private providers, including costs, activities and outcomes. That would allow the public to judge whether spending leads to permanent NHS capacity or just short-term solutions. An NHS first approach must have stronger accountability. For too long, the Welsh Government has taken a hands-off approach to NHS management. Ministers must exercise firmer oversight and set clear expectations when performance, decision making or patient safety falls short. Successful practices should be shared across Wales. Our NHS needs management that is results driven, not process driven. We must allow our front-line health professionals to concentrate on what matters most: their patients.

What's needed is faster treatment, safer care and better use of public money. It is about building capacity and resilience within a national health service that belongs to us all. Let us put the NHS first, break down the barriers that delay care, strengthen democratic oversight and ensure that every decision begins and ends with what is best for the patients in Wales. Diolch yn fawr.

Patients should not be refused access simply because they live on the wrong side of a health board boundary. There must be no postcode lottery in treatment or outcomes. The ministerial advisory group recognised last year that de facto regional arrangements are already widely established and called for stronger regional working.

To support the Bill, there is clear need for more medical staff. I welcome the Government's announcement of 253 additional graduate nursing jobs recently, but the Royal College of Nursing has said that the uncertainty has caused a huge reduction in people accepting nursing degrees in Wales.

This Bill should also call for greater transparency. Health boards should publish clear information about the use of private providers, including costs, activities and outcomes. That would allow the public to judge whether spending leads to permanent NHS capacity or just short-term solutions. An NHS first approach must have stronger accountability. For too long, the Welsh Government has taken a hands-off approach to NHS management. Ministers must exercise firmer oversight and set clear expectations when performance, decision making or patient safety falls short. Successful practices should be shared across Wales. Our NHS needs management that is results driven, not process driven. We must allow our front-line health professionals to concentrate on what matters most: their patients.

What's needed is faster treatment, safer care and better use of public money. It is about building capacity and resilience within a national health service that belongs to us all. Let us put the NHS first, break down the barriers that delay care, strengthen democratic oversight and ensure that every decision begins and ends with what is best for the patients in Wales. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Deputy Llywydd, nobody in this Chamber, obviously, wants patients to have to wait any longer for treatment. And if capacity is available that can safely get somebody their operation done sooner, I understand why Governments, including the previous Welsh Government, have looked at the private sector. But I think today's debate asks us to look beyond the immediate waiting lists and consider what kind of NHS we actually are wanting to build for the future. And that is where I believe the workforce has to be at the heart of this discussion.

Here in Wales, 'Agenda for Change' provides the framework for pay and important terms and conditions for most directly employed NHS staff. Unison Cymru has warned that health boards cannot expect to recruit and retain staff without addressing NHS pay. It has also been absolutely explicit in calling for the NHS in Wales to be protected from privatisation. So, when public money is spent buying additional services and capacity outside of NHS Wales, we should ask not only, 'How many patients will this treat today?' but also, 'What does this actually do in terms of the capacity and workforce issues of our NHS for tomorrow?'

This doesn't need to be an ideological argument. Where private capacity is absolutely necessary to get patients treated sooner, we should be pragmatic. This is why I support the principle of NHS first, but NHS first doesn't, obviously, have to mean NHS only. But our longer term ambition should always be much bigger; it should mean building the strength and capacity of our NHS and the public services around it. It means our NHS and our community care working together rather than treating health and social care as separate systems. It means recognising that health does not begin at the hospital door. It means addressing the socioeconomic inequalities that drive poor health. It means tackling mental health earlier before people reach crisis. And it means confronting some of the deepest causes of trauma and ill health in our communities, including violence against women and children, domestic abuse, and other forms of abuse. Because NHS first cannot simply mean asking where we treat somebody once they become ill. It must also mean creating the conditions in which fewer people become ill, fewer people reach crisis, and fewer families need emergency intervention.

So for me, that is also about holding on to the founding principle of our NHS that healthcare is a public good, there for people when they need it, regardless of their means or their backgrounds. And as, of course, Aneurin Bevan put that principle simply:

'No society can legitimately call itself civilized if a sick person is denied medical aid because of lack of means.'

Deputy Llywydd, our responsibility is obviously not simply to defend that principle, but to make it work for the challenges that Wales faces today. Bringing waiting lists down matters, but so does building the NHS, the workforce, the community services and that healthier society that ensures that we leave our NHS stronger than we first found it.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you to Gwyn for bringing this debate to the Chamber. I'm pleased to contribute to this debate, which shines a light on the importance of keeping our NHS in public ownership, and not fall victim to creeping privatisation. At some point, every one of us will rely on the NHS. It has cared for our loved ones and communities in their times of need. And we must protect a service that provides care free at the point of need.

Cardiff is often a hub for specialist NHS services, serving people from all across Wales. My constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf is home to the University Hospital of Wales, Cardiff Royal Infirmary, Noah's Ark Children's Hospital for Wales and Velindre University NHS Trust. These hospitals have been caring for people from all across Wales for decades, and with roughly 700,000 people on NHS waiting lists in Wales, the answer must be to invest in our public health service.

This is particularly important when it comes to women's health. Despite making up more than half of the population, women-specific healthcare needs have historically been overlooked and underfunded. Endometriosis is just one example. Roughly one in 10 women are affected by this debilitating condition, and given concerns about the future of Wales's only NHS British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy-accredited endometriosis centre in Cardiff, protecting these specialist services must remain our priority.

Greater reliance on private healthcare risks creating a two-tier system, where those who can afford treatment get help sooner, while others who can't are left waiting for years. So, Deputy Llywydd, ultimately, we must invest in our NHS and protect its public provision at the point of need. An NHS Bill that strengthens these principles would only be a positive step forward for the people of Wales. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. I welcome the opportunity to contribute to this debate and to respond to the motion before us. I would also like to thank the Member in question for being a tireless advocate for our health service, and I know that he brings very valuable professional experience to this debate.

There is a great deal in the motion that the majority of Members across the Chamber can support, as we've already heard. We all want a stronger national health service in Wales, with more care provided in NHS settings wherever possible, and patients receiving timely, safe and high-quality care. As a Government, we firmly believe that the health service belongs to the people of Wales, and although certain political figures, along with their wealthy, questionable and unaccountable backers, might think otherwise, our precious health service is not for sale and never will be while we are at the helm.

We inherited a significant backlog of patients who have waited far too long for treatment. Our priority, therefore, is to build NHS capacity, increase activity and provide the support that clinical teams need to treat more patients safely within NHS Wales. The Government agrees with the core principles underpinning the motion. NHS capacity should be developed and utilised wherever possible. Decisions should be guided by clinical considerations. Patient safety must be prioritised and any additional capacity must be transparent with appropriate governance measures in place.

The question is: what is the best way to deliver on the commitments that we have made to the people of Wales, particularly our commitment to reduce waiting times and to eliminate the longest waits?
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r cyfle i gyfrannu i'r ddadl yma ac ymateb i'r cynnig sydd o'n blaenau ni. Dwi hefyd am ddiolch i'r Aelod dan sylw am fod yn eiriolwr diflino dros ein gwasanaeth iechyd, a dwi'n gwybod ei fod yn dod â phrofiad proffesiynol gwerthfawr iawn i'r ddadl hon heddiw.

Mae yna lawer iawn yn y cynnig y gall y rhan fwyaf o Aelodau ar draws y Siambr ei gefnogi, fel rydyn ni wedi ei glywed. Rydyn ni oll eisiau gwasanaeth iechyd gwladol cryfach yng Nghymru, gyda mwy o ofal yn cael ei ddarparu mewn lleoliadau NHS lle bynnag y bo modd, a chleifion yn cael gofal amserol, diogel ac o safon uchel. Fel Llywodraeth, rydyn ni'n gadarn yn ein cred bod y gwasanaeth iechyd yn perthyn i bobl Cymru, ac er y byddai rhai cymeriadau gwleidyddol a'u noddwyr cyfoethog amheus ac anatebol yn hoffi meddwl fel arall, dyw ein gwasanaeth iechyd gwerthfawr ni ddim ar werth a fydd o byth ar werth tra byddwn ni wrth y llyw.

Fe wnaethon ni etifeddu ôl-groniad sylweddol o gleifion sydd wedi aros yn rhy hir am driniaeth. Ein blaenoriaeth ni felly yw adeiladu capasiti'r NHS, cynyddu gweithgarwch a rhoi'r gefnogaeth sydd ei hangen ar dimau clinigol i drin mwy o gleifion yn ddiogel o fewn NHS Cymru. Mae'r Llywodraeth yn cytuno â'r egwyddorion canolog y tu ôl i'r cynnig. Mi ddylai capasiti'r NHS gael ei ddatblygu a'i ddefnyddio bryd bynnag y bo modd. Dylai penderfyniadau gael eu harwain gan ystyriaethau clinigol. Mae'n rhaid rhoi diogelwch cleifion yn gyntaf a rhaid i gapasiti ychwanegol bod yn dryloyw efo mesurau llywodraethiant priodol ar waith.

Y cwestiwn yw: beth yw'r ffordd orau o gyflawni'r ymrwymiadau rydyn ni wedi'u gwneud i bobl Cymru, yn enwedig ein hymrwymiad i leihau amseroedd aros a chael gwared ar yr arosiadau hiraf?

contributions.text_english:
Our planned care reset and delivery plan is firmly focused on that objective. The plan was developed with national clinical leaders, speciality leaders and NHS operational experts. It is increasing NHS capacity and productivity, redesigning pathways and exploring dedicated surgical and diagnostic hubs. Our aim isn't simply to purchase short-term activity, but to build a stronger and more sustainable NHS service.

We're already seeing this approach support progress in tackling waits of more than 104 weeks, with most additional activity being delivered within NHS Wales itself. By drawing on the expertise of our clinical and operational teams, strengthening weekly planning and making better use of existing capacity, we are supporting more patients to receive care within the NHS, with independent capacity used selectively where needed. Clinical leadership runs throughout the plan. Clinical leaders are identifying opportunities to increase productivity, redesign pathways and safely increase activity, keeping decisions focused on what is best for patients.

Dirprwy Lywydd, our overriding responsibility as a Government is to deliver the programme for government. That means reducing waiting times, eliminating excessive waits and ensuring that patients receive treatment when they need it. People waiting for surgery, diagnostics or out-patient appointments are not concerned with organisational boundaries. They are concerned with receiving safe and timely care. Health boards are expected to maximise NHS capacity by improving productivity, by using their workforce effectively and strengthening clinical pathways. But health boards must also make responsible choices. They're expected to consider how NHS capacity can be maximised before commissioning additional provision.

This isn't a new approach; the NHS has long commissioned services from external providers where necessary to supplement its own capacity. Where patients would otherwise face excessive delays, health boards must retain the ability to plan services around clinical need, local capacity and the responsibility to reduce harmful waits. Importantly, there are already robust arrangements in place to ensure accountability and transparency. Health boards publish planned care performance monthly, including progress against delivery trajectories, waiting times, activity and recovery plans. The Welsh Government scrutinises delivery weekly so that emerging issues can be addressed promptly.

Dirprwy Lywydd, patient safety must remain at the heart of every decision we take. Where additional capacity is used, established arrangements must ensure care is safe, clinically appropriate and properly monitored, including quality, outcomes, follow-up and continuity of care. Clinical leaders must be able to raise concerns where proposed arrangements do not provide safe treatment, effective governance or appropriate follow-up, and those concerns must be acted upon.

The motion also raises important questions about the future sustainability of planned care services. Alongside tackling waiting times, we must build a stronger and more resilient system through more day-care surgery, higher productivity, fewer unnecessary follow-ups and better use of diagnostics and theatres. The expert group considering surgical and diagnostic hubs is central to that work. Dedicated elective facilities could protect planned care from emergency pressures, improve access and support a more sustainable NHS-led model.

contributions.text_english:
We do support the principles behind the motion, namely maximising NHS capacity and strengthening sustainable provision within it, wherever this is clinically appropriate. The existing legislation, including the Health Service Procurement (Wales) Act 2024, already supports collaborative delivery and flexible commissioning. Through clear national expectations, robust governance and transparent performance management, these goals can be achieved, enabling health boards to ensure safe and timely care. Therefore, there is no necessity as things currently stand to introduce further new legislation.

There is scope to look at strengthening governance, and we are doing so, and ensuring transparency, which is also something that we are doing. If it becomes apparent that these measures have not yielded the desired results, then we may need to revisit the possibility of new legislation. But there are things that can be done, and that we as a new Government are doing, that do not require new legislation—and, of course, there is no need to legislate unnecessarily either.

Wales has also adopted a different approach to infrastructure investment, having made less use of PFI than England in the past. Furthermore, Wales has developed alternative models designed to strengthen the role of the public sector, enhance transparency and deliver greater benefits to communities. Patients cannot afford to wait if there are actions that can be taken now. They want to see positive change now, and their demands are entirely justified. The ultimate test is whether the care provided is safe, timely, free at the point of use, and delivers the best possible outcomes, wherever it is commissioned. We will always seek to strengthen NHS provision, while also acknowledging that health boards must be able to act responsibly when additional capacity is required to prevent avoidable harm.

For these reasons, we can support the motion, and we do so on the basis that its principles, namely strengthening NHS capacity, safeguarding patient safety, ensuring clinical leadership, and improving transparency, can be achieved without necessarily resorting to additional legislation. We will continue to focus on delivery, namely increasing NHS capacity, reducing the backlog we have inherited, and enabling safe decisions that are informed by clinical judgment and in the best interests of patients. Thank you.

Mi rydym ni'n cefnogi egwyddorion y cynnig, sef gwneud y mwyaf o gapasiti'r NHS a chryfhau darpariaeth gynaliadwy oddi mewn iddo lle bynnag mae hynny'n briodol yn glinigol. Mae'r gyfraith bresennol, gan gynnwys Deddf Caffael y Gwasanaeth Iechyd (Cymru) 2024, eisoes yn cefnogi darparu cydweithredol a chomisiynu hyblyg. Trwy ddisgwyliadau cenedlaethol clir, llywodraethiant cryf a rheoli perfformiad tryloyw, gellir cyflawni'r nodau hyn gan ganiatáu i'r byrddau iechyd sicrhau gofal diogel ac amserol. Felly, does dim rheidrwydd, fel y saif pethau, i gyflwyno Deddf newydd eto.

Mae yna le i edrych ar gryfhau llywodraethiant, ac mi ydyn ni'n gwneud hynny, a sicrhau tryloywder, sydd yn rhywbeth rydym ni hefyd yn ei wneud. Os ydym ni'n gweld nad yw hyn yn cael y canlyniadau rydym ni'n eu dymuno, efallai y gellir dod yn ôl ac edrych eto ar Ddeddf newydd. Ond mae yna bethau y gellir eu gwneud ar hyn o bryd, ac yr ydym ni fel Llywodraeth newydd yn eu gwneud, sydd ddim yn golygu bod angen deddfu—ac wrth gwrs, does dim angen deddfu yn ddiangen chwaith.

Mae Cymru hefyd wedi dilyn dull gwahanol o fuddsoddi mewn seilwaith, gan wneud llai o ddefnydd o PFI na Lloegr yn y gorffennol. Mae Cymru hefyd wedi datblygu modelau eraill i gryfhau rôl y sector cyhoeddus, gwella tryloywder a sicrhau mwy o fudd i gymunedau. All cleifion ddim aros os oes camau gweithredu y gellir eu cymryd rŵan. Maen nhw'n dyheu am weld newid positif rŵan, ac mae eu galwadau nhw'n gwbl gyfiawn. Y prawf yw a yw'r gofal yn ddiogel, yn amserol, yn rhad ac am ddim ar y pwynt o ddefnyddio, ac yn sicrhau'r canlyniadau gorau lle bynnag mae'n cael ei gomisiynu. Mi fyddwn ni bob amser yn ceisio cryfhau darpariaeth yr NHS, gan gydnabod hefyd bod rhaid i fyrddau iechyd allu gweithredu'n gyfrifol pan fydd angen capasiti ychwanegol i atal niwed y gellir ei osgoi.

Am y rhesymau hynny, rydym ni'n cefnogi'r cynnig. Rydym ni'n gwneud hynny ar y sail bod modd cyflawni ei egwyddorion o gryfhau capasiti'r NHS, gwarchod diogelwch cleifion, sicrhau arweinyddiaeth glinigol a gwella tryloywder, a hynny heb ddefnyddio deddfwriaeth o reidrwydd eto. Mi fyddwn ni'n parhau i ganolbwyntio ar gyflawni, sef cynyddu capasiti'r NHS, lleihau'r ôl-groniad yr ydym ni wedi'i etifeddu, a galluogi penderfyniadau diogel sy'n cael eu llywio gan farn glinigol ac sydd er budd gorau cleifion. Diolch.

First of all, I thank everyone who took part in the debate from all sides. Before I come on to the specifics, just to reassure Benjamin and Natasha that this is absolutely not about discriminating against the private sector at all, it's just about doing what we can in-house and what we can't outside of the house. Because there are risks—safety risks, but also continuity-of-care risks, follow-up risks—all kinds of things that make it more desirable to do the work in-house.

I myself have been in a strange position, for example, whereby our waiting lists for seeing patients—out-patient appointments—have been going behind. And I want to see more, but I'm told that, because of outsourcing and because there's a lack of money for doing the work in-house, the only way I would have been able to see my own patients is by joining the company and seeing them in a whole different environment, which is very odd. That's why I wanted to bring this to all of your attention, specifically so that we just put the horse before the cart and we try to do things in a sensible, cheaper and safer way beforehand. So, just to reassure you, we're not going to ban the private companies altogether. This is absolutely not the aim of this. It's just about there being a presumption to do the work in-house first. 

I agree with Shav: this is not an ideological argument at all, it's more of a scientific and commonsense argument. I'm grateful to all the people who spoke. I was going to list them all, but there are too many and time is running out. But also the people who wanted to speak but there was no time as well: Leticia, Sarah Rees and Cristiana Emsley. I'm very grateful to her, again, not that she did speak, but that she wanted to speak, and I'm grateful for that. Thank you. 

And lastly, just to say that this is all just about creating the conditions for allowing the national health service to survive. Aneurin Bevan—who has been quoted already, but I've got a different quote, thankfully—famously said that

'The NHS will last as long as there's folk with faith left to fight for it.'

We're fighting for it. Diolch yn fawr.

I stand today to move the motion tabled in the name of my colleague Llŷr Powell calling on the Government to explicitly include prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy for Wales. Prostate cancer is the most common form of cancer amongst men in Wales. Each year, more than 2,500 are diagnosed, and around 640 sadly die from the condition. If it's caught early, the outlook can be more positive. Nearly everybody diagnosed at stage 1 goes on to live for five years or more. But, if it's caught late, the picture is very different. Too many men in Wales are being diagnosed too late, particularly in our most deprived communities. The consequences of this are severe, and they're measured in lower quality of life, unnecessary suffering for patients and their families and too many people losing their lives too soon. 

The 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026' found that prostate cancer diagnoses in Wales rose by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2024. That growth included more stage 1 diagnoses, which is an encouraging sign if it means that the disease is detected early. But it also shows the need for capacity and careful clinical planning in this area. In Wales, 54 per cent of men with high-risk or locally advanced prostate cancer received radical treatment. That's compared to 69 per cent in England. Serious concerns have also been raised regarding higher rates of emergency readmission after surgery and a significant drop in recorded numbers of radical prostatectomies—try saying that after a night out—and radical radiotherapy.

The audit also raises serious questions about data quality in Wales. It highlights problems with incomplete data, data with linkage issues and underrecording. We also know that waiting times for cancer treatment remain a serious problem here. The 62-day target is still missed routinely, and diagnostic capacity needs to be addressed. Across Wales, particularly in north Wales, patients have faced unacceptable delays that have allowed their cancers to progress. If we don't have adequate data systems in place to track treatment and outcomes, it becomes incredibly difficult to make improvements to the system.

Cancer is the leading cause of death in Wales and, for too long, we have lacked a proper cancer action plan as a nation. There is a clear need to implement a strategy that invests in modern diagnostic technologies and treatments and uses evidence-led screening initiatives that improve patient access. That is why I support the principle of the 10-year national cancer strategy. However, I have heard concerns from clinicians, campaigners and the third sector that prostate cancer will not receive the explicit focus, accountability and resources that it needs. So, today's debate is an opportunity for the Government to address those concerns and ensure that people across Wales who are suffering with prostate cancer get the attention and treatment they deserve.

The fact is that there are serious questions that need to be asked with regard to prostate cancer in Wales. What assessment has the Government made of the UK National Screening Committee decision only to recommend a limited screening programme? Alongside that, what discussions has the Government held with the NHS and third sector about the feasibility of implementing a prostate cancer screening programme? And in the absence of a screening programme for all high-risk men, will the Government consider including other early-detection commitments within the cancer strategy to ensure that more men with prostate cancer are diagnosed early?

A strategy that does not contain firm commitments that prostate cancer will be a priority risks leaving men behind. That is why today's motion was both reasonable and necessary. Prostate cancer needs more than a passing mention in the cancer strategy; it needs clear actions, including targets to increase the proportion of men who are diagnosed at an early stage, particularly in our most deprived communities; measurable improvements in the proportion of men with high-risk disease who receive timely radical treatment; urgent action to fix data quality issues so that progress can be monitored; plans to improve diagnostic and treatment capacity; and an integration with a broader men's health approach that encourages men to come forward sooner.

Patients in Wales deserve to be diagnosed before their cancer has spread so that they can receive proper treatment in a timely manner. By explicitly prioritising prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy, the Government can take a practical step towards that goal. It will give clinicians, health boards and patients the clarity that they need, and it will give this Senedd the ability to hold the Government to account against delivery. Prostate cancer deserves a clear place in Wales's cancer strategy, one that is supported by resources, data and delivery. That way more men can be diagnosed early and more lives can be saved. Therefore, I urge Members to support our motion today. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the amendment tabled in my name. As Members are already aware, I am living with prostate cancer and, as such, I believe that that experience has given me a real insight into the challenges faced by patients and indeed their families across Wales. As has already been said, I'm one of more than 2,500 men who are diagnosed with prostate cancer every year here in Wales and, as we've already heard, around 640 men die from it.

It's because of the high prevalence of men in Wales who are diagnosed with it that I believe it has to be included in the national cancer strategy for Wales. Indeed, in the written questions that I've tabled to the Cabinet Minister, the responses have included actions that would be taken via the national cancer strategy, and so I have no reason to believe that it wouldn't inform some part of the future thinking of this Government.

I have to say that I welcome the consultation on the national cancer strategy, because it's a good opportunity to think a bit more innovatively about how services can be delivered in the future. However, this consultation must be more than a tick-box exercise, and as we've so often heard in the past, whether it's a Welsh Government consultation or a health board consultation, patients' voices must be heard. It's absolutely essential that this consultation is meaningful, that those who engage with it are confident that their views are genuinely being considered, and that the final strategy reflects the submissions it receives. So, I hope that the Cabinet Minister will give that assurance to us today in his response to this debate.

Now, as our amendment makes very clear, the Welsh Conservatives want to see a national screening programme introduced by the Welsh Government. I believe that earlier detection improves patient outcomes, and as Prostate Cancer Research tells us, when prostate cancer is detected early, survival rates are close to 100 per cent. And this is not a party political point. I have worked constructively with colleagues in other parties and in other political institutions to call for a national screening programme. For example, I joined the Labour peer Lord Kevin Brennan to raise awareness of some of the symptoms of prostate cancer. We both shared our different prostate cancer journeys, and we discussed why we believe a national screening programme should be introduced. But whether you agree or disagree with a national screening programme, there is clearly a shared understanding across political parties that more can and should be done when it comes to prostate cancer, so I hope that this spirit of co-operation will continue as this strategy is developed.

Now, a key section of the Welsh Government's national cancer strategy consultation considers the opportunities presented by advances in medical technology. We are witnessing significant developments in diagnostic tools and various innovative treatments, many of which are transforming outcomes for patients, including focal therapy, stereotactic ablative radiotherapy and many other treatments. These technological developments can have huge potential, not only to improve survival rates, but also to enhance quality of life for those living with prostate cancer. These technologies must be available to men in all parts of Wales, irrespective of where they live, and I hope the new strategy will show how patients are able to access these specific treatments. Of course, alongside investment in technology, there must also be a commitment to supporting the workforce and ensuring that healthcare professionals have the capacity, training and resources they need to deliver these treatments effectively.

Llywydd, the forthcoming national cancer strategy presents an important opportunity to improve cancer outcomes across Wales, but to achieve that goal, there must be a meaningful consultation process, a commitment to earlier diagnosis and screening, investment in cutting-edge technologies and a determination to provide equitable access to the care and treatment that patients need wherever they live in Wales. We have a responsibility to the men already living with prostate cancer in Wales and to those that will be diagnosed with prostate cancer to use this opportunity to get this strategy right.

And as for a national screening programme, Wales can lead the way if it wants to. We don't have to follow England, we don't have to follow other parts of the UK. So, I urge the Welsh Government to commit to exploring this further at the very least. We all want to deliver better outcomes for men diagnosed with prostate cancer across Wales, and so we will be supporting this motion this afternoon, and I urge Members to support my amendment.

contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful for the opportunity to speak on this really important issue today. There's real excitement across the cancer charity sector and the cancer workforce because a long-term cancer strategy is a chance to set a new course for patients in Wales. This is a critical moment for how we want to see cancer outcomes improve over the coming years, and I welcome every opportunity to discuss what the strategy should look like, because we will all know someone who is told that they have cancer in their lifetime, if not ourselves.

Cancer will affect one in two people. The figures for prostate cancer are particularly shocking. Prostate cancer will affect one in eight men. For black men, it's one in four. And for men who have a family history of particular cancers or who carry the BRCA2 gene variant, they face a significantly higher risk. Reducing this inequality and the many other inequalities in cancer diagnosis and care must be a focus of the strategy.

The Welsh Government has set itself an ambitious timetable, aiming to publish the strategy on World Cancer Day next year. That is commendable and shows the urgency that is needed. It will be Wales's first national cancer strategy since 2006. And as chair of the cross-party group on cancer, which everyone here is welcome to join—I've e-mailed some of you separately; you're all welcome—I'm not aware of any plans for the strategy, as it is at the moment, to focus on any site-specific cancers, which the debate tabled today calls for, but with such a tight deadline, the strategy must build on existing groundwork. There are already national optimal pathways shaped by clinical specialists and best practice that set out how people with suspected site-specific cancers, including prostate cancer, should be treated and supported, but too many people are not being served quickly and effectively by these pathways. There's often a backlog for diagnosis and waits for treatment often depend on surgical space and workforce availability. As a result, only one in three people with prostate cancer start treatment within 62 days, when the target is 75 per cent.

The strategy must not be a 'one and done'. Too many quality statements and short-term plans have sat on the shelf after publication. This strategy must be a living thing. It must give every national optimal pathway, including for prostate cancer, the chance to work to its full potential and actively unblock the barriers holding them back. Alongside this, it must improve access to clinical trials, awareness of signs and symptoms and so much more, like data and workforce. All these things are vital.

I'd like to acknowledge the amendment tabled by Paul Davies, and I share the urgency behind it. General screening for all men is still not recommended by the UK National Screening Committee based on the evidence currently available, but that evidence is moving. In May, the committee recommended targeted screening every two years for men aged 45 to 61 who carry the BRCA gene variant and have a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer, and the UK Government has accepted that. So, I'd like to ask the Minister: when will this be in place in Wales and will the new strategy commit to it?

I also stand with colleagues in calling for research to go further and faster and for more men to know of their family history. For men facing a prostate cancer diagnosis, support and time to make decisions about their care are essential, but time is not always a luxury patients have. The earlier a diagnosis is made, the more treatment options are available. I hope today's discussion can focus our minds on a near future where prostate cancer is diagnosed quickly and early, where innovative treatments are available and where patients can look forward to life after cancer or to live well for decades to come. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Can I thank the Member for bringing forward this important debate today and also thank Paul Davies for sharing his experience and his insight into such an important subject matter? And as we've heard during this debate already, prostate cancer is the most common cancer amongst men in Wales and far too many families across the country have lost loved ones because a cancer diagnosis came too late. So, Welsh Labour strongly supports this motion and we join calls to include prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy for Wales. We wish to see a strategy that delivers better outcomes, improves support for cancer patients and builds on the progress made under the previous Welsh Labour Government.

In Government, Welsh Labour ensured that record numbers of people got the good news every year that they don't have cancer. We invested tens of millions of pounds in new cancer facilities, diagnostic equipment, treatments, technology and workforce development, and we started construction on the new Velindre Cancer Centre, which is opening next spring. We introduced a £2 million cancer recovery programme to improve how services are delivered, including a specific focus on urological cancers, and we took significant steps to improve cancer screening and early diagnosis. We expanded bowel cancer screening to everyone aged 50 to 74, and increased the sensitivity of the screening test. We also made Wales the first UK nation to introduce human papillomavirus testing as the primary cervical screening test. Furthermore, we announced a new national targeted lung cancer screening programme, and on all of those decisions, Welsh Labour were driven in our determination to deliver better health outcomes for families in Wales.

contributions.text_english:
We were certainly right to set very, very stretching targets for cancer. Obviously, we didn't meet them on all occasions, but I do not apologise for the stretching targets that we set. And of all of those decisions, as I say, Welsh Labour were driven at all times by the determination to deliver better health outcomes for the people that we served.

Now, that's particularly relevant today. Decisions about screening programmes must always be based on the best available evidence. In this case, we know that the independent UK National Screening Committee does not recommend population-wide screening for prostate cancer. It advises that population-wide screening can cause more harm than good, because of the risks that include false positives and also the risk of providing false reassurances. Instead, they recommend targeted screening for prostate cancer, and, of course, the UK Labour Government has followed that advice.

The UK Labour Government has committed more than £20 million to improve prostate cancer research and treatment, including supporting the Transform trial, which aims to deliver better ways of detecting the disease. That research is particularly important for understanding how screening can better support black men who face a higher risk of developing prostate cancer. So, will the Minister now confirm that he too will follow the science and the Plaid Cymru Government will commit to introducing an evidence-based targeted prostate cancer screening programme in Wales, similar to that which the UK Labour Government has announced for England? If the Minister is unable to make that commitment today, he should set out his reasons in detail and explain why the Welsh Government is taking a decision that is not led by the evidence.

I'd also urge the Minister to ensure that the national cancer strategy is focused squarely on outcomes and real-life improvements for patients, and that it builds on the measures delivered by the Welsh Labour Government. Because what matters is early diagnosis, faster treatment and better chances of survival for cancer patients. The Minister already has our support for the motion today. If he can make those further commitments on the national cancer strategy, and a targeted prostate cancer screening programme, he will have the full backing of Labour Members as he delivers those plans.

contributions.text_english:
I'm going to address the men of Wales, and first of all, thank you, Llŷr Powell, for tabling this debate. This is one of those debates where we should be able to put politics to one side. Prostate cancer doesn't care who you vote for, where you live or what you do for a living. When somebody is told they've got cancer, they're not thinking about politics, they're thinking about their family, what happens next and whether they're going to be all right.

This issue is personal to me. My grandfather died from kidney failure caused by prostate cancer, and several other men on my mother's side of the family have been affected by it. That's why it matters to me. I'm thinking about my grandfather and about the families across Wales facing those same worries today. I'm also thinking about the men who may have put off speaking to their GP. I'm 61 now, and because of my family background, I've had the prostate-specific antigen test, and, thankfully, the result was reassuring. But many men don't take that step. Some don't want to make a fuss. Some are worried about what they might be told. Others simply think if they feel fine, there cannot be anything wrong. The reality is that prostate cancer does not always give you a warning. That's why awareness matters and why men need to understand their own risk. But awareness on its own isn't enough. When someone does come forward, the NHS has to be there for them. If they need tests, scans or treatment, they shouldn't be left waiting and worrying about what happens next.

For those of us in rural Wales, there can be additional challenges. A hospital appointment can mean a long journey, time away from work and an entire day spent travelling. If you're already anxious about your health, that only adds to the burden. The latest national prostate cancer audit also raises concerns about variation in treatment in Wales. The figures come with important warnings about data quality, but that itself raises a question: how can we be confident that patients are receiving the right treatment if we cannot reliably measure what is happening?

I also want to say a brief word about the Conservative amendment. I understand the case being made, because I'd like to see more men diagnosed earlier too, particularly given my own family's experience. There is important work taking place around targeted screening for men at particularly high risk, and I believe Wales should continue to follow the evidence and medical advice as that develops.

But today's motion is straightforward. We're asking the Welsh Government to ensure that prostate cancer has a clear place within Wales's national cancer strategy. And inclusion in a strategy must mean more than just a mention in a document.
