I will declare an interest in this debate, because this particular cancer has come knocking at my own door for a loved one of my family.

I would first of all like to thank my colleague, though, Paul Davies MS, for all the brilliant work that he's already done to raise awareness of prostate cancer. By sharing your own experiences, Paul, which was very brave, you've already actively played a part in encouraging more men to come forward for screening. More than 2,500 men are diagnosed with prostate cancer in Wales every year. Around 640 men in Wales die from that disease annually. And the reason I'm speaking up is because what has happened to me and my family, it can happen to anybody.

We shouldn't just stand by and read out numbers any more of how many people have died annually. In my particular case, two years of monitoring—diagnosed two years ago, two years of monitoring—and the condition was going worse and worse during monitoring, to such a degree now that more extensive surgery is required than would have been had this been picked up sooner. Almost 40 per cent of prostate cancer cases are diagnosed at stages 3 or 4. That is not good enough. When the disease is more advanced, the treatment becomes more challenging. These figures should concern everybody sitting here, including you, Cabinet Minister for Health and Care.

Behind every statistic is a man facing the devastating consequences of cancer, prostate cancer being the most common cancer to affect men. Yet it remains one of the cancers where diagnosis too often comes too late. That is why, as has been said many times here today, and I endorse, early detection must be a priority. The Welsh Conservatives firmly believe that a national prostate cancer screening programme could help to identify the disease earlier, improve survival rates, reduce inequality and raise awareness across Wales.

We recognise that screening must be evidence-based and carefully designed. Concerns have rightly been raised about false positive results, unnecessary treatments and the pressure a screening programme could place on NHS capacity. I also understand that there's been a pushback, certainly from our health board, but also the Government, that too much testing can actually identify problems that could lead to more problems. I'm never convinced by that. A raised PSA result does not automatically mean a man has prostate cancer, but an ever-increasing PSA result is very worrying indeed for the family.

Screening can identify some slow-growing cancers that may never cause serious harm. But these challenges should drive us here, as Senedd Members, to develop a far better approach. Advances in diagnostic technology, including MRI and improved testing pathways, offer opportunities to make diagnosis more accurate, and for better treatment decisions when better informed. We should ensure Wales keeps pace with these developments and adopt proven innovation and evidence as it emerges. We should also recognise that a consistent national approach will tackle those very inequalities that have been described today: black men, men with a family history of prostate cancer and men with certain inherited genetic variations. It is fair to say that a very close member of my family has already died with prostate cancer, so why those warnings were not heeded earlier—who knows?

We acknowledge the recommendations of the UK National Screening Committee, including targeted screening for certain men with a confirmed BRCA2 variant and a relevant family history. The Welsh Government must carefully consider these recommendations. However, we also believe Wales should be ambitious. We should work with clinicians, researchers, charities, and patients and their families, to establish the strongest possible screening approach, informed by evidence and designed for the needs of our Welsh men.

We must also ensure that earlier diagnosis is matched by timely access to high-quality treatment, sufficient NHS staffing and the resources needed to meet demand. I will say this here today: patients from north Wales, patients within the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, should not be going to London for operations. Devolution was always supposed to be about providing those kinds of treatments here in Wales, and I was really shocked to learn that the robotic equipment that was purchased in the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board was not the right equipment—that is why we're sending people from north Wales to London. And it has to stop now. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Every Member here will have met a constituent who has lived with prostate cancer or a family who has lost someone to it. A man who put off seeing the GP because he felt fine. A wife who noticed something was wrong before he did. A son who now gets himself checked because his father was diagnosed too late. These are not abstract cases. They are our neighbours, our friends and, for some of us, our own families.

Prostate cancer does not affect all communities equally. In our most deprived communities, most men, or more men, are now diagnosed at a later stage than at an earlier one, while men in more affluent areas are more often caught early. In practice, that means that a man's postcode can decide whether his cancer is found while it can still be treated.

According to the 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026', diagnoses in Wales rose by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2024 to around 2,500 men. That is 2,500 men in a single year who heard the words, 'You have cancer', and 2,500 families whose lives changed in that moment. The same audit found that only 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced disease received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Those are the men whose cancer is the most dangerous, and too many of them do not appear to have received the treatment that could have saved their lives.

At the same time, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment that may not have been needed, compared with 7 per cent in England, with all the lasting consequences that that can bring. The audit urges caution about the Welsh figures because of problems with data quality. Think about what that means. We cannot even say with confidence how many men with prostate cancer are being treated in Wales. That should trouble every one of us, and should be put right.

We also know how hard it is for many men to come forward. Too many have grown up believing that talking about their health is a weakness, and prostate cancer often gives no warning in its early stages. Members of the Senedd have spoken with real courage about their personal experiences, and I pay tribute to them, Paul. Our party leader in Scotland has done the same. But we cannot ask men to be brave enough to come forward and then fail to have a clear plan waiting for them when they do.

Men account for 54 per cent of cancer deaths in Wales. That is why Reform Wales has called for a 10-year cancer strategy, investment in modern diagnostics, targeted screening where need is greatest, and a men's health framework for Wales. So, I call on the Government to name prostate cancer in the strategy, with clear and measurable objectives included, to fix the data, so that we know what is happening to men diagnosed with prostate cancer, and to close the gap between our richest and poorest communities, so that no man is diagnosed too late because of where he lives. I urge all Members to support this motion. Diolch.

Thank you for tabling this debate today. As we've already heard, the statistics regarding the number of men who are impacted by this cruel disease every year cause quite a lot of concern. It's important to recognise that our rural communities are not immune to this challenge. Indeed, as noted in several studies, the burden can be particularly heavy for men in rural areas, where access to health services can be more challenging. A number of factors contribute to this: the distance that some men have to travel to reach a GP; concerns regarding the reduction in GP services, as we currently see in Powys; and the lack of public transport in rural areas. These barriers can all make it more difficult for men to access medical advice and that critical early diagnosis. 

It isn't just the practical challenges that we have to tackle, either. Often, stigma and unwillingness to discuss personal health matters can also lead to delay. We know that some men in farming communities are more prepared to prioritise the health and welfare of their animals over their own. We need to change that. We must foster a culture where men feel comfortable speaking about their health and are willing to ask for advice when something worries them. 

A number of organisations do valuable work in tackling this stigma. Recent work by the FCN charity, in partnership with Macmillan, to draw attention to the challenges in terms of access to cancer services in rural areas is an important example of these efforts. By the same token, I was very pleased to see the FUW adopting Prostate Cymru as the union president’s charity this year. I very much hope that this partnership will help to reach more men in our farming communities and emphasise the importance of identifying potential symptoms and seeking prompt medical advice.

In order to ensure real change, it's vital that any strategy to increase awareness and improve access to diagnosis and treatment aligns with the Welsh Government's broader plans to improve rural health services. To this end, I very much hope that such a strategy will work hand in hand with the Welsh Government's progressive aspiration to establish a new rapid diagnosis centre in Powys.

This is an important development for the region. At present, some patients have to travel outside Powys to receive specialist assessments because there are no suitable diagnostic services available locally. This can mean long journeys, additional costs and further strain for patients and their families at a time already full of worry. A new centre would be an opportunity to improve access to timely assessments and reduce geographical barriers, and it would help to ensure that patients are examined as soon as possible. 

We know that awareness and early diagnosis are vital in order to improve treatment outcomes for prostate cancer. By ensuring that the needs of rural communities are at the heart of any strategy, we can make a genuine difference to men’s lives the length and breadth of Wales. Thank you very much.

Diolch am ddod â'r ddadl yma ymlaen heddiw. Fel rydym eisoes wedi'i glywed, mae'r ystadegau ynghylch nifer y dynion sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan y clefyd creulon hwn bob blwyddyn yn peri cryn bryder. Mae'n bwysig cydnabod nad yw ein cymunedau gwledig yn imiwn i'r her hon. Yn wir, fel nodai sawl astudiaeth, gall y baich fod yn arbennig o drwm ar ddynion mewn ardaloedd gwledig, lle gall mynediad at wasanaethau iechyd fod yn fwy heriol. Mae nifer o ffactorau'n cyfrannu at hyn: y pellter y mae'n rhaid i rai dynion ei deithio i gyrraedd meddygfa; y pryderon ynghylch y gostyngiad mewn gwasanaethau meddygon teulu, fel y gwelwn ym Mhowys ar hyn o bryd; a'r diffyg trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus mewn ardaloedd gwledig. Gall y rhwystrau hyn ei gwneud yn anoddach i ddynion gael cyngor meddygol a'r diagnosis cynnar hollbwysig.

Nid heriau ymarferol yn unig sydd angen inni fynd i'r afael â nhw, ychwaith. Yn aml, gall stigma ac amharodrwydd i drafod materion iechyd personol hefyd arwain at oedi. Gwyddom fod rhai dynion mewn cymunedau amaethyddol yn fwy parod i boeni am iechyd a lles eu hanifeiliaid nag am eu hiechyd eu hunain. Mae hynny'n rhywbeth y mae angen inni ei newid. Rhaid meithrin diwylliant lle gall dynion deimlo'n gyfforddus i siarad am eu hiechyd a bod yn barod i ofyn am gyngor pan fydd rhywbeth yn peri pryder iddynt.

Mae nifer o fudiadau eisoes yn gwneud gwaith gwerthfawr iawn i fynd i'r afael â'r stigma hwn. Mae gwaith diweddar elusen FCN, ar y cyd â Macmillan, i dynnu sylw at yr heriau o ran mynediad at wasanaethau canser mewn ardaloedd gwledig yn enghraifft bwysig o hynny. Yn yr un modd, roeddwn yn falch iawn o weld Undeb Amaethwyr Cymru yn mabwysiadu Prostate Cymru fel elusen llywydd yr undeb eleni. Gobeithiaf yn fawr bydd y bartneriaeth hon yn helpu i gyrraedd mwy o ddynion yn ein cymunedau ffermio a phwysleisio pwysigrwydd adnabod symptomau posibl a chanfod cyngor meddygol yn brydlon.

Er mwyn sicrhau newid gwirioneddol, mae'n hanfodol bod unrhyw strategaeth i wella ymwybyddiaeth a mynediad at ddiagnosis a thriniaeth yn cyd-fynd â chynlluniau ehangach Llywodraeth Cymru i wella gwasanaethau iechyd gwledig. I'r perwyl hwn, rwy'n mawr obeithio y bydd strategaeth o'r fath yn gweithio law yn llaw â dyhead blaengar Llywodraeth Cymru i sefydlu canolfan diagnosis cyflym newydd ym Mhowys.

Mae hwn yn ddatblygiad pwysig i'r rhanbarth. Ar hyn o bryd, mae'n rhaid i rai cleifion deithio y tu allan i Bowys i gael asesiadau arbenigol, gan nad oes gwasanaethau diagnostig priodol ar gael yn lleol. Gall hyn olygu teithiau hir, costau ychwanegol a straen pellach i gleifion a'u teuluoedd ar adeg sydd eisoes yn llawn pryder. Byddai canolfan newydd yn gyfle i wella mynediad at asesiadau amserol, lleihau rhwystrau daearyddol, a helpu i sicrhau bod cleifion yn cael yr ymchwiliadau sydd eu hangen arnynt cyn gynted â phosibl.

Gwyddom fod ymwybyddiaeth a diagnosis cynnar yn hanfodol er mwyn gwella canlyniadau triniaeth ar gyfer canser y prostad. Drwy sicrhau bod anghenion cymunedau gwledig wrth galon unrhyw strategaeth, gallwn wneud gwahaniaeth gwirioneddol i fywydau dynion ledled Cymru. Diolch yn fawr.

Nothing can ever prepare a person for receiving a cancer diagnosis, or indeed hearing about the diagnosis of a family member or a friend. It's one of the most terrifying things that anyone can be told, and it's a disease that touches, in effect, so many of us. Therefore, I welcome the Government's 10-year cancer strategy, because it's badly needed.

We're hearing today about why prostate cancer deserves proper attention within the national cancer strategy for Wales, and I'll be building on those points. But I also want to share with you a personal experience. I'd like to thank Paul and Janet for sharing their experiences also. My father was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2023. It was the most horrendous news to hear and it's been a very tough experience for our family, especially, at one point, we had an agonising wait of seven days to find out whether or not it had actually spread to his bones. I'm relieved to be able to tell the Siambr today that, three years on, he's still in remission. He doesn't like to have a fuss made of him, and he went through the first few weeks of this process alone because he didn't want to worry anybody. Thankfully, we're beginning to turn the page and move on from a very difficult chapter for us.

Early diagnosis and timely treatment were essential for my father, as they are for all men affected by prostate cancer here in Wales. Ensuring that our health service has the ability and the bandwidth to test and treat the thousands of people in Wales being diagnosed annually is crucial. The 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026' recorded around 2,700 prostate cancer diagnoses in Wales in 2024, as we've heard, and it increased 12 per cent on the previous year. And as we've heard a few times, but it does bear emphasis, just 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced prostate cancer received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Meanwhile, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment, with concerns that this may represent over-treatment, compared with the 7 per cent in England.

These figures raise serious questions about whether patients are consistently receiving the right treatment at the right time. However, the audit itself warns that problems with Welsh data quality and completeness mean that these findings must be interpreted with caution. Reliable data, modern systems and effective accountability are needed to deliver on its commitments. How can the Government properly assess performance, allocate resources or establish whether its policies are working if it cannot reliably measure what is happening? Cancer services need reliable systems that allow clinicians to access accurate information, co-ordinate treatment and identify delays. The Government must explain how it will ensure that the new platform delivers and how it will hold those responsible to account if it does not.

Llywydd, there is a wider lesson here about funding. In its evidence to the Senedd's Public Accounts and Public Administration Committee, the Wales Cancer Alliance argued that increased investment in cancer services has not translated into proportional improvements in performance or patient outcomes. It also highlighted that the national target requiring 75 per cent of patients to begin treatment within 62 days of their first suspicion of cancer has not been met across Wales as a whole, or by any individual health board, since August 2020. Let us consider that. Years of missed targets across every health board in Wales. That should concern every Member of this Senedd.

Of course, cancer services need adequate funding so that the NHS can afford modern diagnostic equipment, effective treatments, reliable digital infrastructure and properly staffed services. They all require investment. But we cannot simply assume that spending more money will automatically produce better outcomes. We need clear lines of responsibility, transparent performance measures and accountability when commitments are repeatedly missed. Prostate cancer must be included in the national strategy and that must mean measurable commitments on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment, reliable data and reducing unwarranted variation between health boards. And it must mean publishing progress, identifying failures and directing resources where they will make the greatest difference to patients. We should not accept a situation in which the Government cannot confidently establish what is happening to patients because its data is incomplete. The forthcoming strategy is an opportunity to put these failures right.

The Government must explicitly recognise prostate cancer as a priority and demonstrate how investment, digital transformation and service reform will work together to improve outcomes, because men diagnosed with prostate cancer do not need another promise, they need to know that their health is considered, understood and included. They need a health service that can provide the right treatment, at the right time, and demonstrate that it is getting better. That is what accountability looks like; that is what our motion will deliver. I therefore urge Members to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.

We need clear lines of responsibility, transparent performance measures and accountability when commitments are repeatedly missed. Prostate cancer must be included in the national strategy and that must mean measurable commitments on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment, reliable data and reducing unwarranted variation between health boards. And it must mean publishing progress, identifying failures and directing resources where they will make the greatest difference to patients. We should not accept a situation in which the Government cannot confidently establish what is happening to patients because its data is incomplete. The forthcoming strategy is an opportunity to put these failures right.

The Government must explicitly recognise prostate cancer as a priority and demonstrate how investment, digital transformation and service reform will work together to improve outcomes, because men diagnosed with prostate cancer do not need another promise, they need to know that their health is considered, understood and included. They need a health service that can provide the right treatment, at the right time, and demonstrate that it is getting better. That is what accountability looks like; that is what our motion will deliver. I therefore urge Members to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.

contributions.text_english: I call on the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care, Mabon ap Gwynfor.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal, Mabon ap Gwynfor.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this debate and to recognise the significance of prostate cancer for the large number of men, families and communities across Wales that it affects. Cancer is the leading cause of death in Wales, and prostate cancer is now one of the most common cancers diagnosed in men. Too many men still face delays in receiving a diagnosis, treatment and care, and too many families continue to experience uncertainty and anxiety whilst waiting for answers. We must do better.

Let me be clear. I understand the concerns that have prompted this debate. Members will be aware that cancer services in Wales are a major priority for me. In the field of cancer, performance regarding waiting times remains below the standards that we expect, and this includes parts of the urology pathway. Although NHS staff continue to work tirelessly under significant pressures, I am not satisfied with the current situation and no-one else in this Chamber should be satisfied either. Improving outcomes and experiences for everyone affected by cancer remains a key priority for this Government.

That is exactly why we are developing a new 10-year cancer strategy, the first of its kind since 2006. This work will set out a long-term strategic vision as well as national priorities to guide NHS planning and the transformation of cancer care over the next decade. Our objective is simple, but significant: that more people survive cancer, that more cancers are diagnosed early, that access to care does not depend on where one lives, and that people receive timely, personalised support throughout their cancer journey. This same objective must be delivered for men diagnosed with prostate cancer, just as it must for everyone affected by cancer in Wales.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch, Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r cyfle i ymateb i'r ddadl yma ac i gydnabod pwysigrwydd canser y prostad i'r nifer fawr o ddynion, teuluoedd a chymunedau ledled Cymru y mae e'n effeithio arnyn nhw. Canser yw prif achos marwolaethau yng Nghymru, ac mae canser y prostad bellach yn un o'r canserau mwyaf cyffredin y mae dynion yn cael diagnosis ohonyn nhw. Mae gormod o ddynion yn dal i wynebu oedi cyn cael diagnosis, triniaeth a gofal, ac mae gormod o deuluoedd yn dal i brofi ansicrwydd a phryder wrth aros am atebion. Mae'n rhaid i ni wneud yn well.

Gaf i fod yn glir? Dwi'n deall y pryderon sydd wedi ysgogi'r ddadl hon. Bydd yr Aelodau'n gwybod bod gwasanaethau canser yng Nghymru yn flaenoriaeth fawr i mi. Ym maes canser, mae'r perfformiad o ran amseroedd aros yn parhau i fod yn is na'r safonau rydyn ni'n eu disgwyl, ac mae hynny'n cynnwys rhannau o'r llwybr wroleg. Er bod staff yr NHS yn parhau i weithio'n ddiflino o dan bwysau sylweddol, dwi ddim yn fodlon efo ble rydyn ni heddiw a dylai neb arall yn y Siambr yma fod yn fodlon chwaith. Mae gwellau canlyniadau a phrofiadau i bawb sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yn parhau i fod yn flaenoriaeth allweddol i'r Llywodraeth yma.

Dyna'n union pam rydyn ni'n datblygu strategaeth ganser genedlaethol 10 mlynedd newydd, y cyntaf o'i bath ers 2006. Bydd y gwaith hwn yn gosod gweledigaeth strategol, hirdymor a blaenoriaethau cenedlaethol i lywio gwaith cynllunio'r NHS a thrawsnewid gofal canser dros y ddegawd nesaf. Mae'r nod yn syml ond yn arwyddocaol: bod mwy o bobl yn goroesi canser, bod mwy o ganserau yn cael diagnosis yn gynharach, nad yw mynediad at ofal yn dibynnu ar ble mae rhywun yn byw, a bod pobl yn cael cymorth amserol wedi'i bersonoli drwy gydol eu taith canser. Rhaid i'r un nod gael ei wireddu ar gyfer dynion sy'n cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad ag i bawb sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yng Nghymru.

contributions.text_english:
We intend to publish this strategy on World Cancer Day 2027, alongside a national cancer conference bringing together NHS leaders, clinicians, planners, partners, stakeholders and the third sector to share best practice and explore how our national priorities will be delivered across the next decade. Improving outcomes and experience to match the top quartile in Europe will require sustained effort, long-term commitment and honest recognition of the challenges we face. It's an ambition worthy of the people of Wales.

Cancer doesn't discriminate, and nor should we. Our intention is to support improvements across all cancer types and for people of all ages, backgrounds and communities. Importantly, the strategy will cover the entire cancer pathway, from prevention and screening through to diagnosis, treatment, recovery, survivorship and living well with and beyond cancer. The strategy will address the key challenges facing cancer services, while putting in place the enablers needed to deliver sustained improvement. That means looking at workforce, leadership, research, innovation, digital systems, infrastructure and service design alongside the quality and effectiveness of care itself. We also want to accelerate the adoption of new validated tests, technologies and recommended treatments, while strengthening accountability and transparency to drive improvement across Wales.

The strategy is being informed by one of the most extensive engagement exercises undertaken in cancer policy in Wales. A national call for evidence is currently gathering insights from stakeholders and the public, and I encourage all those with an interest in cancer services to contribute by the 31 October deadline. Alongside this, we are undertaking structured engagement with NHS organisations, professional bodies, key partners and the Wales Cancer Alliance.

To Paul's point on consultation, we are listening directly to people affected by cancer through patient engagement forums across Wales, co-ordinated by the Wales Cancer Alliance, to ensure that lived experience helps shape the priorities and actions needed to improve outcomes and experiences for the future. It's important that this process is allowed to conclude before decisions are taken on the final content of the strategy. The programme of engagement is still under way and the final priorities should be shaped by the views, expertise and lived experiences that we are gathering, rather than by predetermined conclusions.

The challenges facing the urology cancer pathway are not unique, but they bring into sharp focus the changes we must make if we are to improve cancer outcomes in Wales. These ambitions sit at the heart of the strategy. While the Welsh Government doesn't directly fund individual diagnostic tests, the strategy will set out how the NHS and its partners will work together to evaluate and introduce new diagnostic investigations for suspected cancer, including for prostate cancer.

contributions.text_english:
I recognise the anxiety that prostate cancer causes men and their families and why many would welcome screening. The Welsh Government follows the advice of the UK National Screening Committee and, at present, the committee does not recommend population screening for prostate cancer. However, it has recommended targeted screening for men between the ages of 45 and 61 who carry the BRCA2 gene and have a first-degree family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer. We have asked Public Health Wales to consider how this could be implemented in Wales.

It is already established clinical practice to offer active surveillance to patients with low-risk, localised prostate cancer, and we are monitoring rates of radical treatment through the national prostate cancer audit, to support improvements in care. GPs support shared decision-making with any man who is concerned about his risk of developing prostate cancer. We will work with the NHS to consider whether additional guidance is needed to support GPs in conducting these discussions.

I want to reassure Members that we are not waiting for the strategy to improve cancer data. Working with NHS organisations, we are already strengthening the availability, quality and use of data to lay the groundwork for success once the strategy is published. The Welsh Government has taken action and will continue to take action on the findings of the Audit Wales report, with the next phase of this work being driven by the strategy.

Llywydd, everyone in this Chamber shares the same broad objective: better outcomes, better experiences and better services for people affected by cancer in Wales. The national cancer strategy provides a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure that improvement, not only for men diagnosed with prostate cancer, but for everyone affected by cancer in Wales. That is the commitment driving this work, and I look forward to continuing that journey alongside patients, clinicians, charities and Members from across this Chamber. Thank you.
contributions.text_original:
Dwi'n cydnabod y pryder y mae canser y prostad yn achosi i ddynion a'u teuluoedd a pham y byddai llawer yn croesawu sgrinio. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn dilyn cyngor Pwyllgor Sgrinio Cenedlaethol y Deyrnas Gyfunol ac, ar hyn o bryd, dyw'r pwyllgor ddim yn argymell sgrinio poblogaeth ar gyfer canser y prostad. Er hynny, mae wedi argymell sgrinio wedi ei dargedu ar gyfer dynion rhwng 45 a 61 oed gyda'r gennyn BRCA2 a hanes teuluol gradd gyntaf o ganser y fron, yr ofari, y pancreas neu'r prostad. Rydyn ni wedi gofyn i Iechyd Cyhoeddus Cymru i ystyried sut y gallai hyn gael ei gyflawni yng Nghymru.

Mae'n arfer clinigol sefydledig eisoes i gleifion â chanser prostad lleol risg isel gael cynnig gwyliadwriaeth weithredol, ac rydyn ni'n monitro cyfraddau triniaeth radical drwy archwiliad cenedlaethol canser y prostad, i gefnogi gwelliannau mewn gofal. Mae meddygon teulu yn cefnogi gwneud penderfyniadau a rennir gydag unrhyw ddyn sy'n pryderu am ei risg o ddatblygu canser y prostad. Mi fyddwn ni'n gweithio gyda'r NHS i ystyried a oes angen canllawiau ychwanegol i gefnogi meddygon teulu i gynnal y trafodaethau hyn.

Dwi am roi sicrwydd i'r Aelodau nad ydyn ni'n aros i'r strategaeth i wella'r data canser. Gan weithio gyda sefydliadau'r NHS, rydyn ni eisoes yn cryfhau argaeledd, ansawdd a defnydd o'r data i osod amodau llwyddiant ar gyfer pan fydd y strategaeth yn cael ei chyhoeddi. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi gweithredu a bydd yn parhau i weithredu ar ganfyddiadau adroddiad Archwilio Cymru, gyda cham nesaf y gwaith hwn yn cael ei yrru gan y strategaeth.

Lywydd, mae pawb yn y Siambr yn rhannu'r un amcan eang: canlyniadau gwell, profiadau gwell a gwasanaethau gwell i bobl sy'n cael eu heffeithio gan ganser yng Nghymru. Mae'r strategaeth ganser genedlaethol yn darparu cyfle unwaith mewn cenhedlaeth i sicrhau'r gwelliant hwnnw, nid yn unig i ddynion sydd wedi cael diagnosis o ganser y prostad, ond i bawb y mae canser yn effeithio arnyn nhw yng Nghymru. Dyna'r ymrwymiad sy'n gyrru'r gwaith yma, a dwi'n edrych ymlaen at barhau â'r daith honno gyda chleifion, clinigwyr, elusennau ac Aelodau ar draws y Siambr hon. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I call on James Evans to respond to the debate.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf ar James Evans i ymateb i'r ddadl.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Llywydd. Can I just start by thanking all Members who've contributed to this debate, and also the Members who haven't contributed, but have actually sat through and listened to the debate? Because I think it's very nice that we've got a debate that galvanises the whole Chamber together. With all of the rumpus conversations that we have in here, it is quite nice to have some that do bring us together.

Ben opened the debate and, as you said, it's the most common cause of cancer in men: 2,500 people diagnosed and, as many people, like yourself, said, 640 of those sadly passing away—sadly too young, a lot of them as well, because the diagnosis wasn't caught early. And that only 54 per cent of men in Wales are accessing rapid treatment compared to 69 per cent in England, and that's something that should concern us all. I know the Cabinet Secretary highlighted—I'll come on to it later—about wanting to be the best in Europe, and I share that ambition, I'm sure we all do, but we need to put a laser focus on this area of cancer, because it is preventable if it is caught early enough.

You also raised the issue, as a lot of Members did, around data. It's something that a number of us who've been here a long time have always heard about cancer care, that the data just isn't there to inform decision making, so having more accurate data is very, very important. You also raised early screening. I know a number of Members raised that and that's something that's also very important. I know Prostate Cymru, for example, have gone out doing screening themselves on top of what the NHS is doing, and I think they've done an absolutely phenomenal job in finding a number of people across the country. Sometimes, those are men, as Members have talked about, who wouldn't naturally go and see a doctor, but they've had the sessions in rugby clubs, in gyms, for example, or down the local pub. So, it's actually been really good that they've rolled that out.

contributions.text_english:
And then Paul Davies—and thank you, Paul, for giving your own personal experience. You and I have talked a lot about this in the past, about your own personal experience of living with prostate cancer and the need to include it within that cancer strategy. That's something that we need to see, because it is the biggest killer of men in terms of cancer. We do need to make sure that it is included. You also raised the consultation, and we all need to see that, if consultations are had by Government, then the lived experience of people has to come through that consultation. It can't just be a tick-box exercise, as you raised. It actually needs to be considered and thought out. You also raised, and I know you've been a real champion for it, the national screening programme, when it was first discussed, and then the UK screening committee decided not to roll it out. I know that you were deeply disappointed about that, like a lot of others, and I'd just like to thank you for the work you've done, not just in this Parliament but in other Parliaments across the UK, to understand why that screening programme should be happening. You also talked about the advances in medical technology as well, and that men in Wales should have access to that technology and not outdated technology, and that was picked up a little bit by the Cabinet Minister.

Matthew, your commitment to cancer is unmatched, really, in this Chamber. You worked for a number of cancer charities before you even came to this place, and now you're chairman of the cross-party group on cancer. As someone who's been here before, I can say that that cross-party group does an awful lot of very good work, and it's informed a lot of the work of the cancer strategy over the years as well. So thank you for that. You talked about the excitement that there is amongst a number of third sector bodies and our charities about a cancer strategy, something that a number of us have been shouting about for a long time to have, so it's positive that that is coming forward. You raised the cancer pathways as well, and the delays that some people are experiencing through those pathways. I'm sure that's something that the Government will take heed of from your cross-party group as well, to see how we can improve, not just for prostate cancer but all cancers, to improve the pathways.

Ken Skates then opened with his support for the motion. I will give credit to the last Government—I don't give them credit much—for the new Velindre cancer care centre. [Interruption.] You can keep rolling your hand, Ken, but that's as far as it's going. And the work it did with the new cancer centre in Nevill Hall Hospital, the Velindre cancer centre there, and just how that's opened up so many more avenues to get care closer to home. I know the new Cabinet Minister has been there, and I've also been there in a personal capacity with a family member. I know just how important that centre is for so many people. He also talked about the strategy being evidence led by stuff that's going on at a UK level. I think that was really important to highlight.

Adrian, you raised your personal experience, like a lot of others did, with cancer, and that a lot of men don't seek out help. That's something that we do see across men's health across the country. A lot of people don't seek help with their own health problems, they just tend to deal with it quietly, and they don't go to the GP, and they don't go for tests. They just put it in a box somewhere and say, 'We won't talk about it'. I think that's really important. You also raised screening, and that the Welsh Government here should follow the advice as it develops. You also mentioned the support that can be given to patients and their families. I think that's really important.

Janet, thank you very much. I know about your personal experience. As you said, you and I have also talked about that a lot. You raised the point that 40 per cent of people are only caught at stage 3 and 4, which is an absolutely shocking statistic. It's coming well too late. That's probably one of the worst out of all the cancers, actually, except some of our rarer cancers. And you, like others, raised the screening programme as well. So I'm sure the Cabinet Minister has heard that, that a lot of us in this Chamber want that. 

Gareth, you said that cancer can affect everyone, and that men in deprived areas are actually more likely to get diagnosed later than those in more affluent areas, and that's something about health inequalities, which the health committee have looked at on a number of occasions, and how we do need to make sure there is that health equality across Wales, without detriment to anyone in any part of the country. And the postcode lottery—I don't know how many times the Cabinet Minister and I have both heard that before, and others in this Chamber, about how where you live across Wales can really decide how your outcomes and prognosis look, which is also shocking.

Elwyn Vaughan talked about people who live in rural areas. You and I and a lot of others share this as well, about the barriers we face to diagnosis. You talked about the farming community especially. Just raising something from my own community, Shearing is Caring raised an awful lot of money for Prostate Cymru, and that's about the farming community and getting men talking more about their health. You talked about the link with the Farming Community Network at Macmillan. I'll give a shameless plug now that I'm running a Hyrox race next week for Macmillan. So if anybody wants to sponsor me, I'm still taking sponsorship. You also talked about the Welsh Government's plan for the rapid diagnostic centre in Powys. I don't agree with Plaid Cymru on much, but I think this could actually be an area where I think it's really positive for the people who live in rural areas, especially in Powys.

Helen Jenner spoke about her own personal experience in her own family, and I think it's very important that people do talk about their personal experience. I think it's something that really shapes a parliamentary democracy, that we've got people in here who actually do understand the issue, that have got family going through it. You also said about your father not wanting to worry people. How many times have we heard that with men who are going through a diagnosis? ‘I'm just not going to tell my family.’ I've even known people who've passed away from cancer, and their own family don't even know why they've passed away until after, because it's been hidden from them, because they just don't want them to worry. So, making sure that men talk more is important. You also raised the data and the years of missed targets, and I think that's something that the Cabinet Minister needs to reflect on, and perhaps other Members in the Chamber who were in Government before, that actually this is a historical issue and a historical injustice that really does need to be sorted.

Then we moved on to our Cabinet Minister, and I do not pretend that you're not showing commitment to this area. I know you and I have worked closely in the past on cancer pathways and improving cancer care across Wales, so I don't doubt your commitment to that. As you said, cancer is the leading cause of death for men in Wales. It's still too high, and it needs to be addressed. As I said earlier, you talked about us wanting to be the best in Europe. I want us to be the best in the world when it comes to addressing cancer, especially prostate cancer. We're a small nation that spends an awful lot of our public money on the health service. For the money we put into it, we actually get a pretty poor return. Making that money work better to get better outcomes for the people of Wales, and especially men struggling with prostate cancer, is really important.

You also talked about the Welsh Government wanting new technologies and tests. I know there are new lung screening tests that are coming through, but there are new tests coming through as well for prostate cancer, and it would be really good if Wales could be a leading partner with charities and with the university institutions to develop these new technologies so people can get seen quicker.

You mentioned screening. Something I haven't heard before, actually, is the commitment from the Government—that they've asked Public Health Wales to look at the screening. It's perhaps not as wide as some Members want, but it's screening for perhaps a portion of the population who are at higher risk of getting prostate cancer.

The clock has now gone red, but I'm going to make another shameless plug. It's something that I've always been very keen on. It was something in our manifesto—a proper men's health strategy for Wales. I think that is something that is needed. Prostate cancer is a leading cause of death in men, but there are also a lot of other health areas that need to be addressed for our men across the country. We don't talk about it often enough, and I think that's something that the Government should take into serious consideration—a proper men's health strategy for Wales to address the health inequalities of a number of men across our country. I urge all Members to support our motion this afternoon. Diolch.

Gareth, you said that cancer can affect everyone, and that men in deprived areas are actually more likely to get diagnosed later than those in more affluent areas, and that's something about health inequalities, which the health committee have looked at on a number of occasions, and how we do need to make sure there is that health equality across Wales, without detriment to anyone in any part of the country. And the postcode lottery—I don't know how many times the Cabinet Minister and I have both heard that before, and others in this Chamber, about how where you live across Wales can really decide how your outcomes and prognosis look, which is also shocking.

Elwyn Vaughan talked about people who live in rural areas. You and I and a lot of others share this as well, about the barriers we face to diagnosis. You talked about the farming community especially. Just raising something from my own community, Shearing is Caring raised an awful lot of money for Prostate Cymru, and that's about the farming community and getting men talking more about their health. You talked about the link with the Farming Community Network at Macmillan. I'll give a shameless plug now that I'm running a Hyrox race next week for Macmillan. So if anybody wants to sponsor me, I'm still taking sponsorship. You also talked about the Welsh Government's plan for the rapid diagnostic centre in Powys. I don't agree with Plaid Cymru on much, but I think this could actually be an area where I think it's really positive for the people who live in rural areas, especially in Powys.

Helen Jenner spoke about her own personal experience in her own family, and I think it's very important that people do talk about their personal experience. I think it's something that really shapes a parliamentary democracy, that we've got people in here who actually do understand the issue, that have got family going through it. You also said about your father not wanting to worry people. How many times have we heard that with men who are going through a diagnosis? ‘I'm just not going to tell my family.’ I've even known people who've passed away from cancer, and their own family don't even know why they've passed away until after, because it's been hidden from them, because they just don't want them to worry. So, making sure that men talk more is important. You also raised the data and the years of missed targets, and I think that's something that the Cabinet Minister needs to reflect on, and perhaps other Members in the Chamber who were in Government before, that actually this is a historical issue and a historical injustice that really does need to be sorted.

Then we moved on to our Cabinet Minister, and I do not pretend that you're not showing commitment to this area. I know you and I have worked closely in the past on cancer pathways and improving cancer care across Wales, so I don't doubt your commitment to that. As you said, cancer is the leading cause of death for men in Wales. It's still too high, and it needs to be addressed. As I said earlier, you talked about us wanting to be the best in Europe. I want us to be the best in the world when it comes to addressing cancer, especially prostate cancer. We're a small nation that spends an awful lot of our public money on the health service. For the money we put into it, we actually get a pretty poor return. Making that money work better to get better outcomes for the people of Wales, and especially men struggling with prostate cancer, is really important.

You also talked about the Welsh Government wanting new technologies and tests. I know there are new lung screening tests that are coming through, but there are new tests coming through as well for prostate cancer, and it would be really good if Wales could be a leading partner with charities and with the university institutions to develop these new technologies so people can get seen quicker.

You mentioned screening. Something I haven't heard before, actually, is the commitment from the Government—that they've asked Public Health Wales to look at the screening. It's perhaps not as wide as some Members want, but it's screening for perhaps a portion of the population who are at higher risk of getting prostate cancer.

The clock has now gone red, but I'm going to make another shameless plug. It's something that I've always been very keen on. It was something in our manifesto—a proper men's health strategy for Wales. I think that is something that is needed. Prostate cancer is a leading cause of death in men, but there are also a lot of other health areas that need to be addressed for our men across the country. We don't talk about it often enough, and I think that's something that the Government should take into serious consideration—a proper men's health strategy for Wales to address the health inequalities of a number of men across our country. I urge all Members to support our motion this afternoon. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: The next item is the Welsh Labour debate, the M4 around Newport. I call on Jayne Bryant to move the motion.
contributions.text_original: Yr eitem nesaf yw dadl Llafur Cymru, yr M4 o amgylch Casnewydd. Galwaf ar Jayne Bryant i wneud y cynnig.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Newport is the city where I was born, grew up in, and live in, and I speak today as part of a group of Welsh Labour Senedd Members who know that this issue has gone unresolved for far too long. You do not need to live locally to know that the M4 around Newport is broken. Sadly, the Brynglas tunnels have become synonymous with gridlock. The vast majority of M4 traffic is not local, but the motorway was never designed to carry the weight of a modern national economy. This stretch of road is the main gateway to south and west Wales. It is critical to our industries, both established and emerging, our ports and our tourism, yet it bisects a growing city.

While congestion on this stretch of the M4 puts a handbrake on economic growth, it is the people of Newport who pay the price every single day with air pollution, which is a silent killer. Welsh Labour has laid this motion today because the people of Newport and connected communities in Cwmbran, Torfaen and Caerphilly have had enough. These communities are not some theoretical testbed, and the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government is toying with costly and ineffective proposals that will wreak havoc on people's lives.

Let's take the Government's serious proposals to close junctions. Fully closing High Cross and the eastbound slips at Malpas and Caerleon is not a quick fix. The Welsh Government's own report shows that it would only take up to 3 per cent of traffic off the motorway. Not everyone can work from home, and junction closures, whether temporary or permanent, would also affect public transport, access to healthcare, childcare and property prices. It's astounding that the Government is even considering this.

contributions.text_english:
When I asked the Deputy Minister how the remaining junctions at Tredegar Park and the Coldra would cope with the displaced traffic, he had no answer, because it wouldn't cope; it would just funnel toxic air and gridlock into residential streets. That's why, Llywydd, we're asking that this Senedd charts a new course today. Welsh Labour believes that local people should be at the heart of this new Government's approach to the M4 around Newport. Successive Governments—the Conservatives before devolution, a Plaid Cymru Minister in 2009, and Welsh Labour Governments—have all failed to resolve this challenge.

When the independent planning inspector examined the black route nearly a decade ago, he concluded there was a compelling case on economic and human grounds to build the relief road. This was a comprehensive and lengthy process that engaged with communities, including public hearings, and incorporated detailed plans to enhance and protect the environment.

Major infrastructure done right can enhance, rather than destroy, our natural environment. Indeed, the wonderful and much-loved Newport wetlands nature reserve was established to compensate for habitat lost during the construction of the Cardiff Bay barrage. Many of us across the Labour movement have known for a long time how vital a relief road is, and that's why I could not vote to scrap it in this Chamber in 2019. Today, as a party, Welsh Labour is clear: while the decision to reject the inspector's recommendations may have been understandable on narrow financial grounds, it has left the issue unresolved. Innovative funding models should have been explored, like public-private partnerships, regional borrowing by local authorities supported by the Welsh Government, or land value capture, rather than rejecting it outright.

Let's be clear: these decisions are difficult, and for too long the M4 has been put in the 'too difficult' box. The Plaid Cymru Welsh Government's recent report from Arup states, on page 3:

'None of the options or any combination of options considered as part of this review would fully resolve the M4 problem.'

If the Government is serious about solving this issue, why on earth has the Government remained wedded to their belief that a new relief road is out of scope? It seems Plaid Cymru is perfectly content to build roads and bridges elsewhere in Wales, but not when it comes to solving the M4 around Newport.

In addition to junction closures, the review identifies the options of widening the Brynglas tunnels, combined with the ineffective interventions on local roads, and the so-called blue route is back on the table, which would take traffic closer to communities like Liswerry, Ringland, Pill and Duffryn. The blue route might seem like an option for people who don't live in the area, but with thousands of homes built at Glan Llyn and Milton Park since the initial option was proposed, and thousands more being built, turning what's known as the SDR, the southern distributor road, into a quasi motorway is completely divorced from reality. Everyone knows locally how busy that road is.

The option of widening the Brynglas tunnels cannot be regarded in a credible way. The report states that widening the tunnels is not expected to reduce traffic on the M4 as it involves online works and does not create an alternative route elsewhere. The two lanes start back before the tunnels, and whilst we want the traffic to flow better, it will not tackle the air pollution problem. And we must not forget what the disruption to local homes and businesses above and next to the motorway will be.

Plaid Cymru's public transport plans are not new. They were in progress before this Government. The Burns train stations and better public transport are vital. Welsh Labour championed them, and we need them to be delivered. And while we're glad to see Magor and Undy and Cardiff parkway stations progress, these stations alone will not solve congestion at the Brynglas tunnels. We need to see the Plaid Cymru Government act with urgency to deliver the stations in Newport at Somerton, Liswerry and Tredegar Park. Public transport must be regular, reliable and affordable for people to use it. I say this as someone who's long campaigned for the Ebbw Vale to Newport line and commuters on that line still face unacceptable cancellations and overcrowding. Public transport and road infrastructure must meet the needs of a growing population, and Newport is the faster-growing city with the youngest population in Wales. 

So, let's be clear: a new relief road would not be the old black route. Houses and schools have been built, people have moved to the area and the bar for environmental delivery has rightly risen following the roads review. What we need now is an appropriate, modern relief road that acts as a template for responsible infrastructure. Imagine a road built with the lowest possible embedded carbon and strong site of special scientific interest protections.

The way forward should not be shaped by Ministers lecturing, but by people affected in and around Newport. Welsh Labour believes we should empower those local leaders across councils and the south-east Wales capital region, building on the collaborative Burns model, to develop an appropriate relief road and a creative multisource funding package supported by Welsh Government. Contrary to what we've seen so far, the Government must remember that the people of Newport and south-east Wales aren't just data points in a transport policy document, they're individuals, families and businesses. So, I urge the Senedd to back our motion today. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. This is the first time I rise in this Chamber having to admit that I'm in awe of the Labour Party—for the barefaced cheek it takes to bring this motion to the floor of the Senedd, having cancelled the previous scheme in 2019. Let us not forget that, in Government, they spent £135 million not to build the very thing they are now demanding of Plaid Cymru today. Public money spent on a road that they cancelled, and I note that the leader of the Labour group was the transport Minister at the time. Labour cannot expect people to forget simply because they are now sitting on the opposition benches. Indeed, the public have not forgotten. For all of their online sham protests, I would suggest they read the comments from the public on their social media accounts.

Burnham's branch office is entitled to argue for a different road, but it owes the people who paid for the last scheme an explanation of what it would do differently this time. Its motion gives us no way of knowing which road it means or how it would be funded. Labour needs to explain what its motion would add to the work Ministers have already announced. The Government has already accepted that road and engineering improvements are needed around Newport. It has announced an 18-month study to select a third—

contributions.text_english:
—road option alongside improvements to the existing motorway and public transport. The study needs to lead to a decision that Ministers can fund and carry through. I also expect progress on the existing network while this work takes place. People should be able to see what is being delivered within those 18 months and when they can expect to improve their journeys.

For people in Casnewydd Islwyn, the roads that lead to the M4 matter as much as the motorway itself. Changes at the Newport junction could affect journeys from the Valleys and put more traffic through residential areas. The Arup review warns that traffic could be displaced around Malpas, High Cross and Ridgeway, which affects noise and air quality. A proposal could therefore improve the flow of traffic on the motorway while making some local journeys worse. We need to know where that traffic would go and what the consequences would be for the people living around those routes. The Government has said that no decision to implement junction closures has been taken. It is committed to further traffic modelling before any decisions are made. I support the decision and look forward to seeing the updated data before the Government makes any final decision.

Based on the evidence, I am supporting the amendment and urge Members to do the same. The electorate expect us to act in this Chamber on their behalf, and not descend into pantomime politics by pretending that the easy solution exists to solve complex problems. This is how we end up here in the first place.

contributions.text_english:
Oh, have I waited for this one. [Laughter.] Now, we, Reform, will of course support the motion today. It's pretty clear, though, that it's an obvious attempt to cut the strings of Labour's puppet master, Mark Drakeford. Now, we welcome the decision and we congratulate Welsh Labour on taking 27 years to come to the same conclusion that it took us exactly one minute to make. And that one minute was 59 seconds too long, in my opinion.

Now, every day, tens of thousands of motorists sit in queues on the M4. Businesses lose money, workers lose time and families spend more of their lives sitting in traffic than sitting at home with loved ones. And after literally decades of promises, what have they been given? More congestion, more excuses and absolutely no solution. The very politicians responsible for this failure are trying to convince the people of Wales that they have the answer.

Let's start with Labour. Twenty-seven years in Government. Twenty-seven years to deliver a solution to the most important transport problem in recent Welsh history. One hundred and fifty million pounds of taxpayers' money spent on plans, consultations and reviews. And what did the people of Wales receive for that substantial investment? Nothing. Perhaps a few sheets of paper. Mark Drakeford cancelled the M4 relief road, abandoning a project that would have made a real difference. And who was the Government Minister at the time? A gentleman called Ken Skates. [Interruption.] Good timing, sir.

Not at all. Reform has been very clear: we will build the M4 relief road. So, that's our position. That's the one we're currently going down, and it will not be a toll road. It will be paid for out of the sovereign wealth fund from the UK Government. Thank you very much.

But continuing, did you stand up and challenge the decision? No. Did you stand up and fight for businesses, commuters and families who desperately need that road? No. You defended the very Government that cancelled it. Now Labour wants to lecture this Chamber about the importance of building a relief road. It is quite funny. The same party that killed the project want to take credit for bringing it back to life. So, here's my question to Labour: if the M4 relief road is so desperately needed today, why didn't you build it when you were in power? The truth is, Labour hasn't changed. They've discovered the political consequences of ignoring it. And now, frightened of losing even more support to Reform UK, they're desperately trying to distance themselves from the anti-motorist legacy of Mark Drakeford and Lee Waters. But the people of Wales won't forget, and neither will we.

So, let me now turn to Plaid Cymru, a party that promised change but are determined to continue the same failed approach. The black route has apparently been ruled out. But good news, stranded motorists, we've been offered more studies, more assessments and even more delays, and astonishingly, proposals to close motorway junctions and divert traffic onto local roads in Newport and the surrounding towns. Now, think about that for a moment. Their answer to congestion on the M4 is to move that congestion into the communities of Newport. How on earth is that supposed to improve the lives of the people we represent?

Now, thanks to resurfaced tweets, we have greater clarity on the mind behind the junction closures. In 2019, the Minister stated he wanted to discourage car use on the M4 because of the climate emergency, and even went so far as to seriously suggest that the way to solve the M4 issue was that workers in Wales, in the public sector, should work a day fewer a week. Now, they call us climate conspiracy theorists, of course, yet they're the ones blocking the relief road as part of their net-zero agenda. That is their design: punish motorists and push them onto public transport. And if you don't believe me, just take a look at the transport Minister's own words for it. 

Today is about setting the record straight. Labour had the opportunity to build the road and cancelled it. Plaid Cymru had the opportunity to deliver a solution and is ruling out the very project that would provide one. Now, one party cancelled it, the other refuses to build it, but we all know it was the constant pressure of Reform, our historic election result and our grass-roots campaign that has got us here today. The people of Wales already know how they're going to get this M4 road delivered, and that is with a Reform UK Government.

They've discovered the political consequences of ignoring it. And now, frightened of losing even more support to Reform UK, they're desperately trying to distance themselves from the anti-motorist legacy of Mark Drakeford and Lee Waters. But the people of Wales won't forget, and neither will we.

So, let me now turn to Plaid Cymru, a party that promised change but are determined to continue the same failed approach. The black route has apparently been ruled out. But good news, stranded motorists, we've been offered more studies, more assessments and even more delays, and astonishingly, proposals to close motorway junctions and divert traffic onto local roads in Newport and the surrounding towns. Now, think about that for a moment. Their answer to congestion on the M4 is to move that congestion into the communities of Newport. How on earth is that supposed to improve the lives of the people we represent?

Now, thanks to resurfaced tweets, we have greater clarity on the mind behind the junction closures. In 2019, the Minister stated he wanted to discourage car use on the M4 because of the climate emergency, and even went so far as to seriously suggest that the way to solve the M4 issue was that workers in Wales, in the public sector, should work a day fewer a week. Now, they call us climate conspiracy theorists, of course, yet they're the ones blocking the relief road as part of their net-zero agenda. That is their design: punish motorists and push them onto public transport. And if you don't believe me, just take a look at the transport Minister's own words for it. 

Today is about setting the record straight. Labour had the opportunity to build the road and cancelled it. Plaid Cymru had the opportunity to deliver a solution and is ruling out the very project that would provide one. Now, one party cancelled it, the other refuses to build it, but we all know it was the constant pressure of Reform, our historic election result and our grass-roots campaign that has got us here today. The people of Wales already know how they're going to get this M4 road delivered, and that is with a Reform UK Government.

I'm delighted to support this Labour motion today. The gridlock of traffic congestion on the M4 around Newport has been a national embarrassment for over 30 years. The consequences of all Senedd parties being unable to agree a way forward for the M4 around Newport is ever-rising levels of congestion and pollution in Newport, and the connected Valleys communities north of the M4 in Torfaen and Caerphilly. The Confederation of British Industry and local businesses have been advising for years that the gridlock on the M4 is a brake on economic growth and prosperity for communities along the whole of the M4 corridor in south Wales.

One of the key lessons that this Welsh Labour group takes from its losses in the Senedd elections in May is that we must do more for people today. This is why we must speak out against what Plaid Cymru is proposing to visit on the people of Newport and the south-east Wales Valleys through its proposals on the M4 around Newport review.

Every party in this Chamber will, of course, be keen to support the public transport proposals developed under the last Labour Government for more rail services on the south Wales main line, and this will eventually offer many commuters a rail-based public transport option. And bus and active travel solutions also have a role to play. But the problem is that these public transport interventions will only take 7 per cent of traffic off the M4 on completion, and that's after six to seven years of construction. This is less than a third of the 25 per cent or more of traffic that needs to be diverted from the M4 around Newport.

The last Welsh Labour Government commissioned a series of major road studies in readiness for a new Government, looking at the M4 and also the A55 and the A494 corridors in particular. This work under Labour enabled the Minister to make his announcements on the Menai bridge and the M4 in recent weeks.

The most effective intervention for the M4 would be a relief road. It would meet the key criteria of reducing congestion and thereby pollution made worse by stationary and crawl-speed traffic, and improve resilience, providing an alternative route to the M4 in case of accidents. The other options seemingly championed by the Minister are not fit for purpose. For a 3 per cent reduction in traffic on the M4, junction closures will cause congestion mayhem, pollution and economic harm in and around Newport.

Widening the Brynglas tunnels is a surprising option, dismissed by all previous reviews. The A48 and blue route are not credible either. They would destroy health and wealth in Newport, and the proposals will face great challenges from new housing and the urban context. Looking at this Welsh Government's half-baked review options, it would need to implement a combination of these that it sets out, and the cost of these combinations would exceed £3 billion, and take nearly 30 years as the works on them cannot be done concurrently. All this in the context of a Government with an annual borrowing limit of £165 million, and a total borrowing cap of £1.1 billion.

The Welsh Government cannot deliver an M4 solution on its own. It will need partners prepared to pool financial resources, subject to fit-for-purpose options being agreed. It's time to get real. The proposed junction closures must be ruled out for the benefit of the people of Newport. The only option that delivers reduced congestion, better environmental outcomes by keeping traffic moving and releasing the chokehold of the M4 on the economy is a relief road. We need local leaders empowered to lead the planning of a new relief road for the M4—a partnership of the Welsh Government and local authorities able to consider innovative funding and fully grounded in engagement with the community. Diolch, Lywydd.

I'm not going to lie, I do feel like I've walked into the twilight zone today with this particular debate happening. As someone who was born and raised in Newport, I have to say on behalf of myself, as well as all the residents, commuters and businesses, that Newport has been forced to suffer for years with unacceptable traffic chaos, especially when it comes to the M4. This vital stretch of road is regularly clogged, with hotspots like the Brynglas tunnels often gridlocked. Not only does this affect residents going about their daily lives, it has a major impact on visitors and seriously damages our economic prosperity. Something absolutely needs to be done to tackle the M4's never-ending problems. By closing junctions 26, 27 and 25, it's simply not going to be the answer to everyone's prayers. Now, instead of providing any sort of relief, as the Government claims, junction closures will consign Newport to even more misery. Traffic won't magically disappear when these junctions close, it will just be moved to our city's A-roads and residential streets, creating more problems. 

And then there's the price tag. The Government is looking at spending £14 million on closing these three junctions for a measly 3 per cent expected drop in traffic on the M4. Do you really think that's worth it? That £14 million could go towards building an M4 relief road—something that would actually improve the traffic problems across and around Newport. Since news of the junction closure plans came to light, the public uproar in Newport and its surrounding communities has been loud and clear. They do not want to see Plaid politicians spending £14 million on a scheme that is going to make their lives a living misery. And I don't blame them one bit. Residents have been contacting me in their droves over the past few weeks to highlight the problems junction closures will cause for them, and I want to share some of their stories with all of you here in the Chamber today. These are the words of one of my constituents: 'If the Welsh Government continues to pursue these oppressive and poorly thought out policies, it makes me seriously question my future here and I am genuinely considering moving my family and my taxes across the border to England. I know I'm not alone in giving this serious thought.' 

Another constituent told me, 'The closure of these junctions will not only cause chaos on the roads in and around Newport, it will create problems on the roads leading down to the two valleys, which are already congested. It will cause businesses to lose valuable custom, increase their fuel costs and make deliveries a logistical nightmare. It will make commutes longer, more time consuming and more costly.' Another bewildered constituent said, 'Newport residents should not have to pay the price for years of inadequate transport planning and infrastructure investment. Stopping the M4 relief road was, in my view, a major failure in planning towards the future of Wales. Closing M4 junctions is not a solution, it is simply going to move the problem elsewhere. Has anyone seriously considered what the consequences will be for local residents, businesses, commuters and emergency services? We need proper infrastructure investment and long-term thinking. We need additional road capacity and better connectivity across south-east Wales towards England, not measures that make existing congestion even worse. Newport residents deserve better, Wales deserves better.'

Now, that's just a snapshot of the feeling amongst my constituents. I could stand here, genuinely, all afternoon and read you e-mail after e-mail, but I appreciate there's simply not enough time. However, I would be more than happy to share these with the Deputy Minister for Transport so he can get a better understanding of how his plans have gone down in communities across my constituency. Taking feedback and views from residents, businesses and key stakeholders is paramount, Presiding Officer, and whilst I believe these junction closures should be categorically ruled out, if this Government is hell bent on pushing this piece of work through, then there must be a serious consultation. Last week, I raised this point with the Welsh Government, and to say I was disappointed by the response would be an understatement. The Government keeps saying it will engage with communities in Newport about the junction plans, but we haven't heard to date one time—one time alone—how they will be doing this or when this piece of work will indeed be commencing. So, I'm going to try again, and I hope that the Deputy Minister will address these points when he responds to this debate later on.

These are genuine concerns about the impact junction closures will have on emergency services and accessing medical care. One constituent that I spoke to, who has a child with medically complex needs, is sincerely fearful of the potential extra delay she will face as a result of more traffic when getting her daughter to the Grange hospital. The Gwent police and crime commissioner, Jane Mudd, has also sounded the alarm over junction closures, saying it runs the risk of slowing down emergency response times. Not only that, but Malpas fire station is just a stone's throw away from junction 26, which has been earmarked for partial closure. Has the Welsh Government taken this into account? Has the Minister had serious discussions with Gwent Police, the ambulance service, Newport City Council and Aneurin Bevan University Health Board? If so, what has their feedback been so far?

My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I will absolutely be supporting Labour's motion this afternoon, calling for the M4 junction closures to be ruled out and a relief road to be built. But it would be very much remiss of me not to point out the sheer hypocrisy of the Labour Party when it comes to this issue. Let's not all forget, Labour were in power here for 27 years before being turfed out in May. You had more than a quarter of a century to do something to solve the M4 problem, but you did nothing. Labour spent more than £100 million of taxpayers' money on research and development for the M4 relief road, including buying a caravan park, everybody, only for the former First Minister, Mark Drakeford, to scrap the project. And let's not forget that the Conservative Prime Minister, David Cameron, offered your Labour Welsh Government the money to build the relief road, but it was rejected. Where was the outcry from Newport Labour politicians then? Everyone sat there in silence. By not acting when you were in Government, you are equally to blame that these junction closure plans—

Thank you, Llywydd. Obviously, the subject matter of this debate actually predates devolution. It goes all the way back to the early 1990s, to the John Major Government, when there was failure to deliver back then. And of course, some in the Chamber were once Tories failing to deliver. But if we then move to 2019, of course, the planning inspector gave support to the proposed M4 relief lanes promoted through the public inquiry. But the decision made in 2019 not to go ahead with the relief lanes was for very good reason. The cost at the time, at a period of terrible uncertainty, was prohibitive. It was too much money at the time, with too few options available to pay for it. Costs, and estimated costs, had been rising during the course of development and reached £1.4 billion. At the time, we were planning for a no-deal Brexit, with funds being—[Interruption.]—this is a fact—with funds being prepared to help businesses, to help farmers, to help public services with the chaos that would have come. Instead, COVID came and wiped out our budgets.

Now, I'm proud of the work that Lord Burns and the South East Wales Transport Commission did, as well as having secured the money for the south Wales relief line stations, including Cardiff Parkway. And I'm proud that we delivered the south Wales metro. But we now know for sure, because of the independent expert resilience study published this month, that if we wish to solve the problem of M4 congestion through Newport, no single or combined package of solutions will do.

Now, it's worth Members knowing that 25 million km—25 million km—of new road will be built around the world between now and 2050. The M4 black route would have amounted to less than one-millionth of that amount. And that doesn't relieve us of our responsibilities to meet net-zero targets and to promote biodiversity, but it does show that even the most environmentally sensitive nations are building roads. The key is building better, and in suitable places, rather than in not building at all. Ecologists from around the world, from Cairns to Cambridge, are now agreeing that, built in the right way, roads can actually help nature and the environment. And this is why our motion states that a relief road must be appropriate. The policy and consenting environment has changed substantially since 2019, and a relief road would rightly have to meet far more stretching environmental challenges. Revising existing plans would provide an opportunity to include dedicated bus rapid transport and active travel routes along the M4. That would save more than £300 million from the proposed stand-alone bus rapid transport road from Newport to Cardiff. It could also be used as a global exemplar in the use of low-carbon materials, modular construction techniques, and world-leading environmental benefits. The world is building 25 million km of new road. In my view, we must help them build better by leading on sustainable infrastructure.

Now, pages 27-29 of the independent report published this month show how economic growth and investment in road transport infrastructure are tightly coupled together—this is a fact—where an economy is weighted towards manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, construction, automotive and aerospace sectors, the very sectors that drive the future of the Welsh economy. So, whether we like it or not, unless the economy of Wales is changed dramatically and fast, its future growth or contraction is inextricably linked to road transport. Where we are today is a world away from 2019. We have greater economic stability—
