Diolch, Lywydd. In his resignation statement to the Senedd in 2024, the former First Minister, Mark Drakeford, reflected on his first major decision, which was to not proceed with the M4 relief road. He said,

'The easy decision would have been to say, "Go ahead". The powerful voices in Wales were lined up in support of it. My decision, having spent many, many days reading and thinking about it, was that that was not in the long-term interests of Wales.' 

Welsh Labour were also responsible for passing our groundbreaking Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 and many other world-leading initiatives. I guess that's why I find this motion quite sad. The black route is no longer an option; the land is no longer available. But even if it were an option, concreting over the Gwent levels is an option that no serious Government or Parliament could consider, given the environmental devastation it would cause. There is no magic green floating motorway. But I do agree that doing nothing is not an option.

The most important part of the solution to the M4 congestion is further investment in public transport to encourage more drivers to leave their cars at home and take a train or a bus. So, I really welcome the announcement that the new railway stations recommended—[Interruption.]—no, it's all right—by the Burns commission will be brought forward and delivered sooner than originally planned. Increasing accessibility and the number of services on the main line between Cardiff and Severn Tunnel Junction will be incredibly valuable for people across the region, and I look forward to using them myself in the not-too-distant future.

Now, looking at the Government's proposals, lorries travelling between the north of England and west Wales are currently inhibited from using the Heads of the Valleys road due to the lack of rest facilities, which they are, of course, legally required to use. The Government's proposal to invest in rest facilities is common sense, cost-effective, and can remove substantial freight traffic from the M4.

Diolch.

On paper, we're debating the M4 relief road, but scratch the surface of this debate and it's about something else entirely: political credibility, consistency and a spectacular example of political opportunism. When I saw this debate on the agenda, I wondered whether the scriptwriters from The Thick of It had taken over the Labour group, because, Llywydd, you can't make this up. Do Labour Members think we've forgotten who cancelled the M4 relief road?

Let's remind ourselves of the fact that a Labour Government spent over £100 million developing the plans and buying land along the route. A Labour Government commissioned an expensive public inquiry. A Labour Government cancelled the project in June 2019. As we've heard, we know who the transport Minister at the time was—none other than the Labour leader himself. But we don't need to go back seven years to find a contradiction. Seven months will do. In March, speaking as the transport Secretary, he told us this in this Chamber, and I quote:

'When it comes to the M4, this debate has been and gone, and we are ploughing ahead with hugely ambitious plans to improve connectivity by public transport, sustainable connectivity. The cost of building an M4 relief road right now would be enormous, and it does need to be a costed proposition, I believe, and it can't be, whether it's from yourselves or the Conservatives, a back-of-the-fag-packet proposal.'

Seven months ago, Llywydd. So what's changed? Has the cost come down? Is there new evidence, or is the scheme that was unaffordable in Government—

If we were starting from scratch now, the M4 would stretch from the bridge over the Severn estuary to Fishguard. The motorway would be three lanes wide for the whole of its length. There would be fewer junctions, and they would be further apart. It was built piecemeal. But we're not starting from scratch, are we? So, what do we intend to do? It's not just around the Brynglas tunnels that we have problems on the M4. For those of us coming in from the west, we have problems around Port Talbot. We have problems around the junction going on to the Heads of Valleys, and then we all join—and I'm sure, if you're driving here, Presiding Officer, you do—coming off the M4 at junction 33. We have all these traffic jams that affect us. So, I'm asking the Welsh Government: why do we always think we're unique? Why do we think that no other country has ever dealt with these sorts of problems? It's happening all the time.

Can I mention what's happened in Italy? There's a technique known as the Nazzano method, which allows tunnels to be widened while traffic continues to run through them. Originally developed and successfully implemented in Italy, the Nazzano method allows an existing tunnel to be widened while remaining open to traffic. This technique involves constructing a new, larger tunnel shell around the existing bore, maintaining traffic flows through the works, and then removing the old lining once the new structure is complete. This method has been used internationally on busy motorway tunnels where closure was not feasible, and it has consistently delivered increased capacity. Can I urge the Welsh Government to give some serious thought to that?

And it's not just that, is it? [Interruption.] Certainly.

Diolch, Lywydd. I have been asked to shorten this debate, so I'll take no interventions, please, because I'm going to have to cut out as I go, because some people like to talk more than they should need to. [Laughter.]

For more than 30 years, the Welsh Government has wrestled with M4 congestion around Newport, yet we are still here facing the same question today: the problem at Brynglas. The Welsh Government review considers several options, but says none alone or combined would fully resolve the M4 problem.

Despite previous Governments spending £136.5 million already, the review estimates currently that around 25 per cent of peak-time traffic would need to be removed to avoid congestion unless road capacity is increased. Yet the package considered could only achieve 17 per cent, with planning to fail instead of planning to fix things. Take the proposed junction changes: £14 million could be spent closing junctions 27, 26, 25 for an estimated 3 per cent reduction. These are direct questions from residents. So, where does that traffic go? How much moves into Newport local roads? Which communities take that additional traffic? What happens to congestions on routes such as Queensway and the southern distributor road? And what happens to the journey times for drivers that live around those junctions?

These questions matter even more with the housing growth that is coming to the area. Research supplied to me already estimates between 7,100 and 7,400 homes have been built across the four former Gwent authorities since 2019. Most of the councils are now sending out their regional development plans. Newport plans just shy of 400 homes; Monmouth to provide between 5,400 and 6,200 homes. Caerphilly identifies 7,400 new homes by 2035. Torfaen and Blaenau Gwent are still developing theirs, so their numbers will be added at a later date.

Now, Minister, not every home puts another car on the M4, but more homes mean more people, more journeys in the long run. The review says that benefits are uncertain because of future growth and that latent demand could take up capacity over time. It also says that no new transport modelling was undertaken in the review. So, Minister, how long will these proposals work? How quickly could the growing demand wipe out the 3 per cent reduction? Where is the modelling that includes thousands of new homes? The review reflects a greater emphasis on sustainable travel and carbon reduction, but the Minister must answer this: is the primary objective to solve the M4 capacity problem or to get people out of their cars in the pursuit of wider net-zero objectives? They are not necessarily the same thing. The review says public transport improvements will help, but to a limited extent.

I'm going to have to skip over some, because I'm aware you want me to keep the time down.

When Welsh Labour, the Government, cancelled the black route, it was estimated that the cost at the time was £1.4 billion. I'm not suggesting that £1.4 billion would still be today's price, but it would need recalculating. That is precisely the point—why exclude it before the calculation is made? The review says a new motorway was excluded primarily because of likely affordability and environmental and planning challenges. Surely, those must be assessed and compared so that we can compare apples with apples.

So, why not give us today's cost of the black route? Give us the full cost of the alternative packages. Show us the congestion reduction that each would achieve. Show us the additional capacity that each would provide. Include future housing growth in every model. And then tell us how long each option's benefits are expected to last. Show us where the displaced traffic goes. Show us what happens to the 1,000 more homes built. Show us what every option costs and delivers, and give the black route the same test. If the Government alternative provides the best long-term answer, let the evidence demonstrate it. But if it costs more, delivers less, and leaves Newport with a capacity problem, the black route should be put back on the table.

Finally, Minister, a few weeks ago, when we discussed the M4 before, I asked you if you would listen to the residents of Newport. Two petitions have been raised: one by Labour, which has achieved 5,846 signatures as of yesterday morning, and one sponsored by Reform Members, which has reached 13,713. Will you now listen to their voices?

The motion calls for a relief road. If opposition Members are serious about solving this issue, they need to answer some basic questions. What road? On what routes? Through what planning and consenting process? And how quickly could it be realistically delivered? No opposition—[Interruption.] I'm not taking—. You've tried a lot, Ken. No opposition Member has brought forward workable answers to these questions today, but they are exactly the questions a responsible Government must answer before committing to major infrastructure. That is why the announcement I made on 6 October was important. We took a clear strategic decision that road-based and engineering solutions must form part of the long-term answer to congestion on the M4 around Newport.

There is no debate about whether roads should form part of the solution. We have accepted that they should. The task now is to identify the right solution and establish a credible route to delivery. That is why the centrepiece of our approach is an 18-month study of engineering, technical and appraisal work. This is not—[Interruption.] No, Mike. This is not another exercise in deciding whether there is a problem or whether action is needed. Those questions have already been answered. The purpose of this work is to identify the preferred road and engineering solution, assess its deliverability, understand its impacts and establish a realistic pathway to implementation. In short, it is about moving from recognising the problem to delivering the solution. The motion claims that our response is inadequate. What is inadequate is calling for a relief road without identifying which road is being proposed, whether it remains deliverable and how it would actually be taken forward.

The motion also calls on the Government to rule out junction closures. I understand why this issue has generated debate, but I'd like to correct some of the commentary surrounding it, much of it coming from the opposition benches, including from Natasha's contribution earlier. The report published alongside my statement does not recommend the closure of the three junctions. It identifies options for further investigation, including the closure of junction 27 at High Cross and restrictions to east-facing slips at junctions 25 and 26. Those are not Government decisions, they are options for investigation. The purpose of the work now under way is to determine whether any form of junction restriction could contribute to a wider solution and, if so, under what circumstances. That means understanding the impacts on communities, businesses, local roads and road users, alongside any potential benefits for motorway performance and resilience.

This is a question we've been asked a lot in this, about the evidence. One of the things that the report has done—. We've shared that report in full sight of everyone, including the public. We will maintain that level of transparency throughout this process and share it as we go. It means engagement with local authorities, businesses, communities and other stakeholders. And it means following the evidence. If the evidence shows an option will not deliver the outcomes required, it will not be taken forward. In short, we have not announced a programme of junction closures. What we have announced is further technical work to assess whether junction restrictions should form part of a wider solution to improve the operation and resilience of the M4 around Newport.

Llywydd, the most important decision that I announced on 6 October was that a significant road and engineering intervention is required, and that we should begin the detailed work necessary to identify it. This is the fundamental shift this Government has made, but critically, while that long-term solution is developed, we are also acting now. Where previous Labour transport Ministers neglected it, we are investing in the resilience and reliability as a critical national asset. We are progressing maintenance and renewal work on key infrastructure that, to be frank, the previous Government could and should have undertaken, and it didn't.

We are improving freight movement across the region, and we are supporting improvements to rail and bus connectivity—improvements that the previous Government championed, but which Labour has dropped completely from this motion. The motion calls for a relief road. If opposition Members are serious about solving this issue, they need to answer some basic questions. What road? On what routes? Through what planning and consenting process? And how quickly could it be realistically delivered? No opposition—[Interruption.] I'm not taking—. You've tried a lot, Ken. No opposition Member has brought forward workable answers to these questions today, but they are exactly the questions a responsible Government must answer before committing to major infrastructure. That is why the announcement I made on 6 October was important. We took a clear strategic decision that road-based and engineering solutions must form part of the long-term answer to congestion on the M4 around Newport.

There is no debate about whether roads should form part of the solution. We have accepted that they should. The task now is to identify the right solution and establish a credible route to delivery. That is why the centrepiece of our approach is an 18-month study of engineering, technical and appraisal work. This is not—[Interruption.] No, Mike. This is not another exercise in deciding whether there is a problem or whether action is needed. Those questions have already been answered. The purpose of this work is to identify the preferred road and engineering solution, assess its deliverability, understand its impacts and establish a realistic pathway to implementation. In short, it is about moving from recognising the problem to delivering the solution. The motion claims that our response is inadequate. What is inadequate is calling for a relief road without identifying which road is being proposed, whether it remains deliverable and how it would actually be taken forward.

The motion also calls on the Government to rule out junction closures. I understand why this issue has generated debate, but I'd like to correct some of the commentary surrounding it, much of it coming from the opposition benches, including from Natasha's contribution earlier. The report published alongside my statement does not recommend the closure of the three junctions. It identifies options for further investigation, including the closure of junction 27 at High Cross and restrictions to east-facing slips at junctions 25 and 26. Those are not Government decisions, they are options for investigation. The purpose of the work now under way is to determine whether any form of junction restriction could contribute to a wider solution and, if so, under what circumstances. That means understanding the impacts on communities, businesses, local roads and road users, alongside any potential benefits for motorway performance and resilience.

This is a question we've been asked a lot in this, about the evidence. One of the things that the report has done—. We've shared that report in full sight of everyone, including the public. We will maintain that level of transparency throughout this process and share it as we go. It means engagement with local authorities, businesses, communities and other stakeholders. And it means following the evidence. If the evidence shows an option will not deliver the outcomes required, it will not be taken forward. In short, we have not announced a programme of junction closures. What we have announced is further technical work to assess whether junction restrictions should form part of a wider solution to improve the operation and resilience of the M4 around Newport.

These are practical actions that can deliver benefits now while the longer term engineering solution is developed. Success will not come—

I'm not taking interventions, sorry, Stephen. 

Success will not come from a single measure in isolation. That is the balanced approach we have set out.

We are looking to reduce peak traffic on the M4 around Newport by around 10 per cent. That would be an order of magnitude greater than anything Labour ever attempted in 27 years. That represents a clear ambition to make measurable progress whilst longer term solutions are developed. 

As the work progresses, people and businesses must have a genuine opportunity to contribute. The decisions we will take will affect communities across the region. People rightly expect to be informed, consulted and listened to, and I have made a commitment to do it. [Interruption.] I'm coming towards the end. 

Llywydd, the people and businesses who rely on the M4 have waited long enough for progress. We have made a clear decision that road and engineering interventions must form part of the long-term solution. This is a serious and credible approach, focused on delivery, rather than opportunism and slogans. Others may want to play politics here—[Laughter.]

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Llywydd. One way to start is to have a bit of a laugh after that one, about not playing politics. I'd just like to thank everybody for their contributions to this debate today. Since being elected in 2016, I've always said that inaction is not an option, but the people of Newport and the surrounding area must not pay the price of costly options that this Government's report says won't solve the problem on the M4 around Newport.

What has been missing as well, for many Members who perhaps don't realise, is that this report was actually commissioned by the previous Labour Government and the Labour transport Minister at the time. So, what we're discussing, which the report is based on, is actually something that has come out from the previous Government. 

I realise that many Members might not have realised my contributions in the past Senedds, and that I did not vote to scrap the M4 relief road. I think that many Members here perhaps don't realise that. I spoke up at every opportunity throughout that time when it was being discussed, so just to be aware of that.

You might think that junction closures are quick fixes, but they will make next to no difference to congestion on the M4 and certainly cause havoc on local roads. And we've heard that from many Members across the Chamber today. 

Lyn Ackerman spoke earlier, and I think, from your contribution, Lyn, we weren't clear, and perhaps we could assume that you are not against the proposed junction closures. And also, to other Plaid Members as well, if you remember the time of a junction closure which was junction 41 around Swansea, that was temporarily closed by a Labour Government, but it was campaigned on by Plaid Cymru Members to reopen that junction at the time. And I would be interested to know—at the time, the Labour Government listened to Plaid Cymru Members—if the Plaid Cymru Government will listen to other Members in this Chamber, so I look forward to seeing that. 

Natasha, I absolutely do agree with your points on the junction closures. I went to visit a group of pensioners a couple of weeks ago, and the only thing they wanted to talk to me about was proposed junction closures, whether temporary or permanent. They were very, very concerned about that.

The other thing that has been missing from a number of people's contributions is a collective memory loss, that, actually, Plaid Cymru also voted to reject the M4 relief road at the time, and it was a Plaid Cymru Minister in 2009 who rejected the M4 relief road that put us back, and Plaid Cymru voted with the Labour Party, so not myself, to stop the M4 relief road last time.

Paul Rock, I should say, 'pen-blwydd hapus', first of all. I think we'd all like to say that to you, Paul, on your birthday. I have said that the black route is not an option, but I do think—and I would encourage you to look at the Arup report—when you talk about the freight that would go off, the Arup report also highlights that would only take up to 1 per cent of traffic off the road. So, just be aware of that, because there are a number of these issues that I think people haven't looked into, into that depth yet. But it would only take 1 per cent of traffic off the M4 around Newport.

Public transport absolutely does have a role to play, and Welsh Labour championed the Burns stations, and we now need to see that similar level of commitment to these stations from Plaid Cymru. The evidence is, though, clear that public transport interventions have to be delivered alongside a revised relief road, and that's the only option that provides resilience and reduces congestion.

We've heard some warm words from the Welsh Government today and I am hopeful of engagement with local people. I know the Deputy Minister has said again today about the importance of that, something I very strongly place an importance on. I feel, too many times over the years, the people of Newport's voice has not been heard to the extent that it should have been heard—[Interruption.] Pardon? Of all parties, as I said, of all parties. I have championed my constituents over that time, and I've spoken up, and I feel that these—. I would hope that the Government would also take that engagement with local people seriously. Unfortunately, we haven't seen that at the moment. Some decisions and options have been presented to local people, and they feel that they haven't had their say in all of this so far. So, I look forward to understanding, as does Natasha, how you will engage with local people throughout this time, because their voice absolutely needs to be heard.

This is why we in Welsh Labour believe that local people do need to shape this answer to the decades-old problem at the M4 around Newport, and we know that it shouldn't be an experiment that I feel like we're seeing today. The Welsh Government should begin work immediately on what an appropriate relief road could look like to meet the needs of a growing city. And that has changed: Newport is, as I said, the fastest growing city, it's a young city, so we have to be aware of that.

Mike Hedges talked about that this is not just a particular—. This, obviously, is an issue we're talking about today, but we do know there are other resilience issues around the road network in Wales. Mike mentioned the M4 around Swansea.

Ken talked about building roads better and investment in growth. I think an appropriate relief road would have the innovation to drive down and embed carbon and promote alternatives to private transport, and it should act as a template for responsible road building that others can follow. I think it's something that we can do to lead the world here.

Art mentioned—[Interruption.] I'd like to go to Art, sorry, James; I'm out of time otherwise. But I would like to mention Art, who contributed as well, who mentioned the homes that have been built, and mentioned the points in the report, and that the Government is at the moment planning to fail. But different funding options should be explored, as we have said. We need to listen to the local leaders who work with local communities to solve this problem. Give it to leaders who innovate and inspire an effective solution. So, let's put people above politics and vote for this motion today. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. It's good to see the Chamber so full for a short debate. I had no idea I was so popular. I'd like to give a minute's time in this debate to Joe Martin, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, Francesca O'Brien, Carrie Harper, Steven Rodaway and Kiera Marshall.

Llywydd, our town centres were once the bright and beating heart of our communities, where businesses thrived and families felt safe. But years of economic decline and political failure have let our town centres, sadly, rot. As a result, a new dangerous culture has emerged. From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe. For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable. And while Governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says, 'Enough is enough'.

contributions.text_english:
Face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society. Let's take a look at the city of Newport, the city that holds the unenviable title of the worst high street in Britain. Disaffected young people have run through businesses, causing a decimated high street and rundown shopfronts, leading to a loss of inward investment and hope for the future deserted, thanks, in part, to balaclava-covered youths running riot over those that are just trying to make a living—people who've worked hard, paid their taxes, and contributed to their communities. But this is not just about one Welsh city; this is a Wales-wide issue.

Plaid will say this is a pointless debate because it's a non-devolved matter reserved to Westminster. But that doesn't mean UK councils are powerless. Look at what Nottingham has achieved as an example. They introduced a targeted restriction against face coverings, and they've seen a 40 per cent reduction in city-centre anti-social behaviour. Newport City Council has voted to explore similar options, and I, alongside every Reform MS, will be encouraging all Welsh councils to do the same.

Adam Price disappointed me today with his response to spokespersons' questions. Imagine being a victim of crime, of violent theft or some kind of violent robbery, only to listen to Plaid's economy minister today saying balaclava bans are a gimmick, that businesses don't care. But the reality is that Plaid doesn't care. Plaid cares more about promoting foreign cultures than our own. They clearly don't care about keeping Welsh people and businesses safe.

When a Welsh person supports Reform, Plaid often accuses them of questioning their loyalty to Wales. But when foreign people who can't speak any British language enter Wales for a life on the welfare system, they are celebrated as trophies of the benefits of mass migration. They don't care about how a lack of integration by face-clad unknown people impacts Wales, our working-class communities. All they care about is supporting mass migration in all its forms, no matter the cost to our communities. We see this today. They defend balaclavas, all because they want some in our society to be able to hide their faces. Some will lazily say we're being Islamophobic, whatever that means. Some, no doubt, will roll out the old classic and shriek, 'Racists!' These tropes are tired, ineffective, and clearly wildly inaccurate, but I will address them.

Reform supports freedom of religion in all its forms. But where that freedom oppresses women and damages assimilation into Welsh communities, a line must be drawn. In Afghanistan, under Taliban rule, women are under a system of gender apartheid. They can't study above the age of 12, they can't speak loudly in public, and they're forced, by law, to wear the burqa. If they don't, they could be denied healthcare, they could be beaten, or even worse. For these women, raised under an extremist form of Islam, the burqa is a symbol of oppression. This symbol is what Plaid Members are attempting to back today: an extreme ideology that is anti British, anti women and against assimilation, forced on young girls and carried on into adulthood.

In numerous countries, the burqa is already banned. But we cannot allow this form of oppression to become the norm in Wales. Walk through any areas across Wales, and you will see it for yourself. The Muslim Council of Wales has tried to silence this debate today, saying we are hateful and divisive. So, I say again, and let me be very clear: Reform has no issue with the hijab, we have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims, but we do have an issue with people living in our communities hiding their identities. We say the same thing to protesters that cover their faces, whatever their political persuasion. In modern Britain, we are polite people. We say 'hello' to our neighbours, and we do not hide our faces. That is our culture, that is our way, regardless of race, creed or religion. Reform wants safer streets and strong communities for our families to live, work and thrive. Diolch.

Diolch, Lywydd. I think we're all entitled to question Reform's real intentions when they raise a debate on face coverings, especially given, just in the last fortnight, a very similar debate was raised in the Scottish Parliament as well, which explicitly called for banning the burqa and the niqab, and we've heard the same statements here today. So, let's not pretend that this is about criminality and balaclavas. That's nonsense, and we can all see through that. This is a thinly veiled attack on the religious rights of women. That's blatantly obvious to everybody.

I think it's really ironic as well that Reform have chosen to frame this debate about values in the same week that we've had an ITV investigation exposing deep-rooted racism and sexism in your party. One of the worst things that I heard from that programme was then Reform councillor Chris Whelan talking about a fellow Reform candidate. He said, 'If she were my daughter, it would still be bath night on a Thursday'. Vile, disgusting and disturbing in the way it sexualised a child. There were multiple examples of sexism and racism in that programme, from the party that claims to want to protect women.

So, seriously, how can Reform lecture us about values when they're in the midst of a scandal about racism and sexism? How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear? Complete hypocrisy—complete hypocrisy.

The burqa and niqab are two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with western civilisation. They represent ideas that are oppressive, misogynistic and anti-British. Mass immigration was sold to the public with the assertion that those arriving would assimilate into British culture. That was a lie—we can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burqas, how are we meant to tell them apart? I can't believe this needs to be said, but being able to tell people apart is an important part of British culture.

Proponents will argue that they promote modesty and stop women from being sexualised. For thousands of years, the west achieved the same result—not by oppressing women, but by requiring men to employ an ounce of self-control. If the people who've moved here can't do that, they should live in countries where it's accepted that men can't control themselves. I've also seen children wearing face coverings; anyone who struggles not to feel lust when looking at a child should not be free to walk around in our society. There are countries where that might be normal. This is not one of them. Assimilation means losing religious face coverings, and to encourage that, they should be banned.

contributions.text_english:
We are being asked to debate about people on the basis of what we imagine their lives to be. Their lives are not fictional, they are real, and what we debate here deeply matters to them, and affects their perception of their home here in Wales. I want to focus my remarks on a territory I'm sure is familiar to Reform of civil liberties. Members opposite speak a great deal about this, but instead of advocating for freedom, they have brought us a list of things a woman may not do, and are asking the state to enforce it.

I want to add a bit of philosophy to help frame my remarks. I choose it deliberately because I feel it has some resemblance to this debate today. Burke's argument against revolutionaries was that a nation cannot be remade by decree, and this goes back as far as 1700. A society is not an arrangement between people who happen to be alive. It is a partnership between the living, the dead and those that are yet to be born. That is the essence of the social contract.

The liberties we hold in these countries were not granted to us by anyone in this room. They were fought for, often at huge cost. Lives were lost, people were imprisoned, and often people were hanged for them. We did not earn any of that, we inherited it, and it is our role as stewards of these liberties to protect them for future generations. We are not entitled to erode that liberty just because Reform finds it politically expedient.

contributions.text_english:
I am proud to be Welsh, proud to be British, and unapologetic in defending our culture. In Britain we show our faces. It builds trust and, more importantly, it keeps us safe. In certain Islamic countries, under Islamic law, girls from puberty must cover their faces, and some countries will arrest females above the age of nine for showing too much hair. Whether balaclava or burqa, face coverings have no place on our streets here in Wales. It is oppressive, and it is a risk to Welsh public safety. We have written to the First Minister urging him to make a much-needed representation to the UK Government.

This summer, the Prime Minister and the First Minister managed to meet together to ban the barbecue. While those on the left want us to ban the barbecue, we in Reform want to ban the burqa, or the balaclava. Face coverings are incompatible with our British way of life. It is an outright betrayal of the dignity and freedom of women.

Beyond this, we must look at banning cousin marriages and address religious attitudes towards women and homosexuals. Women's freedom and their safety here in Wales deserve urgency, which is why we must, at the very first possible opportunity, ban face coverings in public, and I urge every Member across this house to support this motion. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
This summer, a Muslim woman in my constituency in Cardiff was subject to a physical violent attack in broad daylight. The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf, and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her. And this is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence where Muslim women are being targeted. This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing.

Reform claims to protect women and girls, but they don't really, do they? Because only over the weekend did we hear about one of Reform's own MPs say that Reform is chauvinistic and has a male issue. And today, they're trying to control what women wear, and it's quite frankly disgusting and creepy that they're trying to do this. Meanwhile in Wales, 31 per cent of our children live in poverty, the unemployment rate has consistently remained above the UK average, and in this context, it's bizarre that they've chosen to focus their taxpayer-funded time on a debate like this today.

To all the Muslim women—to all the Muslim women—who might be watching today, who might be feeling afraid and let down by this debate, Reform may claim that this attack on your faith is in line with British values, but it is not in line with Welsh values. Plaid Cymru stands with you, we will stand up for you, and we will always call out this hate where we see it.

Gosh, I don't know how to follow some of this. Thank you, Presiding Officer, and thank you, Jason O'Connell, for tabling the debate. We're a nation that prides itself on our tradition of constitutional liberty, which has always included freedom of expression to dress as one chooses, including garments that most people find offensive or objectionable, such as face coverings. This stands in opposition to the tradition on the continent where restrictions are commonplace. However, I think we need to re-examine our position on this, as the wearing of face coverings has become normalised in recent years, and consider banning them.

In Swansea, Neath and many other areas of Wales, there has been a growing problem with anti-social behaviour committed by youths wearing face coverings. No-one should have to tolerate this sort of hooliganism. We should recognise too that face coverings are not normal practice in any religion, and they're only employed by a tiny minority of ultra-conservative adherents. Whilst religious freedom is an important tenet of British values, our laws and cultural norms should not bend to the whims of an ultra-conservative minority. We should recognise too that many countries across Europe, the middle east and central Asia ban the use of face coverings and do not make religious exceptions. So, I agree with Jason that the use of face coverings is a growing issue and we must look to banning them.

Absolutely, and properly represent their communities and the voice of their communities. Absolutely. That dog whistle varies in volume, it's always there, but it's getting louder. It lingers over those benches, a deliberately intangible thing that leaves too many wondering whether a line has been crossed. Llywydd, I am not afraid to speak up and say that, since May, that line has too often been crossed. It hides itself in plain sight: hateful speech dressed up as free speech over concerns—[Interruption.] No, we've heard enough from those benches, thank you very much. It lurks beneath what is disingenuously tonight presented as the language of common sense and—I'm not taking interventions—in today's case, British values. [Interruption.] Llywydd, can I carry on?

I want the Members who have spoken in support of this debate to know that not only do we hear you but we see you. We see you for what you are. We see you weaponising discontent, driving division and stirring hate. We see you in this debate conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs—those whose protests can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims—with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour.

Llywydd, let me say clearly that I do not accept the premise that face coverings are in themselves contrary to our values. Such a catch-all position ignores the many legitimate reasons why face coverings are worn. People's rights to do so can, of course, be subject already to lawful and proportionate restrictions when necessary, including to prevent crime and disorder. But the justification comes from the situation and the behaviour, not from a judgment that covering one's face in itself is unacceptable and dangerous.

contributions.text_english: We've heard a lot of nonsense tonight. What I haven't heard is any condemnation of the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across the south coast last month. Would you join me, Minister, in condemning those protesters and agree with me that a fine representation of British values is the decency and courage shown by the lifeboat crews out in the English channel saving lives, regardless of creed or skin or race or religion?

contributions.text_english:
Absolutely. And the people of Neath showed—. We had a food fair recently where they were there out in the street. They had never had so much support and so many donations after those. The people of Neath came out and they spoke in support of the fine men and women of the RNLI.

One of the reasons for wearing a face covering is, of course, an important one that I am determined to use my voice to defend: religious expression. The values of our nation are centred not on exclusion but on respect, and we as representatives of our communities should respect people of every religion within them and we should never suggest that they are in any way less or inferior because they exercise their human right to freedom of religion. People of every religion or belief should feel that they belong in Wales. I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values. Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less because their religious practice differs from that of others.

Framing religious dress as contrary to British values without demonstrating any harm that justifies interference with fundamental rights risks deepening division rather than strengthening cohesion. But this is clearly Reform UK's aim here. The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg laws that stated they were no longer German, laws that led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of their German-ness, enabled by those who believed German-ness could not accommodate diversity. Who is the arbiter of Britishness or Welshness? Who decides that a woman who wears a face covering is less British or less Welsh? We have a moral duty and responsibility in this place to be careful about the language we use and the message we send and not to engage or encourage discrimination on the basis of race, religion or belief.

Thank you. It was a statement of fact about what happened in Germany in the 1930s. The face coverings debate, when it is spoken about by Reform UK, is always referencing connection with religious dress. On 6 October, the deputy leader set out their position in this Chamber: they would ban the burqa and every full-face covering in public. The debate put forward on this subject in the Scottish Parliament also specifically references the burqa and niqab as the only face coverings mentioned. This dog-whistle politics, while almost always a disturbing undercurrent where Reform UK is concerned, pierces the surface of this debate and other debates more and more often.

But then there are occasions where the racism, sexism and misogyny of Reform UK is plain to see. ITV's exposure Undercover: A Year in Reform, broadcast just a few days ago, recorded Reform UK members and representatives describing Asian families as parasites. A Reform candidate in Wales who was employed by the Member that brought this debate to the Chamber was recorded using abhorrent racist terms. Unsurprisingly, it also exposed the misogyny and sexism within the party—so much for a party who so often claims to want to protect women and girls. And we, as women of all races and religions, stand as one against this behaviour, this language and the so-called values of your party.

Roedd ffigurau'r Swyddfa Gartref a gyhoeddwyd yr wythnos diwethaf yn dangos cynnydd o 13 y cant mewn troseddau casineb crefyddol a gofnodwyd gan yr heddlu yn ystod y flwyddyn hyd at Fawrth eleni. Gyda chyfanswm o 11,419 o droseddau wedi eu cofnodi, o'r rheini roedd cynnydd o 15 y cant mewn troseddau casineb sy'n targedu Mwslimiaid. Rhannodd ymatebwyr brofiadau o gael eu hymosod yn gorfforol, eu bygwth, cael pobl yn poeri arnynt a gweld eu gwisg crefyddol yn cael ei gwawdio a'i thargedu.

contributions.text_english: These crimes aren't just happening in faraway towns and cities, as we heard from Kiera Marshall, they're happening in our communities. When I visited a mosque in September, members of the Muslim community told me about the profound impact that Islamaphobia is having on them and how that attack, in which a Welsh Muslim woman had had her hijab torn from her head, was affecting their sense of safety and belonging.

contributions.text_english: Diolch yn fawr. I'll be very brief. Would you not agree with this: that actually Reform UK's recent debates, including this one, are designed to divide and are designed to bring fear—[Interruption.]—to bring fear to our communities? And on this day, where you started, we should be in unity together. Would you not agree that this is shameful by Reform UK?

And on this day, where you started, we should be in unity together. Would you not agree that this is shameful by Reform UK?

contributions.text_english:
I absolutely agree that it's shameful. And what's also shameful is the claim that Muslim women are somehow voiceless and forced to dress against their will. That's as sexist as it is Islamaphobic. These experiences and the stubbornly high rates of hate crime don't happen by accident, they happen by design. They do so by deliberately pitting communities against each other for political gain, which is as shameful as it is hateful.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt, herself deemed 'un-German' and forced to flee her native land, warned that the death of human empathy is one of the earliest and most telling signs of a culture on the verge of descending into barbarism. What can stop that descent is the power and protection of universal human rights. So, if we are to talk about British values, let us talk first and foremost about those rights, those freedoms that are enshrined in British laws: the freedom of religion—everyone in Wales is protected by the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998—a freedom that Reform appear to have a problem with. Because the pattern is always the same: they claim to be champions of freedom—[Interruption.]—no, I won't—but only when it fits their narrow and singular definition, a dangerous, exclusionary definition. We must never be bystanders to bigotry and hatred.

And, Llywydd, this Government will always celebrate the plurality of our communities. We will always challenge those who claim that our differences divide us. Our values are demonstrated by how we treat one another. In her report on the war crimes trial of the Nazi Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt suggested that his evil stemmed from an inability to think from the standpoint of someone else. That lack of empathy, that ability to see others as less, is what we must constantly guard against in this society. And that empathy must be expressed by those with power and influence through the language they use.

So, finally, Llywydd, at a time when racism and Islamaphobia, fuelled by deliberate political discourse, are becoming increasingly normalised, we should remind ourselves that we, as elected Members in this Chamber, hold a position of privilege and of power. Our words matter and we can't afford to stay silent. [Applause.]

tabled_texts.text_english:
Motion NDM9335 Lynne Neagle

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Believes that the Welsh Government’s proposals for the relief of congestion on the M4 around Newport are inadequate.

2. Calls on the Welsh Government to:

a) rule out junction closures; and

b) begin work on an appropriate relief road for the M4.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Cynnig NDM9335 Lynne Neagle

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn credu bod cynigion Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer lliniaru tagfeydd ar yr M4 o amgylch Casnewydd yn annigonol.

2. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i:

a) diystyru cau cyffyrdd; a

b) dechrau ar y gwaith o adeiladu ffordd liniaru briodol ar gyfer yr M4.

tabled_texts.text_english:
Amendment 1—Heledd Fychan

Delete all and replace with:

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Regrets previous Welsh Governments’ failure to tackle the long-standing issue of congestion and poor resilience on the M4 around Newport, which continues to affect communities, businesses and economic activity across south-east Wales.

2. Notes that the decision to scrap the M4 relief road was taken by a previous Welsh Government, and that the proposed route is therefore no longer viable.

3. Welcomes the Welsh Government’s decision that road and engineering improvements must form part of the long-term response to congestion on the M4 around Newport and its commitment to identify a preferred, deliverable solution.

4. Notes the programme of immediate and medium-term measures announced by the Welsh Government, including investment in the existing motorway, improvements to network resilience, support for rail and bus connectivity, and measures to improve freight movement.

5. Supports the Welsh Government’s approach of taking action now to improve reliability and connectivity while developing the long-term solution.

6. Welcomes the Welsh Government’s commitment to sustained engagement with people, businesses and communities in and around Newport as solutions are developed and implemented.
tabled_texts.text_original:
Gwelliant 1—Heledd Fychan

Dileu popeth a rhoi yn ei le:

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn gresynu at fethiant Llywodraeth flaenorol Cymru i fynd i’r afael â phroblem hirdymor tagfeydd a gwydnwch gwael ar yr M4 o amgylch Casnewydd, sy’n parhau i effeithio ar gymunedau, busnesau a gweithgarwch economaidd ar draws de-ddwyrain Cymru.

2. Yn nodi mai penderfyniad Llywodraeth flaenorol Cymru oedd gwaredu cynllun ffordd liniaru’r M4, ac felly nid yw’r llwybr arfaethedig bellach yn hyfyw.

3. Yn croesawu penderfyniad Llywodraeth Cymru fod yn rhaid i welliannau i ffyrdd a pheirianneg fod yn rhan o’r ymateb hirdymor i dagfeydd ar yr M4 o amgylch Casnewydd a’i hymrwymiad i bennu datrysiad ymarferol a ffefrir.

4. Yn nodi’r rhaglen o fesurau i’w cyflwyno ar unwaith ac yn y tymor canolig a gyhoeddwyd gan Lywodraeth Cymru, gan gynnwys buddsoddi yn y draffordd bresennol, gwelliannau i wydnwch y rhwydwaith, cymorth ar gyfer cysylltedd trenau a bysiau a mesurau i hwyluso cludo nwyddau.

5. Yn cefnogi dull Llywodraeth Cymru o weithredu yn awr i wella dibynadwyedd a chysylltedd tra bo datrysiad hirdymor yn cael ei ddatblygu.

6. Yn croesawu ymrwymiad Llywodraeth Cymru i barhau i ymgysylltu â phobl, busnesau a chymunedau yng Nghasnewydd a’r cyffiniau wrth i ddatrysiadau gael eu datblygu a’u gweithredu.
Gohiriwyd y pleidleisio tan y cyfnod pleidleisio.
Daeth y cyfarfod i ben am 19:19.
